abstract: We propose a new neural network model and its learning algorithm. The proposed neural network consists of four layers - input, hidden, output and final output layers. The hidden and output layers are multiple. Using the proposed SICL(Spread Pattern Information and Cooperative Learning) algorithm, it is possible to learn analog data accurately and to obtain smooth outputs. Using this neural network, we have developed a speech production system consisting of a phonemic symbol production subsystem and a speech parameter production subsystem. We have succeeded in producing natural speech waves with high accuracy.

The hidden and output layers are multiple. paragraphs: This paper introduces a neural network and learning algorithm for producing accurate, smoothly varying outputs from analog data. The architecture has input, hidden, output, and final-output stages, with multiple hidden and output layers. The learning procedure is called SICL, short for Spread Pattern Information and Cooperative Learning.

The stated purpose of SICL is to combine accurate learning of analog values with smooth output behavior. These are complementary requirements for the proposed speech-production application: the system must generate the desired values while also producing outputs that vary smoothly. The network architecture and cooperative learning mechanism are presented together as the means of achieving this.

The authors build a speech-production system with two subsystems, one producing phonemic symbols and the other producing speech parameters. They report successfully generating natural speech waveforms with high accuracy. The contribution therefore spans a proposed learning mechanism and its use in a complete speech-production arrangement, connecting the network’s analog-output properties to the resulting speech signals.
summary.tldr: A cooperative-learning network produces smooth analog outputs and is used in a system reported to generate accurate, natural speech waveforms.

title: Speech Production Using A Neural Network with a Cooperative Learning Mechanism

abstract: We describe an electronic photoreceptor circuit that is sensitive to small changes in incident light intensity. The sensitivity to change8 in the intensity is achieved by feeding back to the input a filtered version of the output. The feedback loop includes a hysteretic el(cid:173) ement. The circuit behaves in a manner reminiscent of the gain control properties and temporal responses of a variety of retinal cells, particularly retinal bipolar cells. We compare the thresholds for detection of intensity increments by a human and by the cir(cid:173) cuit. Both obey Weber's law and for both the temporal contrast sensitivities are nearly identical. We previously described an electronic photoreceptor that outputs a voltage that is logarithmic in the light intensity (Mead, 1985). This report describes an extension of this circuit which was based on a suggestion by Frank Werblin that biological retinas may achieve greater sensitivity to change8 in the illumination by feeding back a filtered version of the output. OPERATION OF THE CIRCUIT The circuit (Figure 1) consists of a phototransistor (P), exponential feedback to P (Ql, Q2, and Q3), a transconductance amplifier (A), and the hysteretic element (Q4 and Qs). In general terms the operation of the circuit consists of two stages of amplification with hysteresis in the feedback loop. The light falls on the parasitic bipolar transistor P. (The rest of the circuit is shielded by metal.) P's collector is the substrate and the base is an isolated well. P and Ql form the first stage of amplification. The light produces a base current Is for P. The emitter current IE is PIs, neglecting collector resistance for now. P is typically a few hundred. The feedback current IQl is set by the gate voltage on QdQ2' which is set by the current through Q3, which is set by the feedback voltage Vjb. In equilibrium Vjb will be such that IQl = IE and some voltage Vp will be the output of the first stage. The DC output of the circuit will be Vout ~ V/b = Vdd - (2kT /q) log IE, neglecting the back-gate effect for Q2. paragraphs: The paper describes an electronic light receptor designed to detect small changes in illumination. It extends an earlier circuit whose output voltage varies logarithmically with light intensity. The key addition sends a filtered version of the output back to the input, making feedback central to the circuit's sensitivity to changes.

The feedback loop includes a hysteretic element, whose behavior depends on its prior state. Together with two amplification stages, this produces responses resembling the gain control and timing behavior of retinal cells, particularly bipolar cells. The circuit therefore provides a physical implementation of a proposed sensory principle: feedback can help a receptor respond to changes around its illumination level.

The authors compare intensity-increment detection thresholds in the circuit and a human observer. Both follow Weber's law, meaning that detectable increments scale with the background intensity, and their temporal contrast sensitivities are nearly identical. The supplied circuit analysis also reports logarithmic operation under a subthreshold assumption valid across about four orders of magnitude, connecting the observed behavior to the electronics.
summary.tldr: Filtered feedback makes an electronic photoreceptor sensitive to small light changes, with detection behavior closely resembling human vision.

title: An Electronic Photoreceptor Sensitive to Small Changes in Intensity

abstract: In the electrosensory system of weakly electric fish, descending pathways to a first-order sensory nucleus have been shown to influ(cid:173) ence the gain of its output neurons. The underlying neural mecha(cid:173) nisms that subserve this descending gain control capability are not yet fully understood. We suggest that one possible gain control mechanism could involve the regulation of total membrane conduc(cid:173) tance of the output neurons. In this paper, a neural model based on this idea is used to demonstrate how activity levels on descend(cid:173) ing pathways could control both the gain and baseline excitation of a target neuron .

The underlying neural mecha(cid:173) nisms that subserve this descending gain control capability are not yet fully understood. We suggest that one possible gain control mechanism could involve the regulation of total membrane conduc(cid:173) tance of the output neurons. In this paper, a neural model based on this idea is used to demonstrate how activity levels on descend(cid:173) ing pathways could control both the gain and baseline excitation of a target neuron .

paragraphs: This paper investigates how descending neural signals could adjust sensory responses in weakly electric fish. Biological observations show that these pathways influence the gain of output neurons in an early sensory nucleus. Gain describes how strongly a neuron's response changes with its input, so controlling it changes the sensitivity of sensory processing.

The authors propose that this control could operate by regulating the output neurons' total membrane conductance. They build a neural model around that possibility and examine how activity in the descending pathways affects a target neuron. The proposed mechanism links signals arriving from those pathways to a physical property of the neuron's membrane.

The model demonstrates control over both response gain and baseline excitation. These are distinct effects: changing sensitivity affects the response to input, while changing baseline excitation shifts the neuron's underlying level of activation. The result establishes a possible mechanism for the observed descending influence. The authors present it as a candidate explanation because the biological mechanisms responsible are not yet fully understood.
summary.tldr: A neural model shows how regulating membrane conductance could let descending signals control sensory gain and baseline excitation.

title: A Neural Model of Descending Gain Control in the Electrosensory System

abstract: We show how an "Elman" network architecture, constructed from recurrently connected oscillatory associative memory network mod(cid:173) ules, can employ selective "attentional" control of synchronization to direct the flow of communication and computation within the architecture to solve a grammatical inference problem. Previously we have shown how the discrete time "Elman" network algorithm can be implemented in a network completely described by continuous ordinary differential equations. The time steps (ma(cid:173) chine cycles) of the system are implemented by rhythmic variation (clocking) of a bifurcation parameter. In this architecture, oscilla(cid:173) tion amplitude codes the information content or activity of a mod(cid:173) ule (unit), whereas phase and frequency are used to "softwire" the network. Only synchronized modules communicate by exchang(cid:173) ing amplitude information; the activity of non-resonating modules contributes incoherent crosstalk noise. Attentional control is modeled as a special subset of the hidden modules with ouputs which affect the resonant frequencies of other hidden modules. They control synchrony among the other mod(cid:173) ules and direct the flow of computation (attention) to effect transi(cid:173) tions between two subgraphs of a thirteen state automaton which the system emulates to generate a Reber grammar. The internal crosstalk noise is used to drive the required random transitions of the automaton.

paragraphs: The paper shows how an Elman-style recurrent architecture can control computation through synchronization among oscillating modules. The system is described by continuous ordinary differential equations. Rhythmic variation of a bifurcation parameter supplies its computational cycles, connecting continuous dynamics with the stepwise operation of the Elman algorithm.

Different aspects of an oscillation serve different purposes. Amplitude carries a module's activity or information, while phase and frequency determine communication. Synchronized modules exchange amplitude information; modules that are out of resonance contribute incoherent crosstalk. A special group of hidden modules changes the resonant frequencies of other hidden modules, selectively controlling which parts of the network communicate.

The authors use this mechanism to direct transitions between two subgraphs of a thirteen-state automaton that generates a Reber grammar. Internal crosstalk noise supplies the automaton's required random transitions. The demonstration gives attentional control a concrete dynamical meaning: changing synchrony redirects computation within the architecture. It also assigns useful roles to both coordinated oscillations and the noise produced by uncoordinated activity.
summary.tldr: An oscillating Elman network uses selective synchronization to route information and emulate a grammar-generating automaton.

title: Grammatical Inference by Attentional Control of Synchronization in an Oscillating Elman Network

abstract: We introduce a recurrent architecture having a modular structure and we formulate a training procedure based on the EM algorithm. The resulting model has similarities to hidden Markov models, but supports recurrent networks processing style and allows to exploit the supervised learning paradigm while using maximum likelihood estimation.
originalAbstract: We introduce a recurrent architecture having a modular structure and we formulate a training procedure based on the EM algorithm. The resulting model has similarities to hidden Markov models, but supports recurrent networks processing style and allows to exploit the supervised learning paradigm while using maximum likelihood estimation.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a modular recurrent architecture for learning relationships between inputs and outputs. Recurrence means that processing can depend on an evolving internal state, giving the model a way to handle information across a sequence. Its modular organization brings this style of processing together with a model resembling a hidden Markov model.

The authors also formulate a training procedure based on expectation maximization, or EM. This connects the architecture to maximum likelihood estimation: learning seeks parameters that make the observed training outputs more probable. Hidden-state structure and supervised learning therefore fit within the same framework, with supplied input-output examples guiding the statistical estimation process.

The main contribution is this architectural and training combination. It allows the model to retain a recurrent-network style of computation while using a probabilistic learning objective associated with hidden Markov models. For sequence modeling, that combination matters because the representation of temporal state and the use of supervised targets can be designed together, rather than treated as separate modeling choices.
summary.tldr: A modular recurrent architecture combines hidden-Markov-model structure with supervised maximum likelihood learning through EM.

title: An Input Output HMM Architecture

abstract: This paper presents a new method for image compression by neural networks. First, we show that we can use neural networks in a py(cid:173) ramidal framework, yielding the so-called PCA pyramids. Then we present an image compression method based on the PCA pyramid, which is similar to the Laplace pyramid and wavelet transform. Some experimental results with real images are reported. Finally, we present a method to combine the quantization step with the learning of the PCA pyramid.
originalAbstract: This paper presents a new method for image compression by neural networks. First, we show that we can use neural networks in a py(cid:173) ramidal framework, yielding the so-called PCA pyramids. Then we present an image compression method based on the PCA pyramid, which is similar to the Laplace pyramid and wavelet transform. Some experimental results with real images are reported. Finally, we present a method to combine the quantization step with the learning of the PCA pyramid.

paragraphs: The paper introduces an image compression method built around a neural network structure called a PCA pyramid. Its first step is to show how neural networks can operate within a pyramidal framework. This makes a hierarchy of representations the organizing structure for the compression method, connecting neural learning with pyramid-based image processing.

The resulting compression approach is described as similar to the Laplace pyramid and wavelet transform. Those comparisons locate its contribution in a family of structured image representations, with the PCA pyramid supplying the learned component. The authors report experiments on real images, applying the representation to the image compression task that motivates the work.

The paper also presents a way to combine quantization with learning the pyramid. Quantization concerns the discrete values used to encode a representation, so incorporating it into learning connects representation formation with the encoding stage. The overall contribution brings together the neural pyramid, its use for compression, and a method for learning it alongside quantization.
summary.tldr: PCA pyramids combine neural network image representations with a compression method that can learn alongside quantization.

title: PCA-Pyramids for Image Compression

abstract: In this paper, we propose a memory-based Q-Iearning algorithm called predictive Q-routing (PQ-routing) for adaptive traffic con(cid:173) trol. We attempt to address two problems encountered in Q-routing (Boyan & Littman, 1994), namely, the inability to fine-tune rout(cid:173) ing policies under low network load and the inability to learn new optimal policies under decreasing load conditions. Unlike other memory-based reinforcement learning algorithms in which mem(cid:173) ory is used to keep past experiences to increase learning speed, PQ-routing keeps the best experiences learned and reuses them by predicting the traffic trend. The effectiveness of PQ-routing has been verified under various network topologies and traffic con(cid:173) ditions. Simulation results show that PQ-routing is superior to Q-routing in terms of both learning speed and adaptability.

paragraphs: This paper proposes predictive Q-routing, a memory-based reinforcement learning method for adapting network traffic routes. It targets two weaknesses of Q-routing: difficulty refining routing policies when network load is low, and difficulty learning new optimal policies as load decreases. Both concern adjustment when traffic conditions become less demanding.

The method retains the best experiences it has learned and reuses them according to a prediction of the traffic trend. Memory therefore serves a selective, forward-looking role. The approach connects previously successful experience with an estimate of how conditions are changing, so that past learning can inform routing decisions under a different load.

The authors evaluate predictive Q-routing in simulations spanning multiple network topologies and traffic conditions. They report improvements over Q-routing in both learning speed and adaptability. These findings support the proposed combination of selective memory and traffic-trend prediction. The contribution addresses how a routing learner can respond to changing conditions, especially the low-load and decreasing-load cases identified as problems for the earlier method.
summary.tldr: Predictive Q-routing reuses its best experiences according to traffic trends, improving simulated learning speed and adaptability over Q-routing.

title: Predictive Q-Routing: A Memory-based Reinforcement Learning Approach to Adaptive Traffic Control

abstract: Symmetrically connected recurrent networks have recently been used as models of a host of neural computations. However, be(cid:173) cause of the separation between excitation and inhibition, biolog(cid:173) ical neural networks are asymmetrical. We study characteristic differences between asymmetrical networks and their symmetri(cid:173) cal counterparts, showing that they have dramatically different dynamical behavior and also how the differences can be exploited for computational ends. We illustrate our results in the case of a network that is a selective amplifier.
originalAbstract: Symmetrically connected recurrent networks have recently been used as models of a host of neural computations. However, be(cid:173) cause of the separation between excitation and inhibition, biolog(cid:173) ical neural networks are asymmetrical. We study characteristic differences between asymmetrical networks and their symmetri(cid:173) cal counterparts, showing that they have dramatically different dynamical behavior and also how the differences can be exploited for computational ends. We illustrate our results in the case of a network that is a selective amplifier.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how connection symmetry affects computation in recurrent neural networks. Symmetrically connected networks have been used to model many neural computations, but the authors emphasize a biological motivation for asymmetry: excitation and inhibition are separated in biological networks. That distinction raises the question of how well symmetric models capture relevant dynamics.

The authors compare asymmetric networks with their symmetric counterparts and show that their dynamical behavior can differ dramatically. The issue is therefore more than a change in how connections are represented. Altering symmetry can change the activity produced by the network as it evolves, with consequences for the computations that activity can support.

They also show how these differences can be used computationally, illustrating the results with a selective-amplifier network. The example connects the dynamical comparison to a concrete computational role. The contribution is an argument, supported by the studied networks, that asymmetry deserves attention as a source of computational behavior when modeling recurrent neural systems.
summary.tldr: Connection asymmetry produces major changes in recurrent-network dynamics that can be used for computation.

title: Computational Differences between Asymmetrical and Symmetrical Networks

abstract: A recent neural model of illusory contour formation is based on a distribution of natural shapes traced by particles moving with constant speed in directions given by Brownian motions. The input to that model consists of pairs of position and direction constraints and the output consists of the distribution of contours joining all such pairs. In general, these contours will not be closed and their distribution will not be scale-invariant. In this paper, we show how to compute a scale-invariant distribution of closed contours given position constraints alone and use this result to explain a well known illusory contour effect.
originalAbstract: A recent neural model of illusory contour formation is based on a distribution of natural shapes traced by particles moving with constant speed in directions given by Brownian motions. The input to that model consists of pairs of position and direction constraints and the output consists of the distribution of contours joining all such pairs. In general, these contours will not be closed and their distribution will not be scale-invariant. In this paper, we show how to compute a scale-invariant distribution of closed contours given position constraints alone and use this result to explain a well known illusory contour effect.

paragraphs: This paper develops a probabilistic account of illusory contours, the boundaries perceived between supplied visual cues. It builds on a model in which candidate shapes are traced by particles moving at constant speed while their directions change according to Brownian motion. Such a construction describes a distribution of possible contours rather than selecting a single connecting curve.

The earlier model takes constraints specifying both position and direction, then produces contours joining pairs of constraints. Two shortcomings motivate the new work: those contours generally remain open, and their distribution depends on scale. This leaves closure and consistent treatment across sizes unresolved within that formulation.

The authors show how to compute a scale-invariant distribution of closed contours using position constraints alone. Closing the contours makes complete boundaries part of the construction, while removing explicit directional inputs reduces what must be specified beforehand. They use the resulting distribution to explain a known illusory-contour effect, linking the mathematical treatment of contour shape to a perceptual phenomenon.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic contour model derives closed, scale-invariant boundaries from position cues alone and explains an illusory-contour effect.

title: Orientation, Scale, and Discontinuity as Emergent Properties of Illusory Contour Shape

abstract: We develop a hierarchical generative model to study cue combination. The model maps a global shape parameter to local cuespecific parameters, which in tum generate an intensity image. Inferring shape from images is achieved by inverting this model. Inference produces a probability distribution at each level; using distributions rather than a single value of underlying variables at each stage preserves information about the validity of each local cue for the given image. This allows the model, unlike standard combination models, to adaptively weight each cue based on general cue reliability and specific image context. We describe the results of a cue combination psychophysics experiment we conducted that allows a direct comparison with the model. The model provides a good fit to our data and a natural account for some interesting aspects of cue combination.

The model maps a global shape parameter to local cuespecific parameters, which in tum generate an intensity image. Inferring shape from images is achieved by inverting this model. Inference produces a probability distribution at each level; using distributions rather than a single value of underlying variables at each stage preserves information about the validity of each local cue for the given image. paragraphs: The paper studies how information from different visual cues can be combined to infer shape. It builds a hierarchical generative model: a global shape parameter determines local parameters for individual cues, and those local parameters generate an intensity image. Shape inference works backward through this model from the observed image.

At every level, inference maintains a probability distribution rather than committing to a single estimate. This preserves information about how informative or valid each local cue is for the particular image. As a result, cue weighting can reflect both a cue's general reliability and the specific context in which it appears.

The authors conduct a psychophysics experiment designed to allow direct comparison with the model and report a good fit to the resulting data. The model also offers an account of interesting aspects of cue combination. The contribution is an explanation of adaptive cue weighting through retained uncertainty: cues can receive different weights because their usefulness depends on the image being interpreted.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical model preserves uncertainty to weight visual cues by reliability and image context, fitting the authors' psychophysics data well.

title: Managing Uncertainty in Cue Combination

abstract: The standard reinforcement learning view of the involvement of neuromodulatory systems in instrumental conditioning in(cid:173) cludes a rather straightforward conception of motivation as prediction of sum future reward. Competition between actions is based on the motivating characteristics of their consequent states in this sense. Substantial, careful, experiments reviewed in Dickinson & Balleine, 12,13 into the neurobiology and psychol(cid:173) ogy of motivation shows that this view is incomplete. In many cases, animals are faced with the choice not between many dif(cid:173) ferent actions at a given state, but rather whether a single re(cid:173) sponse is worth executing at all. Evidence suggests that the motivational process underlying this choice has different psy(cid:173) chological and neural properties from that underlying action choice. We describe and model these motivational systems, and consider the way they interact.

paragraphs: The paper examines a distinction within motivation: selecting among possible actions and deciding whether a particular response is worth making at all. A standard reinforcement-learning account frames motivation through predicted cumulative future reward, with actions competing according to the value of the states they lead to.

The authors argue that this account is incomplete in light of experimental work on the psychology and neurobiology of motivation. Animals often face a question about whether to execute one available response. The reviewed evidence suggests that this decision involves motivational processes with psychological and neural properties different from those involved in choosing among actions.

The paper describes and models these motivational systems and considers their interaction. Its contribution is to make the distinction part of a computational account, broadening what motivation must explain in instrumental conditioning. The evidence supports treating response execution and action choice as distinguishable processes, while the modeling addresses how those processes can interact within an account of motivated behavior.
summary.tldr: The paper models the interaction between motivation to execute a response and motivation governing choice among actions.

title: Motivated Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Acetylcholine (ACh) has been implicated in a wide variety of tasks involving attentional processes and plasticity. Following extensive animal studies, it has previously been suggested that ACh reports on uncertainty and controls hippocampal, cortical and cortico-amygdalar plasticity. We extend this view and consider its effects on cortical representational inference, arguing that ACh controls the balance between bottom-up inference, in(cid:3)uenced by input stimuli, and top-down inference, in(cid:3)uenced by contextual information. We illustrate our proposal using a hierarchical hid- den Markov model.
originalAbstract: Acetylcholine (ACh) has been implicated in a wide variety of tasks involving attentional processes and plasticity. Following extensive animal studies, it has previously been suggested that ACh reports on uncertainty and controls hippocampal, cortical and cortico-amygdalar plasticity. We extend this view and consider its effects on cortical representational inference, arguing that ACh controls the balance between bottom-up inference, in(cid:3)uenced by input stimuli, and top-down inference, in(cid:3)uenced by contextual information. We illustrate our proposal using a hierarchical hid- den Markov model.

paragraphs: The paper proposes an account of how acetylcholine, or ACh, could influence the brain's interpretation of sensory information. Earlier animal research had motivated the suggestion that ACh signals uncertainty and regulates plasticity in several brain systems. The authors extend that perspective from changes in neural connections to the ongoing process of deciding what incoming information represents.

Their proposal concerns the balance between two sources of evidence. Bottom-up inference draws on the current sensory input, while top-down inference draws on context. The authors argue that ACh controls the relative influence of these sources. This gives uncertainty a role in determining how a cortical representation is formed, connecting the proposed chemical signal to the interpretation of stimuli.

A hierarchical hidden Markov model illustrates the idea computationally. It provides a way to express the proposed relationship between contextual information and incoming observations within a layered inference model. The contribution is a mechanistic hypothesis and its illustration: it suggests how ACh's previously proposed uncertainty role could also organize cortical inference.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes that acetylcholine regulates how cortical inference balances sensory input against contextual information.

title: ACh, Uncertainty, and Cortical Inference

abstract: We present a hierarchical Bayesian model for learning efﬁcient codes of higher-order structure in natural images. The model, a non-linear gen- eralization of independent component analysis, replaces the standard as- sumption of independence for the joint distribution of coefﬁcients with a distribution that is adapted to the variance structure of the coefﬁcients of an efﬁcient image basis. This offers a novel description of higher- order image structure and provides a way to learn coarse-coded, sparse- distributed representations of abstract image properties such as object location, scale, and texture.
originalAbstract: We present a hierarchical Bayesian model for learning efﬁcient codes of higher-order structure in natural images. The model, a non-linear gen- eralization of independent component analysis, replaces the standard as- sumption of independence for the joint distribution of coefﬁcients with a distribution that is adapted to the variance structure of the coefﬁcients of an efﬁcient image basis. This offers a novel description of higher- order image structure and provides a way to learn coarse-coded, sparse- distributed representations of abstract image properties such as object location, scale, and texture.

paragraphs: The paper develops a hierarchical Bayesian model for representing structure in natural images. Its starting point is independent component analysis, which describes an image through coefficients associated with an image basis. The proposed model extends this approach nonlinearly to capture relationships that an independence assumption would leave out.

The key change concerns the joint distribution of those coefficients. Instead of treating them as independent, the model adapts their distribution to the way their variances are structured. This shifts attention toward patterns in how strongly different coefficients vary, providing a description of higher-order image structure beyond the individual coefficients themselves.

The resulting representation offers a way to learn abstract properties such as object location, scale, and texture. These properties are represented through sparse, distributed activity with coarse coding: the representation spreads information across components rather than assigning every property to a single exact indicator. The contribution is a modeling framework connecting variance structure to more abstract image descriptions.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian extension of independent component analysis models image-coefficient variance structure to learn sparse representations of abstract image properties.

title: A Model for Learning Variance Components of Natural Images

abstract: Super-resolution aims to produce a high-resolution image from a set of one or more low-resolution images by recovering or inventing plausible high-frequency image content. Typical approaches try to reconstruct a high-resolution image using the sub-pixel displacements of several low- resolution images, usually regularized by a generic smoothness prior over the high-resolution image space. Other methods use training data to learn low-to-high-resolution matches, and have been highly successful even in the single-input-image case. Here we present a domain-speciﬁc im- age prior in the form of a p.d.f. based upon sampled images, and show that for certain types of super-resolution problems, this sample-based prior gives a signiﬁcant improvement over other common multiple-image super-resolution techniques.

paragraphs: Super-resolution seeks a detailed image from one or more lower-resolution observations. Some fine detail can be recovered from the inputs, while other detail must be supplied as a plausible reconstruction. The paper focuses on the prior that guides this choice: the assumptions about what a reasonable high-resolution image should look like.

Common multiple-image methods use small displacements between observations to reconstruct detail and apply a general preference for smooth images. The proposed approach instead represents domain-specific image knowledge as a probability density built from sampled images. This lets examples from the relevant image domain shape which reconstructions are considered plausible, rather than relying only on generic smoothness.

The authors report significant improvement over other common multiple-image super-resolution techniques for certain types of problems. That qualification matters because the prior is explicitly domain-specific. The stated finding supports using sampled image structure where it suits the reconstruction problem; it does not establish an improvement for every kind of image or every super-resolution setting.
summary.tldr: A domain-specific prior built from sampled images improves reconstruction for certain multiple-image super-resolution problems.

title: A Sampled Texture Prior for Image Super-Resolution

abstract: We introduce a new algorithm based on linear programming that approximates the differential value function of an average-cost Markov decision process via a linear combination of pre-selected basis functions. The algorithm carries out a form of cost shaping and minimizes a version of Bellman error. We establish an error bound that scales gracefully with the number of states without imposing the (strong) Lyapunov condition required by its counterpart in [6]. We propose a path-following method that automates selection of important algorithm parameters which represent counterparts to the “state-relevance weights” studied in [6].

paragraphs: This paper studies how to approximate the differential value function of an average-cost Markov decision process. This function captures differences in the long-term consequences of states under an average-cost objective. The proposed algorithm represents it as a weighted combination of basis functions selected beforehand, turning the search for a value function into a search for suitable coefficients.

The algorithm uses linear programming to carry out a form of cost shaping while reducing a version of Bellman error. That error measures a mismatch with the consistency relationship that a value function should satisfy. Connecting this approximation objective to an error guarantee gives the optimization procedure a theoretical basis beyond simply fitting its chosen representation.

The authors establish a bound that scales favorably with the number of states without requiring the strong Lyapunov condition used by the referenced counterpart. They also propose a path-following procedure for choosing important parameters automatically. These parameters play a role analogous to state-relevance weights, making their selection part of the method rather than leaving it entirely to manual adjustment.
summary.tldr: A linear-programming method approximates average-cost value functions with an error guarantee and a procedure for selecting important parameters.

title: A Cost-Shaping LP for Bellman Error Minimization with Performance Guarantees

abstract: We describe a vision-based obstacle avoidance system for off-road mobile robots. The system is trained from end to end to map raw in put images to steering angles. It is trained in supervised mode to predict the steering angles provided by a human driver during training r uns collected in a wide variety of terrains, weather conditions, lighting conditions, and obstacle types. The robot is a 50cm off-road truck, with two f orwardpointing wireless color cameras. A remote computer process es the video and controls the robot via radio. The learning system is a lar ge 6-layer convolutional network whose input is a single left/right pair of unprocessed low-resolution images. The robot exhibits an excellent ability to detect obstacles and navigate around them in real time at speeds of 2 m/s.

The collected driving runs span varied terrain, weather, lighting, and obstacle types, giving the supervised learning system examples from a broad set of operating conditions.

The robot is a 50-centimeter truck equipped with two forward-facing wireless color cameras. A six-layer convolutional network receives one pair of unprocessed, low-resolution left and right images and predicts a steering angle. Video processing runs on a remote computer, which sends control commands to the vehicle by radio.

The authors report strong obstacle detection and avoidance in real time at speeds of two meters per second. The key contribution is the complete connection from visual observations to driving commands through supervised learning. The demonstrated system shows that human steering examples can train a convolutional network to produce useful obstacle-avoidance behavior on a physical off-road vehicle.
summary.tldr: A convolutional network trained on human steering examples guides an off-road robot around obstacles directly from paired camera images.

title: Off-Road Obstacle Avoidance through End-to-End Learning

abstract: We present a novel Bayesian model for semi-supervised part-of-speech tagging. Our model extends the Latent Dirichlet Allocation model and incorporates the intuition that words’ distributions over tags, p(t|w), are sparse. In addition we in- troduce a model for determining the set of possible tags of a word which captures important dependencies in the ambiguity classes of words. Our model outper- forms the best previously proposed model for this task on a standard dataset.

Our model outper- forms the best previously proposed model for this task on a standard dataset.

Its starting point is Latent Dirichlet Allocation, extended to express a particular intuition about language: a word's probability distribution over grammatical tags should be sparse.

Sparsity here means that a word places substantial probability on relatively few tags. The model therefore incorporates information about how narrowly or broadly individual words can behave grammatically. The authors also introduce a model for determining which tags are possible for each word. This captures dependencies within ambiguity classes, the sets of grammatical categories associated with words.

These two contributions address related aspects of uncertainty: how probability is distributed across tags, and how the possible tag sets are structured. On a standard dataset, the resulting system outperforms the strongest previously proposed model identified in the abstract. The stated finding supports incorporating these linguistic regularities into Bayesian tagging for the evaluated task.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian extension of LDA improves semi-supervised tagging by modeling sparse word–tag distributions and dependencies in possible tag sets.

title: A Bayesian LDA-based model for semi-supervised part-of-speech tagging

abstract: The recent emergence of Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) as general-purpose parallel computing devices provides us with new opportunities to develop scalable learning methods for massive data. In this work, we consider the problem of parallelizing two inference methods on GPUs for latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) models, collapsed Gibbs sampling (CGS) and collapsed variational Bayesian (CVB). To address limited memory constraints on GPUs, we propose a novel data partitioning scheme that effectively reduces the memory cost. Furthermore, the partitioning scheme balances the computational cost on each multiprocessor and enables us to easily avoid memory access conflicts. We also use data streaming to handle extremely large datasets. Extensive experiments showed that our parallel inference methods consistently produced LDA models with the same predictive power as sequential training methods did but with 26x speedup for CGS and 196x speedup for CVB on a GPU with 30 multiprocessors; actually the speedup is almost linearly scalable with the number of multiprocessors available. The proposed partitioning scheme and data streaming can be easily ported to many other models in machine learning.

paragraphs: The paper accelerates inference for latent Dirichlet allocation by running two established methods on graphics processors: collapsed Gibbs sampling and collapsed variational Bayes. Its focus is making effective use of parallel hardware while managing the memory constraints that arise when training models on large datasets.

The authors introduce a data-partitioning scheme that reduces memory requirements, balances computation across multiprocessors, and helps avoid conflicting memory accesses. They also use streaming to accommodate extremely large datasets. These choices address how data and work are distributed, enabling the inference procedures to use the available parallel resources efficiently.

Experiments produce models with the same predictive power as sequential training, with speedups of 26 times for Gibbs sampling and 196 times for variational Bayes on a GPU with 30 multiprocessors. Speedup scales almost linearly with the available multiprocessor count in the reported results. The authors also identify the partitioning and streaming techniques as readily transferable to many other machine-learning models.
summary.tldr: GPU partitioning and streaming substantially accelerate two LDA inference methods while preserving predictive power in the reported experiments.

title: Parallel Inference for Latent Dirichlet Allocation on Graphics Processing Units

abstract: Dimensionality reduction is commonly used in the setting of multi-label supervised classification to control the learning capacity and to provide a meaningful representation of the data. We introduce a simple forward probabilistic model which is a multinomial extension of reduced rank regression; we show that this model provides a probabilistic interpretation of discriminative clustering methods with added benefits in terms of number of hyperparameters and optimization. While expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm is commonly used to learn these models, its optimization usually leads to local minimum because it relies on a non-convex cost function with many such local minima. To avoid this problem, we introduce a local approximation of this cost function, which leads to a quadratic non-convex optimization problem over a product of simplices. In order to minimize such functions, we propose an efficient algorithm based on convex relaxation and low-rank representation of our data, which allows to deal with large instances. Experiments on text document classification show that the new model outperforms other supervised dimensionality reduction methods, while simulations on unsupervised clustering show that our probabilistic formulation has better properties than existing discriminative clustering methods.

paragraphs: Supervised dimensionality reduction seeks a compact representation that helps classification while controlling learning capacity. This paper introduces a forward probabilistic model that extends reduced-rank regression to multinomial outcomes. It also gives a probabilistic interpretation of discriminative clustering, with stated benefits in hyperparameter requirements and optimization.

A central difficulty is that expectation-maximization optimizes a nonconvex objective containing many local minima. The authors introduce a local approximation that produces a quadratic, still nonconvex problem over a product of simplices, or collections of probability vectors. They then develop an efficient optimization algorithm using convex relaxation and a low-rank representation of the data, allowing larger instances to be handled.

Text document classification experiments show the model outperforming other supervised dimensionality reduction methods in the reported comparisons. Separate unsupervised clustering simulations show advantages of the probabilistic formulation over existing discriminative clustering approaches. The contribution combines a model interpretation with an optimization strategy, and the two experimental settings provide evidence for benefits in both supervised representation learning and clustering.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic latent-class model uses local approximation, convex relaxation, and low-rank structure to improve optimization and reported classification and clustering results.

title: Efficient Optimization for Discriminative Latent Class Models

abstract: In many real world applications we do not have access to fully-labeled training data, but only to a list of possible labels. This is the case, e.g., when learning visual classifiers from images downloaded from the web, using just their text captions or tags as learning oracles. In general, these problems can be very difficult. However most of the time there exist different implicit sources of information, coming from the relations between instances and labels, which are usually dismissed. In this paper, we propose a semi-supervised framework to model this kind of problems. Each training sample is a bag containing multi-instances, associated with a set of candidate labeling vectors. Each labeling vector encodes the possible labels for the instances in the bag, with only one being fully correct. The use of the labeling vectors provides a principled way not to exclude any information. We propose a large margin discriminative formulation, and an efficient algorithm to solve it. Experiments conducted on artificial datasets and a real-world images and captions dataset show that our approach achieves performance comparable to SVM trained with the ground-truth labels, and outperforms other baselines.

paragraphs: Training data sometimes identifies several possible labels without specifying the correct assignment. Images accompanied by captions or tags illustrate this ambiguity: the text provides useful information, but its relationship to individual image instances may be uncertain. This paper develops a semi-supervised framework that retains information contained in relationships among instances and their possible labels.

Each training example is represented as a bag of multiple instances together with candidate labeling vectors. A vector specifies a possible assignment of labels to all instances in the bag, and the formulation assumes that exactly one candidate is fully correct. Keeping complete candidate assignments provides a principled way to preserve information about how possible labels fit together.

The authors introduce a large-margin discriminative formulation and an efficient solution algorithm. On artificial datasets and a real image-caption dataset, the method performs comparably to an SVM trained with ground-truth labels and outperforms the other tested baselines. These findings show the value of representing labeling ambiguity jointly in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Learning from complete candidate label assignments preserves relationships within bags and performs well despite ambiguous supervision.

title: Learning from Candidate Labeling Sets

abstract: We consider the hypothesis testing problem of detecting a shift between the means of two multivariate normal distributions in the high-dimensional setting, allowing for the data dimension p to exceed the sample size n. Our contribution is a new test statistic for the two-sample test of means that integrates a random projection with the classical Hotelling T squared statistic. Working within a high- dimensional framework that allows (p,n) to tend to infinity, we first derive an asymptotic power function for our test, and then provide sufficient conditions for it to achieve greater power than other state-of-the-art tests. Using ROC curves generated from simulated data, we demonstrate superior performance against competing tests in the parameter regimes anticipated by our theoretical results. Lastly, we illustrate an advantage of our procedure with comparisons on a high-dimensional gene expression dataset involving the discrimination of different types of cancer.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to detect a difference between the means of two multivariate normal distributions when there are many measured variables. The setting allows the number of variables to exceed the sample size. Its proposed test combines a random projection of the observations with the classical Hotelling T-squared statistic.

The theoretical analysis considers a regime in which both dimension and sample size grow. Within that framework, the authors derive the test’s asymptotic power, describing its ability to detect a mean shift. They then establish sufficient conditions under which it has greater power than other leading tests. The advantage is therefore tied to specified conditions, rather than asserted for every high-dimensional problem.

Simulated comparisons using ROC curves show stronger performance in the parameter regimes predicted by the theory. A further comparison on gene-expression data illustrates an advantage when distinguishing cancer types. Together, these results connect the mathematical conditions to observed behavior and support random projection as a useful component of high-dimensional mean testing.
summary.tldr: Combining random projection with Hotelling’s statistic yields a high-dimensional mean test with greater power under sufficient conditions supported by experiments.

title: A More Powerful Two-Sample Test in High Dimensions using Random Projection

abstract: Focusing on short term trend prediction in a financial context, we consider the problem of selective prediction whereby the predictor can abstain from prediction in order to improve performance. We examine two types of selective mechanisms for HMM predictors. The first is a rejection in the spirit of Chow’s well-known ambiguity principle. The second is a specialized mechanism for HMMs that identifies low quality HMM states and abstain from prediction in those states. We call this model selective HMM (sHMM). In both approaches we can trade-off prediction coverage to gain better accuracy in a controlled manner. We compare performance of the ambiguity-based rejection technique with that of the sHMM approach. Our results indicate that both methods are effective, and that the sHMM model is superior.

The second is a specialized mechanism for HMMs that identifies low quality HMM states and abstain from prediction in those states. We call this model selective HMM (sHMM). In both approaches we can trade-off prediction coverage to gain better accuracy in a controlled manner. We compare performance of the ambiguity-based rejection technique with that of the sHMM approach. Our results indicate that both methods are effective, and that the sHMM model is superior.

paragraphs: The paper studies short-term financial trend prediction when a model is allowed to abstain. The objective is to improve accuracy on the predictions it chooses to make, accepting that some cases will receive no prediction. This introduces a trade-off between coverage, meaning how often the model predicts, and accuracy on those selected cases.

The authors examine two selection mechanisms for hidden Markov model predictors. The first rejects predictions according to an ambiguity principle. The second identifies low-quality hidden states and avoids predicting when the model is in those states. This second approach, called a selective HMM, uses the model's internal state structure to guide abstention.

Both mechanisms allow coverage to be traded for accuracy in a controlled way. The reported comparison finds both effective and favors the selective HMM approach. The findings concern selective prediction performance: the benefit comes from making predictions on a chosen subset of cases. They support using state-level quality information as a useful basis for deciding when an HMM should predict.
summary.tldr: Allowing HMMs to abstain improves financial trend prediction accuracy at reduced coverage, with state-based selection performing best in the reported comparison.

title: Selective Prediction of Financial Trends with Hidden Markov Models

abstract: Margin is one of the most important concepts in machine learning. Previous margin bounds, both for SVM and for boosting, are dimensionality independent. A major advantage of this dimensionality independency is that it can explain the excellent performance of SVM whose feature spaces are often of high or infinite dimension. In this paper we address the problem whether such dimensionality independency is intrinsic for the margin bounds. We prove a dimensionality dependent PAC-Bayes margin bound. The bound is monotone increasing with respect to the dimension when keeping all other factors fixed. We show that our bound is strictly sharper than a previously well-known PAC-Bayes margin bound if the feature space is of finite dimension; and the two bounds tend to be equivalent as the dimension goes to infinity. In addition, we show that the VC bound for linear classifiers can be recovered from our bound under mild conditions. We conduct extensive experiments on benchmark datasets and find that the new bound is useful for model selection and is significantly sharper than the dimensionality independent PAC-Bayes margin bound as well as the VC bound for linear classifiers.

paragraphs: Margin bounds help explain classification performance through how confidently examples are separated. Familiar bounds for support vector machines and boosting do not depend on feature-space dimension, which helps explain their usefulness in very large feature spaces. This paper asks whether dimension independence is unavoidable, or whether explicitly accounting for dimension can produce a tighter guarantee.

The authors prove a PAC-Bayes margin bound that increases with dimension when all other factors remain fixed. For finite-dimensional feature spaces, it is strictly sharper than a particular established dimension-independent PAC-Bayes margin bound. As dimension tends to infinity, the two bounds approach equivalence. The result therefore identifies a finite-dimensional improvement while retaining a connection to the earlier guarantee.

Under mild conditions, the new bound also recovers the VC bound for linear classifiers. Experiments on benchmark datasets find that it is useful for model selection and substantially sharper than both comparison bounds. These findings concern the informativeness of the guarantee; its increasing dependence on dimension does not by itself assert that actual classification performance must worsen whenever dimension grows.
summary.tldr: A dimension-dependent PAC-Bayes margin bound tightens an established bound in finite-dimensional feature spaces and proves useful for model selection.

title: Dimensionality Dependent PAC-Bayes Margin Bound

abstract: Many scientific data occur as sequences of multidimensional arrays called tensors. How can hidden, evolving trends in such data be extracted while preserving the tensor structure? The model that is traditionally used is the linear dynamical system (LDS), which treats the observation at each time slice as a vector. In this paper, we propose the multilinear dynamical system (MLDS) for modeling tensor time series and an expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm to estimate the parameters. The MLDS models each time slice of the tensor time series as the multilinear projection of a corresponding member of a sequence of latent, low-dimensional tensors. Compared to the LDS with an equal number of parameters, the MLDS achieves higher prediction accuracy and marginal likelihood for both simulated and real datasets.

paragraphs: Some time series contain a multidimensional array at every time step. These arrays, called tensors, have a structure that is lost when each observation is treated simply as a vector. This paper introduces multilinear dynamical systems to extract hidden, changing trends while preserving the tensor form of the observations.

The model represents each observed tensor as a multilinear projection of a corresponding low-dimensional latent tensor. A sequence of these hidden tensors describes the evolving underlying representation. The authors also develop an expectation-maximization algorithm to estimate the model's parameters, giving a fitting procedure alongside the new model.

On both simulated and real datasets, the method achieves higher prediction accuracy and marginal likelihood than a linear dynamical system with the same number of parameters. Matching parameter counts makes the comparison informative about the value of the tensor-based structure. The stated results support modeling multidimensional observations directly when extracting temporal trends, rather than assuming that a vector representation uses the modeling capacity equally well.
summary.tldr: Multilinear dynamical systems preserve tensor structure and outperform equally parameterized linear dynamical systems on the evaluated time-series datasets.

title: Multilinear Dynamical Systems for Tensor Time Series

abstract: We propose a class of closed-form estimators for sparsity-structured graphical models, expressed as exponential family distributions, under high-dimensional settings. Our approach builds on observing the precise manner in which the classical graphical model MLE ``breaks down'' under high-dimensional settings. Our estimator uses a carefully constructed, well-defined and closed-form backward map, and then performs thresholding operations to ensure the desired sparsity structure. We provide a rigorous statistical analysis that shows that surprisingly our simple class of estimators recovers the same asymptotic convergence rates as those of the $\ell_1$-regularized MLEs that are much more difficult to compute. We corroborate this statistical performance, as well as significant computational advantages via simulations of both discrete and Gaussian graphical models.

Our approach builds on observing the precise manner in which the classical graphical model MLE ``breaks down'' under high-dimensional settings. Our estimator uses a carefully constructed, well-defined and closed-form backward map, and then performs thresholding operations to ensure the desired sparsity structure. We provide a rigorous statistical analysis that shows that surprisingly our simple class of estimators recovers the same asymptotic convergence rates as those of the $\ell_1$-regularized MLEs that are much more difficult to compute. We corroborate this statistical performance, as well as significant computational advantages via simulations of both discrete and Gaussian graphical models.

paragraphs: Learning a graphical model means estimating a structured description of relationships among variables. In high-dimensional settings, classical maximum-likelihood estimation can break down. This paper studies the precise form of that failure and uses it to construct simple estimators for sparse graphical models expressed as exponential-family distributions.

The method first applies a carefully designed backward map that is well-defined and available in closed form. It then uses thresholding to enforce the intended sparsity structure. This separates the estimation procedure into a direct calculation and a sparsification step, providing a computationally simpler alternative to solving an optimization problem for an l1-regularized maximum-likelihood estimate.

The statistical analysis shows that these elementary estimators achieve the same asymptotic convergence rates as the more computationally demanding regularized estimators. Matching rates concerns how estimation error scales asymptotically; it does not assert identical estimates. Simulations involving both discrete and Gaussian graphical models support the statistical findings and show substantial computational advantages. The contribution demonstrates that a carefully constructed direct estimator can retain strong statistical performance.
summary.tldr: Closed-form maps followed by thresholding estimate sparse graphical models with convergence rates matching l1-regularized maximum likelihood.

title: Elementary Estimators for Graphical Models

abstract: Lifted inference algorithms for probabilistic first-order logic frameworks such as Markov logic networks (MLNs) have received significant attention in recent years. These algorithms use so called lifting rules to identify symmetries in the first-order representation and reduce the inference problem over a large probabilistic model to an inference problem over a much smaller model. In this paper, we present two new lifting rules, which enable fast MAP inference in a large class of MLNs. Our first rule uses the concept of single occurrence equivalence class of logical variables, which we define in the paper. The rule states that the MAP assignment over an MLN can be recovered from a much smaller MLN, in which each logical variable in each single occurrence equivalence class is replaced by a constant (i.e., an object in the domain of the variable). Our second rule states that we can safely remove a subset of formulas from the MLN if all equivalence classes of variables in the remaining MLN are single occurrence and all formulas in the subset are tautology (i.e., evaluate to true) at extremes (i.e., assignments with identical truth value for groundings of a predicate). We prove that our two new rules are sound and demonstrate via a detailed experimental evaluation that our approach is superior in terms of scalability and MAP solution quality to the state of the art approaches.

In this paper, we present two new lifting rules, which enable fast MAP inference in a large class of MLNs. Our first rule uses the concept of single occurrence equivalence class of logical variables, which we define in the paper. The rule states that the MAP assignment over an MLN can be recovered from a much smaller MLN, in which each logical variable in each single occurrence equivalence class is replaced by a constant (i.e., an object in the domain of the variable). Our second rule states that we can safely remove a subset of formulas from the MLN if all equivalence classes of variables in the remaining MLN are single occurrence and all formulas in the subset are tautology (i.e., evaluate to true) at extremes (i.e., assignments with identical truth value for groundings of a predicate). We prove that our two new rules are sound and demonstrate via a detailed experimental evaluation that our approach is superior in terms of scalability and MAP solution quality to the state of the art approaches.

paragraphs: Lifted inference exploits symmetry in a first-order probabilistic model to reduce a large inference problem to a smaller one. This paper introduces two rules for maximum a posteriori, or MAP, inference in Markov logic networks. The goal is to recover the most probable assignment while working with a reduced model whenever the rules apply.

The first rule uses a defined structure called a single-occurrence equivalence class of logical variables. Variables in these classes can be replaced by domain constants in a smaller network from which the original MAP assignment can be recovered. The second rule permits removing certain formulas when every remaining variable equivalence class is single-occurrence and the removed formulas are true at extreme assignments, where each predicate's groundings share a truth value.

The authors prove both rules sound, so the reductions have a formal justification under their stated conditions. A detailed experimental evaluation reports better scalability and MAP solution quality than the compared state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution expands the structural situations in which symmetry can simplify MAP inference.
summary.tldr: Two sound lifting rules reduce qualifying Markov logic networks and improve MAP inference in the reported experiments.

title: New Rules for Domain Independent Lifted MAP Inference

abstract: Extracting 3D shape of deforming objects in monocular videos, a task known as non-rigid structure-from-motion (NRSfM), has so far been studied only on synthetic datasets and controlled environments. Typically, the objects to reconstruct are pre-segmented, they exhibit limited rotations and occlusions, or full-length trajectories are assumed. In order to integrate NRSfM into current video analysis pipelines, one needs to consider as input realistic -thus incomplete- tracking, and perform spatio-temporal grouping to segment the objects from their surroundings. Furthermore, NRSfM needs to be robust to noise in both segmentation and tracking, e.g., drifting, segmentation leaking'', optical flow bleeding'' etc. In this paper, we make a first attempt towards this goal, and propose a method that combines dense optical flow tracking, motion trajectory clustering and NRSfM for 3D reconstruction of objects in videos. For each trajectory cluster, we compute multiple reconstructions by minimizing the reprojection error and the rank of the 3D shape under different rank bounds of the trajectory matrix. We show that dense 3D shape is extracted and trajectories are completed across occlusions and low textured regions, even under mild relative motion between the object and the camera. We achieve competitive results on a public NRSfM benchmark while using fixed parameters across all sequences and handling incomplete trajectories, in contrast to existing approaches. We further test our approach on popular video segmentation datasets. To the best of our knowledge, our method is the first to extract dense object models from realistic videos, such as those found in Youtube or Hollywood movies, without object-specific priors.

For each trajectory cluster, the method computes multiple reconstructions under different bounds on the trajectory matrix's rank. Grouping and reconstruction therefore work with the incomplete motion evidence available in the video.

summary.tldr: Combining motion grouping with low-rank reconstruction enables dense three-dimensional object recovery from realistic videos with incomplete trajectories.

title: Grouping-Based Low-Rank Trajectory Completion and 3D Reconstruction

abstract: Finding communities in networks is a problem that remains difficult, in spite of the amount of attention it has recently received. The Stochastic Block-Model (SBM) is a generative model for graphs with communities for which, because of its simplicity, the theoretical understanding has advanced fast in recent years. In particular, there have been various results showing that simple versions of spectralclustering using the Normalized Laplacian of the graph can recoverthe communities almost perfectly with high probability. Here we show that essentially the same algorithm used for the SBM and for its extension called Degree-Corrected SBM, works on a wider class of Block-Models, which we call Preference Frame Models, with essentially the same guarantees. Moreover, the parametrization we introduce clearly exhibits the free parameters needed to specify this class of models, and results in bounds that expose with more clarity the parameters that control the recovery error in this model class.

paragraphs: The paper asks how widely a familiar method for finding network communities can be trusted. Earlier theory had established strong recovery results for the Stochastic Block Model and its degree-corrected extension. These models describe networks with community structure, but guarantees for them leave open whether the same algorithm works for a broader range of network models.

The authors introduce Preference Frame Models, a wider class of block models, and show that essentially the same spectral clustering algorithm applies. The algorithm uses the graph's normalized Laplacian to extract information about its community structure. Within the proposed model class, it retains essentially the same high-probability, nearly perfect recovery guarantees associated with the earlier models.

A second contribution is the way the model class is described mathematically. Its parametrization makes the available degrees of freedom explicit, and the recovery bounds clarify which parameters govern error. The result therefore extends the reach of an existing algorithm while making its theoretical behavior easier to interpret within this broader class.
summary.tldr: Preference Frame Models broaden the network models for which familiar spectral clustering methods have strong community-recovery guarantees.

title: A class of network models recoverable by spectral clustering

abstract: We develop a sequential low-complexity inference procedure for Dirichlet process mixtures of Gaussians for online clustering and parameter estimation when the number of clusters are unknown a-priori. We present an easily computable, closed form parametric expression for the conditional likelihood, in which hyperparameters are recursively updated as a function of the streaming data assuming conjugate priors. Motivated by large-sample asymptotics, we propose a noveladaptive low-complexity design for the Dirichlet process concentration parameter and show that the number of classes grow at most at a logarithmic rate. We further prove that in the large-sample limit, the conditional likelihood and datapredictive distribution become asymptotically Gaussian. We demonstrate through experiments on synthetic and real data sets that our approach is superior to otheronline state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: The paper addresses online clustering when the number of groups is unknown beforehand. It develops a sequential inference procedure for Dirichlet process mixtures of Gaussians, updating cluster information and model parameters as data arrive. The emphasis is on keeping these updates computationally inexpensive.

Assuming conjugate priors, the authors derive a closed-form expression for the conditional likelihood. Its hyperparameters are updated recursively from streaming observations. They also propose an adaptive choice of the Dirichlet process concentration parameter, motivated by large-sample behavior. Under this design, they show that the number of classes grows no faster than logarithmically, providing a theoretical description of how model complexity develops.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets report better performance than other leading online methods, supporting the proposed combination of adaptive complexity and efficient sequential inference.
summary.tldr: An efficient online Gaussian mixture procedure adapts to an unknown number of clusters while controlling their growth.

title: Adaptive Low-Complexity Sequential Inference for Dirichlet Process Mixture Models

abstract: This paper is concerned with the problem of representing and learning a linear transformation using a linear neural network. In recent years, there is a growing interest in the study of such networks, in part due to the successes of deep learning. The main question of this body of research (and also of our paper) is related to the existence and optimality properties of the critical points of the mean-squared loss function. An additional primary concern of our paper pertains to the robustness of these critical points in the face of (a small amount of) regularization. An optimal control model is introduced for this purpose and a learning algorithm (backprop with weight decay) derived for the same using the Hamilton's formulation of optimal control. The formulation is used to provide a complete characterization of the critical points in terms of the solutions of a nonlinear matrix-valued equation, referred to as the characteristic equation. Analytical and numerical tools from bifurcation theory are used to compute the critical points via the solutions of the characteristic equation.

paragraphs: This paper examines how a linear neural network learns a linear transformation under mean-squared loss. Its focus is the loss function’s critical points, where first-order changes provide no direction of improvement. The authors investigate their existence and optimality properties, with particular attention to how robust these points are when a small amount of regularization is introduced.

They formulate the problem using optimal control and derive backpropagation with weight decay through Hamilton’s formulation of that framework. This provides a common mathematical description of the learning procedure and the critical points it encounters. The resulting characterization expresses all critical points through solutions of a nonlinear matrix-valued characteristic equation.

The authors then use analytical and numerical tools from bifurcation theory to compute critical points from that equation. This makes the effects of regularization accessible through a structured mathematical problem. The contribution is a complete characterization within the proposed formulation and a way to investigate those solutions, rather than a blanket claim that regularization makes every critical point optimal.
summary.tldr: An optimal-control formulation characterizes critical points of regularized linear networks through a nonlinear matrix equation.

title: How regularization affects the critical points in linear networks

abstract: We study randomly initialized residual networks using mean field theory and the theory of difference equations. Classical feedforward neural networks, such as those with tanh activations, exhibit exponential behavior on the average when propagating inputs forward or gradients backward. The exponential forward dynamics causes rapid collapsing of the input space geometry, while the exponential backward dynamics causes drastic vanishing or exploding gradients. We show, in contrast, that by adding skip connections, the network will, depending on the nonlinearity, adopt subexponential forward and backward dynamics, and in many cases in fact polynomial. The exponents of these polynomials are obtained through analytic methods and proved and verified empirically to be correct. In terms of the "edge of chaos" hypothesis, these subexponential and polynomial laws allow residual networks to "hover over the boundary between stability and chaos," thus preserving the geometry of the input space and the gradient information flow. In our experiments, for each activation function we study here, we initialize residual networks with different hyperparameters and train them on MNIST. Remarkably, our initialization time theory can accurately predict test time performance of these networks, by tracking either the expected amount of gradient explosion or the expected squared distance between the images of two input vectors. Importantly, we show, theoretically as well as empirically, that common initializations such as the Xavier or the He schemes are not optimal for residual networks, because the optimal initialization variances depend on the depth. Finally, we have made mathematical contributions by deriving several new identities for the kernels of powers of ReLU functions by relating them to the zeroth Bessel function of the second kind.

In classical feedforward networks, average forward and backward behavior can be exponential, rapidly collapsing distinctions between inputs or making gradients vanish or explode. The authors investigate how skip connections alter those depth-dependent dynamics.

Depending on the activation function, skip connections produce subexponential dynamics, often polynomial ones. The authors derive polynomial exponents analytically and verify them empirically. These slower changes support preservation of input geometry and gradient information, giving a mathematical interpretation of residual networks remaining near the boundary between stable and chaotic behavior.
