The paper also shows theoretically and empirically that Xavier and He initializations are not optimal for residual networks in the studied setting: optimal initialization variances depend on depth. Additional mathematical results derive identities for kernels of powers of ReLU functions through a connection to a Bessel function.
summary.tldr: The analysis shows how skip connections can slow signal distortion and links depth-dependent initialization choices to residual-network performance.

title: Mean Field Residual Networks: On the Edge of Chaos

abstract: Agnostophobia, the fear of the unknown, can be experienced by deep learning engineers while applying their networks to real-world applications. Unfortunately, network behavior is not well defined for inputs far from a networks training set. In an uncontrolled environment, networks face many instances that are not of interest to them and have to be rejected in order to avoid a false positive. This problem has previously been tackled by researchers by either a) thresholding softmax, which by construction cannot return "none of the known classes", or b) using an additional background or garbage class. In this paper, we show that both of these approaches help, but are generally insufficient when previously unseen classes are encountered. We also introduce a new evaluation metric that focuses on comparing the performance of multiple approaches in scenarios where such unseen classes or unknowns are encountered. Our major contributions are simple yet effective Entropic Open-Set and Objectosphere losses that train networks using negative samples from some classes. These novel losses are designed to maximize entropy for unknown inputs while increasing separation in deep feature space by modifying magnitudes of known and unknown samples. Experiments on networks trained to classify classes from MNIST and CIFAR-10 show that our novel loss functions are significantly better at dealing with unknown inputs from datasets such as Devanagari, NotMNIST, CIFAR-100 and SVHN.

This paper examines that rejection problem and shows that thresholding softmax scores or adding a background class can help but is generally insufficient for previously unseen classes.

The authors introduce Entropic Open-Set and Objectosphere losses, trained using negative examples from some classes. The losses encourage uncertainty for unknown inputs and separate known from unknown examples in the network's learned feature space by changing feature magnitudes. Experiments train classifiers on MNIST and CIFAR-10 classes and test unknown inputs drawn from datasets including Devanagari, NotMNIST, CIFAR-100, and SVHN. The new losses handle those unknown inputs significantly better in the reported experiments. The contribution is to make rejection behavior part of training and evaluation, rather than relying only on the classifier's ordinary category scores.
summary.tldr: Two training losses improve rejection of unknown inputs by encouraging uncertainty and separating known and unknown feature representations.

title: Reducing Network Agnostophobia

abstract: Risk management in dynamic decision problems is a primary concern in many fields, including financial investment, autonomous driving, and healthcare. The mean-variance function is one of the most widely used objective functions in risk management due to its simplicity and interpretability. Existing algorithms for mean-variance optimization are based on multi-time-scale stochastic approximation, whose learning rate schedules are often hard to tune, and have only asymptotic convergence proof. In this paper, we develop a model-free policy search framework for mean-variance optimization with finite-sample error bound analysis (to local optima). Our starting point is a reformulation of the original mean-variance function with its Fenchel dual, from which we propose a stochastic block coordinate ascent policy search algorithm. Both the asymptotic convergence guarantee of the last iteration's solution and the convergence rate of the randomly picked solution are provided, and their applicability is demonstrated on several benchmark domains.

paragraphs: A decision policy can have a high average return while producing outcomes that vary widely. Mean-variance optimization accounts for both considerations, making it useful for decisions where consistency matters alongside performance. The paper addresses how to learn such policies without a model of the environment, while providing guarantees about learning from a finite amount of experience.

The authors first rewrite the mean-variance objective using a mathematical construction called the Fenchel dual. This reformulation leads to a stochastic block coordinate ascent algorithm: policy search proceeds by updating different blocks of the optimization variables. Existing approaches rely on multiple learning-rate schedules that can be difficult to tune.

The analysis provides an asymptotic guarantee for the final iterate and a convergence rate for a randomly selected iterate. Its finite-sample error analysis concerns local optima, so the guarantee does not establish globally best policies. Benchmark demonstrations support the framework's applicability, connecting a risk-sensitive objective with more explicit information about its optimization behavior.
summary.tldr: A model-free policy-search algorithm optimizes mean-variance objectives with finite-sample analysis concerning local optima.

title: A Block Coordinate Ascent Algorithm for Mean-Variance Optimization

abstract: In this paper we present a hybrid active sampling strategy for pairwise preference aggregation, which aims at recovering the underlying rating of the test candidates from sparse and noisy pairwise labeling. Our method employs Bayesian optimization framework and Bradley-Terry model to construct the utility function, then to obtain the Expected Information Gain (EIG) of each pair. For computational efficiency, Gaussian-Hermite quadrature is used for estimation of EIG. In this work, a hybrid active sampling strategy is proposed, either using Global Maximum (GM) EIG sampling or Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) sampling in each trial, which is determined by the test budget. The proposed method has been validated on both simulated and real-world datasets, where it shows higher preference aggregation ability than the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Pairwise preference aggregation tries to recover candidates’ underlying ratings from judgments comparing two candidates at a time. When judgments are sparse and noisy, the choice of which comparison to request becomes part of the problem. Hybrid-MST uses active sampling to direct the available testing budget toward informative pairs.

The method combines a Bayesian optimization framework with the Bradley-Terry preference model to construct a utility function and estimate each pair’s expected information gain. Gaussian-Hermite quadrature makes that estimation computationally efficient. The resulting information scores guide comparison selection, connecting the current uncertainty about ratings to the next data the procedure seeks.

At each trial, the strategy uses either the pair with globally maximal expected information gain or a minimum-spanning-tree sampling approach, with the choice determined by the test budget. Evaluations on simulated and real-world datasets show stronger preference aggregation than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The stated contribution is this budget-dependent combination of sampling strategies, supported by a probabilistic measure of how useful each comparison is expected to be.
summary.tldr: Hybrid-MST uses expected information gain and a budget-dependent sampling strategy to recover ratings from sparse, noisy pairwise preferences.

title: Hybrid-MST: A Hybrid Active Sampling Strategy for Pairwise Preference Aggregation

abstract: Adversarial sample attacks perturb benign inputs to induce DNN misbehaviors. Recent research has demonstrated the widespread presence and the devastating consequences of such attacks. Existing defense techniques either assume prior knowledge of specific attacks or may not work well on complex models due to their underlying assumptions. We argue that adversarial sample attacks are deeply entangled with interpretability of DNN models: while classification results on benign inputs can be reasoned based on the human perceptible features/attributes, results on adversarial samples can hardly be explained. Therefore, we propose a novel adversarial sample detection technique for face recognition models, based on interpretability. It features a novel bi-directional correspondence inference between attributes and internal neurons to identify neurons critical for individual attributes. The activation values of critical neurons are enhanced to amplify the reasoning part of the computation and the values of other neurons are weakened to suppress the uninterpretable part. The classification results after such transformation are compared with those of the original model to detect adversaries. Results show that our technique can achieve 94% detection accuracy for 7 different kinds of attacks with 9.91% false positives on benign inputs. In contrast, a state-of-the-art feature squeezing technique can only achieve 55% accuracy with 23.3% false positives.

The approach turns that proposed relationship between attacks and interpretability into a detection procedure.

summary.tldr: Attribute-guided changes to face recognition networks help detect adversarial inputs by comparing predictions before and after the transformation.

title: Attacks Meet Interpretability: Attribute-steered Detection of Adversarial Samples

abstract: The process of learning new behaviors over time is a problem of great interest in both neuroscience and artificial intelligence. However, most standard analyses of animal training data either treat behavior as fixed or track only coarse performance statistics (e.g., accuracy, bias), providing limited insight into the evolution of the policies governing behavior. To overcome these limitations, we propose a dynamic psychophysical model that efficiently tracks trial-to-trial changes in behavior over the course of training. Our model consists of a dynamic logistic regression model, parametrized by a set of time-varying weights that express dependence on sensory stimuli as well as task-irrelevant covariates, such as stimulus, choice, and answer history. Our implementation scales to large behavioral datasets, allowing us to infer 500K parameters (e.g. 10 weights over 50K trials) in minutes on a desktop computer. We optimize hyperparameters governing how rapidly each weight evolves over time using the decoupled Laplace approximation, an efficient method for maximizing marginal likelihood in non-conjugate models. To illustrate performance, we apply our method to psychophysical data from both rats and human subjects learning a delayed sensory discrimination task. The model successfully tracks the psychophysical weights of rats over the course of training, capturing day-to-day and trial-to-trial fluctuations that underlie changes in performance, choice bias, and dependencies on task history. Finally, we investigate why rats frequently make mistakes on easy trials, and suggest that apparent lapses can be explained by sub-optimal weighting of known task covariates.

For rats, it captures daily and trial-level changes underlying performance, bias, and dependence on task history. They also investigate mistakes on easy trials and suggest that apparently unexplained lapses can arise from suboptimal weighting of known task variables, providing a possible account of those errors.
summary.tldr: A scalable dynamic regression model tracks changing behavioral strategies and suggests that misweighted task variables can explain apparent lapses.

title: Efficient inference for time-varying behavior during learning

abstract: There has been tremendous recent progress on equilibrium-finding algorithms for zero-sum imperfect-information extensive-form games, but there has been a puzzling gap between theory and practice. First-order methods have significantly better theoretical convergence rates than any counterfactual-regret minimization (CFR) variant. Despite this, CFR variants have been favored in practice. Experiments with first-order methods have only been conducted on small- and medium-sized games because those methods are complicated to implement in this setting, and because CFR variants have been enhanced extensively for over a decade they perform well in practice. In this paper we show that a particular first-order method, a state-of-the-art variant of the excessive gap technique---instantiated with the dilated entropy distance function---can efficiently solve large real-world problems competitively with CFR and its variants. We show this on large endgames encountered by the Libratus poker AI, which recently beat top human poker specialist professionals at no-limit Texas hold'em. We show experimental results on our variant of the excessive gap technique as well as a prior version. We introduce a numerically friendly implementation of the smoothed best response computation associated with first-order methods for extensive-form game solving. We present, to our knowledge, the first GPU implementation of a first-order method for extensive-form games. We present comparisons of several excessive gap technique and CFR variants.

title: Solving Large Sequential Games with the Excessive Gap Technique

abstract: Label noise is one of the critical sources that degrade generalization performance of deep neural networks significantly. To handle the label noise issue in a principled way, we propose a unique classification framework of constructing multiple models in heterogeneous coarse-grained meta-class spaces and making joint inference of the trained models for the final predictions in the original (base) class space. Our approach reduces noise level by simply constructing meta-classes and improves accuracy via combinatorial inferences over multiple constituent classifiers. Since the proposed framework has distinct and complementary properties for the given problem, we can even incorporate additional off-the-shelf learning algorithms to improve accuracy further. We also introduce techniques to organize multiple heterogeneous meta-class sets using $k$-means clustering and identify a desirable subset leading to learn compact models. Our extensive experiments demonstrate outstanding performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency compared to the state-of-the-art methods under various synthetic noise configurations and in a real-world noisy dataset.

paragraphs: Incorrect training labels can substantially damage a neural classifier’s ability to generalize. This paper tackles the problem by changing the classification tasks used during training. It constructs several different groupings of the original classes into broader meta-classes, then trains a separate constituent model for each grouping.

Grouping classes reduces the noise level in these coarser prediction spaces. Because the groupings differ, the constituent classifiers provide complementary information. Their outputs are combined through combinatorial inference to predict a class in the original label space. This separates learning broader distinctions from recovering the final detailed prediction, allowing multiple coarse views to contribute to a single decision.

The authors also use k-means clustering to organize heterogeneous meta-class sets and select a useful subset for compact models. The framework can incorporate additional existing learning algorithms to further improve accuracy. Experiments with several synthetic noise configurations and a real-world noisy dataset report strong accuracy and efficiency relative to state-of-the-art methods. The findings support combining different class groupings as a practical strategy for learning from unreliable labels.
summary.tldr: Multiple classifiers learn different coarse class groupings and combine their predictions to improve classification with noisy labels.

title: Combinatorial Inference against Label Noise

abstract: Empowerment is an information-theoretic method that can be used to intrinsically motivate learning agents. It attempts to maximize an agent's control over the environment by encouraging visiting states with a large number of reachable next states. Empowered learning has been shown to lead to complex behaviors, without requiring an explicit reward signal. In this paper, we investigate the use of empowerment in the presence of an extrinsic reward signal. We hypothesize that empowerment can guide reinforcement learning (RL) agents to find good early behavioral solutions by encouraging highly empowered states. We propose a unified Bellman optimality principle for empowered reward maximization. Our empowered reward maximization approach generalizes both Bellman’s optimality principle as well as recent information-theoretical extensions to it. We prove uniqueness of the empowered values and show convergence to the optimal solution. We then apply this idea to develop off-policy actor-critic RL algorithms which we validate in high-dimensional continuous robotics domains (MuJoCo). Our methods demonstrate improved initial and competitive final performance compared to model-free state-of-the-art techniques.

paragraphs: Empowerment motivates an agent to reach situations where it has many possible ways to influence what happens next. This paper studies how that intrinsic motivation can work alongside an externally supplied reward. The authors hypothesize that seeking empowered states can help an agent discover useful behavior early in learning, while it is still learning how to obtain task rewards.

They formulate a unified Bellman optimality principle that combines empowerment with reward maximization. The principle generalizes both the conventional reward-based formulation and recent information-theoretic extensions. For this formulation, the authors prove that the empowered values are unique and establish convergence to the optimal solution. This gives the combined objective a mathematical foundation beyond simply adding an informal exploration preference.

The authors then develop off-policy actor-critic algorithms and evaluate them in high-dimensional continuous robotics tasks in MuJoCo. The methods show better initial performance and competitive final performance against model-free state-of-the-art techniques. The empirical result supports the proposed early-learning benefit without claiming uniformly superior final performance.
summary.tldr: A unified reinforcement-learning objective combines reward with empowerment and yields improved early performance in continuous robotics experiments.

title: A Unified Bellman Optimality Principle Combining Reward Maximization and Empowerment

abstract: We consider the problem of estimating the mean of a set of vectors, which are stored in a distributed system. This is a fundamental task with applications in distributed SGD and many other distributed problems, where communication is a main bottleneck for scaling up computations. We propose a new sparsity-aware algorithm, which improves previous results both theoretically and empirically. The communication cost of our algorithm is characterized by Hoyer's measure of sparseness. Moreover, we prove that the communication cost of our algorithm is information-theoretic optimal up to a constant factor in all sparseness regime. We have also conducted experimental studies, which demonstrate the advantages of our method and confirm our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Estimating the mean of vectors spread across a distributed system requires communication between the places holding the data. That communication can become a major obstacle to scaling computations, including distributed stochastic gradient descent. This paper develops an algorithm that accounts for vector sparsity when estimating the mean, aiming to reduce the communication burden.

The algorithm's communication cost is characterized using Hoyer's measure of sparseness. This makes the guarantee sensitive to how sparse the vectors are, rather than treating every input as having the same communication requirements. The authors show theoretical improvements over previous results and establish a matching limit on how much the cost can be reduced.

Specifically, the communication cost is information-theoretically optimal up to a constant factor across all sparseness regimes. That claim concerns communication efficiency, with the constant-factor qualification preserved. Experimental studies also demonstrate advantages and support the theoretical findings. The result identifies sparsity as a useful resource for distributed mean estimation and quantifies how efficiently the proposed algorithm exploits it.
summary.tldr: A sparsity-aware distributed mean estimator achieves communication costs optimal up to a constant factor across sparsity regimes.

title: Optimal Sparsity-Sensitive Bounds for Distributed Mean Estimation

abstract: Inferring effective connectivity between spatially segregated brain regions is important for understanding human brain dynamics in health and disease. Non-invasive neuroimaging modalities, such as electroencephalography (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), are often used to make measurements and infer connectivity. However most studies do not consider integrating the two modalities even though each is an indirect measure of the latent neural dynamics and each has its own spatial and/or temporal limitations. In this study, we develop a linear state-space model to infer the effective connectivity in a distributed brain network based on simultaneously recorded EEG and fMRI data. Our method first identifies task-dependent and subject-dependent regions of interest (ROI) based on the analysis of fMRI data. Directed influences between the latent neural states at these ROIs are then modeled as a multivariate autogressive (MVAR) process driven by various exogenous inputs. The latent neural dynamics give rise to the observed scalp EEG measurements via a biophysically informed linear EEG forward model. We use a mean-field variational Bayesian approach to infer the posterior distribution of latent states and model parameters. The performance of the model was evaluated on two sets of simulations. Our results emphasize the importance of obtaining accurate spatial localization of ROIs from fMRI. Finally, we applied the model to simultaneously recorded EEG-fMRI data from 10 subjects during a Face-Car-House visual categorization task and compared the change in connectivity induced by different stimulus categories.

Both measurements reflect underlying neural activity indirectly, and each has spatial or temporal limitations. The approach combines their information within a linear state-space model of otherwise unobserved neural dynamics.

The method first uses fMRI to identify brain regions relevant to the particular subject and task. The authors also apply the approach to simultaneous EEG-fMRI recordings from 10 people performing a visual categorization task involving faces, cars, and houses. They compare connectivity changes across stimulus categories, illustrating how the model can investigate task-related differences in directed neural interactions.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian state-space model combines simultaneous EEG and fMRI to estimate directed interactions between hidden neural activities.

title: A state-space model for inferring effective connectivity of latent neural dynamics from simultaneous EEG/fMRI

abstract: Transfer learning from natural image datasets, particularly ImageNet, using standard large models and corresponding pretrained weights has become a de-facto method for deep learning applications to medical imaging. However, there are fundamental differences in data sizes, features and task specifications between natural image classification and the target medical tasks, and there is little understanding of the effects of transfer. In this paper, we explore properties of transfer learning for medical imaging. A performance evaluation on two large scale medical imaging tasks shows that surprisingly, transfer offers little benefit to performance, and simple, lightweight models can perform comparably to ImageNet architectures. Investigating the learned representations and features, we find that some of the differences from transfer learning are due to the over-parametrization of standard models rather than sophisticated feature reuse. We isolate where useful feature reuse occurs, and outline the implications for more efficient model exploration. We also explore feature independent benefits of transfer arising from weight scalings.

paragraphs: Medical imaging models often start from large architectures and weights pretrained on natural images such as ImageNet. This paper investigates what that transfer actually contributes, given differences in dataset sizes, visual features, and task requirements. It separates the question of final performance from the question of which learned features are being reused.

On two large-scale medical imaging tasks, the authors find that transfer provides little performance benefit and that simple, lightweight models can perform comparably to ImageNet architectures. Analysis of learned representations suggests that some differences associated with transfer arise from having more model parameters than needed, rather than from sophisticated reuse of pretrained features.

The study also identifies where useful feature reuse occurs and explores benefits from weight scaling that do not depend on transferred features. These distinctions matter for efficient model exploration: pretrained weights may affect learning through several mechanisms, and a large pretrained architecture is not automatically the source of better performance. The findings apply to the evaluated tasks and motivate closer examination of what transfer contributes in a particular setting.
summary.tldr: On two large medical-imaging tasks, ImageNet transfer offers little performance benefit, and some effects arise from model size and weight scaling rather than feature reuse.

title: Transfusion: Understanding Transfer Learning for Medical Imaging

abstract: Understanding if classifiers generalize to out-of-sample datasets is a central problem in machine learning. Microscopy images provide a standardized way to measure the generalization capacity of image classifiers, as we can image the same classes of objects under increasingly divergent, but controlled factors of variation. We created a public dataset of 132,209 images of mouse cells, COOS-7 (Cells Out Of Sample 7-Class). COOS-7 provides a classification setting where four test datasets have increasing degrees of covariate shift: some images are random subsets of the training data, while others are from experiments reproduced months later and imaged by different instruments. We benchmarked a range of classification models using different representations, including transferred neural network features, end-to-end classification with a supervised deep CNN, and features from a self-supervised CNN. While most classifiers perform well on test datasets similar to the training dataset, all classifiers failed to generalize their performance to datasets with greater covariate shifts. These baselines highlight the challenges of covariate shifts in image data, and establish metrics for improving the generalization capacity of image classifiers.

paragraphs: An image classifier can work well on familiar-looking test data yet lose that performance when acquisition conditions change. This paper introduces COOS-7, a public dataset of 132,209 mouse-cell images across seven classes, to study that problem. Microscopy makes it possible to retain object classes while varying imaging conditions in controlled ways.

The dataset supplies four test sets with increasing covariate shift. Their relationship to training data ranges from random subsets to experiments reproduced months later and recorded with different instruments. This setup lets researchers examine performance as the image distribution moves further from the training distribution, rather than relying on a single test condition.

The benchmarks compare transferred neural-network features, an end-to-end supervised convolutional network, and features from a self-supervised network. Most classifiers perform well when test data resemble training data, but every evaluated classifier fails to maintain its performance under larger shifts. The dataset and baselines therefore provide a concrete basis for measuring progress on generalization across changing image-acquisition conditions.
summary.tldr: COOS-7 uses controlled shifts in microscopy images to show that all evaluated classifiers lose their familiar-data performance under larger distribution changes.

title: The Cells Out of Sample (COOS) dataset and benchmarks for measuring out-of-sample generalization of image classifiers

abstract: How do animals learn? This remains an elusive question in neuroscience. Whereas reinforcement learning often focuses on the design of algorithms that enable artificial agents to efficiently learn new tasks, here we develop a modeling framework to directly infer the empirical learning rules that animals use to acquire new behaviors. Our method efficiently infers the trial-to-trial changes in an animal’s policy, and decomposes those changes into a learning component and a noise component. Specifically, this allows us to: (i) compare different learning rules and objective functions that an animal may be using to update its policy; (ii) estimate distinct learning rates for different parameters of an animal’s policy; (iii) identify variations in learning across cohorts of animals; and (iv) uncover trial-to-trial changes that are not captured by normative learning rules. After validating our framework on simulated choice data, we applied our model to data from rats and mice learning perceptual decision-making tasks. We found that certain learning rules were far more capable of explaining trial-to-trial changes in an animal's policy. Whereas the average contribution of the conventional REINFORCE learning rule to the policy update for mice learning the International Brain Laboratory's task was just 30%, we found that adding baseline parameters allowed the learning rule to explain 92% of the animals' policy updates under our model. Intriguingly, the best-fitting learning rates and baseline values indicate that an animal's policy update, at each trial, does not occur in the direction that maximizes expected reward. Understanding how an animal transitions from chance-level to high-accuracy performance when learning a new task not only provides neuroscientists with insight into their animals, but also provides concrete examples of biological learning algorithms to the machine learning community.

title: Inferring learning rules from animal decision-making

abstract: We introduce a generic \emph{two-loop} scheme for smooth minimax optimization with strongly-convex-concave objectives. Our approach applies the accelerated proximal point framework (or Catalyst) to the associated \emph{dual problem} and takes full advantage of existing gradient-based algorithms to solve a sequence of well-balanced strongly-convex-strongly-concave minimax problems. Despite its simplicity, this leads to a family of near-optimal algorithms with improved complexity over all existing methods designed for strongly-convex-concave minimax problems. Additionally, we obtain the first variance-reduced algorithms for this class of minimax problems with finite-sum structure and establish even faster convergence rate. Furthermore, when extended to the nonconvex-concave minimax optimization, our algorithm again achieves the state-of-the-art complexity for finding a stationary point. We carry out several numerical experiments showcasing the superiority of the Catalyst framework in practice.

paragraphs: Minimax optimization involves variables with opposing goals: one side minimizes an objective while the other maximizes it. This paper develops a general acceleration framework for smooth objectives that are strongly convex on the minimizing side and concave on the maximizing side. Its contribution is a reusable scheme that builds on existing gradient algorithms.

The method has two nested loops. It applies Catalyst, an accelerated proximal point framework, to the associated dual problem. Within this outer procedure, existing algorithms solve a sequence of better-balanced problems that have both strong convexity and strong concavity. This organization lets the framework benefit from available solvers while improving the overall theoretical computational cost.

The authors establish a family of near-optimal algorithms and introduce variance-reduced versions for objectives with finite-sum structure, obtaining faster convergence. They also extend the approach to nonconvex-concave problems, where the target is a stationary point, and report state-of-the-art complexity for that setting. Numerical experiments support the framework’s practical benefits alongside its theoretical guarantees.
summary.tldr: A two-loop Catalyst framework accelerates minimax optimization by wrapping existing gradient methods around a sequence of better-conditioned subproblems.

title: A Catalyst Framework for Minimax Optimization

abstract: Prevailing methods for graphs require abundant label and edge information for learning. When data for a new task are scarce, meta-learning can learn from prior experiences and form much-needed inductive biases for fast adaption to new tasks. Here, we introduce G-Meta, a novel meta-learning algorithm for graphs. G-Meta uses local subgraphs to transfer subgraph-specific information and learn transferable knowledge faster via meta gradients. G-Meta learns how to quickly adapt to a new task using only a handful of nodes or edges in the new task and does so by learning from data points in other graphs or related, albeit disjoint, label sets. G-Meta is theoretically justified as we show that the evidence for a prediction can be found in the local subgraph surrounding the target node or edge. Experiments on seven datasets and nine baseline methods show that G-Meta outperforms existing methods by up to 16.3%. Unlike previous methods, G-Meta successfully learns in challenging, few-shot learning settings that require generalization to completely new graphs and never-before-seen labels. Finally, G-Meta scales to large graphs, which we demonstrate on a new Tree-of-Life dataset comprising 1,840 graphs, a two-orders of magnitude increase in the number of graphs used in prior work.

paragraphs: Graph learning often depends on having plentiful labels and edges, which may be unavailable for a new task. G-Meta addresses this scarcity through meta-learning: it uses experience from other graphs or related tasks to learn how to adapt quickly. The target is adaptation from only a handful of nodes or edges.

The method organizes transferable information around local subgraphs. It uses meta gradients to learn knowledge that can support new tasks, including tasks with disjoint label sets. The authors provide theoretical support by showing that evidence for a node or edge prediction can be found in its surrounding local subgraph.

A Tree-of-Life dataset containing 1,840 graphs demonstrates scaling to a collection two orders of magnitude larger than those used in prior work. Together, these findings support local subgraphs as a useful unit for transferring knowledge across graph-learning tasks.
summary.tldr: G-Meta learns transferable knowledge from local subgraphs to adapt to new graph tasks with very few labeled nodes or edges.

title: Graph Meta Learning via Local Subgraphs

abstract: We present a multi-agent actor-critic method that aims to implicitly address the credit assignment problem under fully cooperative settings. Our key motivation is that credit assignment among agents may not require an explicit formulation as long as (1) the policy gradients derived from a centralized critic carry sufficient information for the decentralized agents to maximize their joint action value through optimal cooperation and (2) a sustained level of exploration is enforced throughout training. Under the centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) paradigm, we achieve the former by formulating the centralized critic as a hypernetwork such that a latent state representation is integrated into the policy gradients through its multiplicative association with the stochastic policies; to achieve the latter, we derive a simple technique called adaptive entropy regularization where magnitudes of the entropy gradients are dynamically rescaled based on the current policy stochasticity to encourage consistent levels of exploration. Our algorithm, referred to as LICA, is evaluated on several benchmarks including the multi-agent particle environments and a set of challenging StarCraft II micromanagement tasks, and we show that LICA significantly outperforms previous methods.
originalAbstract: We present a multi-agent actor-critic method that aims to implicitly address the credit assignment problem under fully cooperative settings. Our key motivation is that credit assignment among agents may not require an explicit formulation as long as (1) the policy gradients derived from a centralized critic carry sufficient information for the decentralized agents to maximize their joint action value through optimal cooperation and (2) a sustained level of exploration is enforced throughout training. Under the centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) paradigm, we achieve the former by formulating the centralized critic as a hypernetwork such that a latent state representation is integrated into the policy gradients through its multiplicative association with the stochastic policies; to achieve the latter, we derive a simple technique called adaptive entropy regularization where magnitudes of the entropy gradients are dynamically rescaled based on the current policy stochasticity to encourage consistent levels of exploration. Our algorithm, referred to as LICA, is evaluated on several benchmarks including the multi-agent particle environments and a set of challenging StarCraft II micromanagement tasks, and we show that LICA significantly outperforms previous methods.

paragraphs: In cooperative multi-agent learning, a shared outcome leaves the question of how each agent should change its behavior. LICA explores whether this credit assignment can emerge implicitly from learning signals. Its motivation is conditional: centralized policy gradients must carry enough information for effective cooperation, and agents must maintain exploration throughout training.

The method uses centralized training with decentralized execution. Its centralized critic is a hypernetwork that multiplicatively connects a latent state representation with the agents’ stochastic policies. This construction incorporates state information into the policy gradients used to improve individual agents. It is designed to make those gradients informative about joint action value without explicitly assigning each agent a separate share of credit.

LICA also introduces adaptive entropy regularization, dynamically rescaling entropy gradients according to current policy randomness to encourage sustained exploration. The authors evaluate the combined method on multi-agent particle environments and challenging StarCraft II micromanagement tasks, reporting significant improvements over previous methods. The results support the combination of informative centralized gradients and continued exploration in the tested cooperative settings.
summary.tldr: LICA combines a hypernetwork critic with adaptive exploration to learn cooperative behavior through implicit credit assignment.

title: Learning Implicit Credit Assignment for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We show how to learn a neural topic model with discrete random variables---one that explicitly models each word's assigned topic---using neural variational inference that does not rely on stochastic backpropagation to handle the discrete variables. The model we utilize combines the expressive power of neural methods for representing sequences of text with the topic model's ability to capture global, thematic coherence. Using neural variational inference, we show improved perplexity and document understanding across multiple corpora. We examine the effect of prior parameters both on the model and variational parameters, and demonstrate how our approach can compete and surpass a popular topic model implementation on an automatic measure of topic quality.

paragraphs: The paper combines two ways of representing text: neural sequence modeling, which captures how words unfold, and topic modeling, which captures the themes connecting a document. Its model explicitly assigns a discrete topic variable to each word. These assignments make thematic structure part of the model rather than leaving it entirely implicit in a neural representation.

The central contribution concerns how to train this combination. The authors use neural variational inference without relying on stochastic backpropagation to handle the discrete variables. This matters because the model retains explicit word-level topic choices while benefiting from neural methods for representing text sequences. The approach brings local sequence information and global thematic coherence into the same learning framework.

Across multiple corpora, the authors report improved perplexity and document understanding. They also study how prior parameters affect both the model and its variational parameters. On an automatic topic-quality measure, the approach can match and surpass a popular topic-model implementation. Together, these findings support the usefulness of the proposed combination for both text prediction and thematic representation.
summary.tldr: A neural topic model learns explicit word-level topic assignments without stochastic backpropagation through discrete variables, improving reported text and topic-quality results.

title: A Discrete Variational Recurrent Topic Model without the Reparametrization Trick

abstract: Feature distillation, a primary method in knowledge distillation, always leads to significant accuracy improvements. Most existing methods distill features in the teacher network through a manually designed transformation. In this paper, we propose a novel distillation method named task-oriented feature distillation (TOFD) where the transformation is convolutional layers that are trained in a data-driven manner by task loss. As a result, the task-oriented information in the features can be captured and distilled to students. Moreover, an orthogonal loss is applied to the feature resizing layer in TOFD to improve the performance of knowledge distillation. Experiments show that TOFD outperforms other distillation methods by a large margin on both image classification and 3D classification tasks. Codes have been released in Github.

paragraphs: Feature distillation transfers information from a teacher network's internal features to a student network. Many existing methods use a manually designed transformation to prepare the teacher features for this transfer. This paper asks how that transformation can instead be learned so that the transferred information is oriented toward the prediction task.

Task-oriented feature distillation uses convolutional layers as the transformation and trains them through the task loss. This makes the transformation data-driven and allows task-relevant feature information to be captured for the student. The method also applies an orthogonal loss to its feature-resizing layer as an additional component intended to improve distillation performance.

Experiments on image classification and 3D classification show TOFD outperforming other distillation methods by a large margin. These findings support learning how features are transformed as part of the task itself. The contribution places the transformation inside the optimization process, giving the task objective a direct role in determining what information is passed from teacher to student.
summary.tldr: TOFD learns feature transformations through task loss to transfer task-relevant information from teacher networks to students.

title: Task-Oriented Feature Distillation

abstract: We propose a simple interpolation-based method for the efficient approximation of gradients in neural ODE models. We compare it with reverse dynamic method (known in literature as “adjoint method”) to train neural ODEs on classification, density estimation and inference approximation tasks. We also propose a theoretical justification of our approach using logarithmic norm formalism. As a result, our method allows faster model training than the reverse dynamic method what was confirmed and validated by extensive numerical experiments for several standard benchmarks.

The intended benefit is faster training through a different gradient-computation procedure, making this step of the learning process the central object of study.

The comparison is with the reverse dynamic method, also known as the adjoint method. The authors evaluate both approaches on classification, density estimation, and inference approximation tasks. Studying these different uses lets them examine the proposed procedure across several kinds of neural ODE training rather than relying on a single application.

The paper also offers a theoretical justification using logarithmic norm formalism, alongside extensive numerical experiments on several standard benchmarks. Those experiments confirm faster training than the reverse dynamic method in the evaluated settings. The resulting contribution connects an interpolation-based gradient approximation with both mathematical support and observed training-speed benefits; the empirical comparison is specifically against the stated adjoint approach.
summary.tldr: An interpolation-based gradient approximation speeds neural ODE training relative to the adjoint method in the reported benchmark experiments.

title: Interpolation Technique to Speed Up Gradients Propagation in Neural ODEs

abstract: This paper proposes a simple self-supervised approach for learning a representation for visual correspondence from raw video. We cast correspondence as prediction of links in a space-time graph constructed from video. In this graph, the nodes are patches sampled from each frame, and nodes adjacent in time can share a directed edge. We learn a representation in which pairwise similarity defines transition probability of a random walk, such that prediction of long-range correspondence is computed as a walk along the graph. We optimize the representation to place high probability along paths of similarity. Targets for learning are formed without supervision, by cycle-consistency: the objective is to maximize the likelihood of returning to the initial node when walking along a graph constructed from a palindrome of frames. Thus, a single path-level constraint implicitly supervises chains of intermediate comparisons. When used as a similarity metric without adaptation, the learned representation outperforms the self-supervised state-of-the-art on label propagation tasks involving objects, semantic parts, and pose. Moreover, we demonstrate that a technique we call edge dropout, as well as self-supervised adaptation at test-time, further improve transfer for object-centric correspondence.

paragraphs: Visual correspondence involves connecting image regions across video frames. This paper learns a representation for that task directly from raw video without supervision. It represents video as a space-time graph whose nodes are sampled image patches and whose directed edges connect patches in neighboring frames.

Similarity between patch representations defines the transition probabilities of a random walk. Following a walk through multiple frames therefore provides a way to predict longer-range correspondence. Training uses a sequence of frames arranged forward and then backward, like a palindrome, and rewards walks that return to their starting node. One constraint on the complete path thus supplies learning signals for the intermediate comparisons.

Used directly as a similarity metric, the learned representation outperforms the reported self-supervised state of the art on label propagation involving objects, semantic parts, and pose. Edge dropout and self-supervised test-time adaptation further improve transfer for object-centered correspondence. The approach matters because temporal consistency supplies supervision for chains of matches without requiring manually labeled correspondences at every step.
summary.tldr: A random walk through video patches learns correspondence by rewarding return paths through forward-and-backward frame sequences.

title: Space-Time Correspondence as a Contrastive Random Walk

abstract: We present an approach to contrastive representation learning for semantic segmentation. Our approach leverages the representational power of existing feature extractors to find corresponding regions across images. These cross-image correspondences are used as auxiliary labels to guide the pixel-level selection of positive and negative samples for more effective contrastive learning in semantic segmentation. We show that auxiliary labels can be generated from a variety of feature extractors, ranging from image classification networks that have been trained using unsupervised contrastive learning to segmentation models that have been trained on a small amount of labeled data. We additionally introduce a novel metric for rapidly judging the quality of a given auxiliary-labeling strategy, and empirically analyze various factors that influence the performance of contrastive learning for semantic segmentation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method both in the low-data as well as the high-data regime on various datasets. Our experiments show that contrastive learning with our auxiliary-labeling approach consistently boosts semantic segmentation accuracy when compared to standard ImageNet pretraining and outperforms existing approaches of contrastive and semi-supervised semantic segmentation.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns meaning at the pixel level, so useful representations must distinguish image regions precisely. This paper improves contrastive representation learning by finding corresponding regions across different images. Those relationships provide auxiliary labels that guide which pixels should be treated as positive or negative examples during contrastive learning.

The method uses existing feature extractors to generate the correspondences. These can include classification networks trained through unsupervised contrastive learning or segmentation models trained on a small labeled dataset. The paper also introduces a metric for quickly assessing an auxiliary-labeling strategy and empirically examines factors that affect contrastive segmentation performance.

The findings support cross-image correspondence as useful supervision for learning pixel representations, with the quality and source of auxiliary labels becoming explicit parts of the method's design.
summary.tldr: Cross-image region correspondences supply auxiliary labels that improve contrastive learning for semantic segmentation.

title: Looking Beyond Single Images for Contrastive Semantic Segmentation Learning

abstract: Recent work introduced deep kernel processes as an entirely kernel-based alternative to NNs (Aitchison et al. 2020). Deep kernel processes flexibly learn good top-layer representations by alternately sampling the kernel from a distribution over positive semi-definite matrices and performing nonlinear transformations. A particular deep kernel process, the deep Wishart process (DWP), is of particular interest because its prior can be made equivalent to deep Gaussian process (DGP) priors for kernels that can be expressed entirely in terms of Gram matrices. However, inference in DWPs has not yet been possible due to the lack of sufficiently flexible distributions over positive semi-definite matrices. Here, we give a novel approach to obtaining flexible distributions over positive semi-definite matrices by generalising the Bartlett decomposition of the Wishart probability density. We use this new distribution to develop an approximate posterior for the DWP that includes dependency across layers. We develop a doubly-stochastic inducing-point inference scheme for the DWP and show experimentally that inference in the DWP can improve performance over doing inference in a DGP with the equivalent prior.

paragraphs: Deep kernel processes learn representations by repeatedly sampling kernel matrices and transforming them nonlinearly. The deep Wishart process is one such model. Its prior can match that of a deep Gaussian process when the kernels can be expressed entirely through Gram matrices, which describe relationships among representations.

The obstacle addressed here is inference: learning from observations requires a flexible approximation to the posterior distribution over positive semidefinite matrices. The authors construct such a distribution by generalizing the Bartlett decomposition of the Wishart density. They use it to build an approximate posterior that includes dependencies between layers, allowing uncertainty at different depths to be represented together.

The paper also develops a doubly stochastic inference procedure using inducing points. Experiments show that inference with the deep Wishart process can outperform inference with a deep Gaussian process having the equivalent prior. This result highlights the importance of the inference formulation: matching prior assumptions does not imply that different approximate inference methods will achieve the same empirical performance.
summary.tldr: A flexible distribution over positive semidefinite matrices enables approximate inference in deep Wishart processes, with potential gains over equivalent-prior deep Gaussian processes.

title: A variational approximate posterior for the deep Wishart process

abstract: Recently many algorithms were devised for reinforcement learning (RL) with function approximation. While they have clear algorithmic distinctions, they also have many implementation differences that are algorithm-independent and sometimes under-emphasized. Such mixing of algorithmic novelty and implementation craftsmanship makes rigorous analyses of the sources of performance improvements across algorithms difficult. In this work, we focus on a series of off-policy inference-based actor-critic algorithms -- MPO, AWR, and SAC -- to decouple their algorithmic innovations and implementation decisions. We present unified derivations through a single control-as-inference objective, where we can categorize each algorithm as based on either Expectation-Maximization (EM) or direct Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence minimization and treat the rest of specifications as implementation details. We performed extensive ablation studies, and identified substantial performance drops whenever implementation details are mismatched for algorithmic choices. These results show which implementation or code details are co-adapted and co-evolved with algorithms, and which are transferable across algorithms: as examples, we identified that tanh Gaussian policy and network sizes are highly adapted to algorithmic types, while layer normalization and ELU are critical for MPO's performances but also transfer to noticeable gains in SAC. We hope our work can inspire future work to further demystify sources of performance improvements across multiple algorithms and allow researchers to build on one another's both algorithmic and implementational innovations.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning methods often differ both in their mathematical algorithms and in implementation choices. This paper studies MPO, AWR, and SAC to separate their underlying algorithmic distinctions from the implementation decisions that accompany them.

The authors derive all three from one control-as-inference objective. These findings show that some implementation improvements transfer, while others depend on their algorithmic context. The unified analysis helps explain why a successful component cannot always be evaluated independently of the method around it.
summary.tldr: A unified analysis of MPO, AWR, and SAC shows that implementation choices can be tightly adapted to particular algorithms, though some improvements transfer.

title: Co-Adaptation of Algorithmic and Implementational Innovations in Inference-based Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Methods for inference and simulation of linearly constrained Gaussian Markov Random Fields (GMRF) are computationally prohibitive when the number of constraints is large. In some cases, such as for intrinsic GMRFs, they may even be unfeasible. We propose a new class of methods to overcome these challenges in the common case of sparse constraints, where one has a large number of constraints and each only involves a few elements. Our methods rely on a basis transformation into blocks of constrained versus non-constrained subspaces, and we show that the methods greatly outperform existing alternatives in terms of computational cost. By combining the proposed methods with the stochastic partial differential equation approach for Gaussian random fields, we also show how to formulate Gaussian process regression with linear constraints in a GMRF setting to reduce computational cost. This is illustrated in two applications with simulated data.

paragraphs: Gaussian Markov random fields can be subject to linear constraints that their values must satisfy. Inference and simulation become computationally expensive when there are many such constraints, and existing approaches can be infeasible for intrinsic GMRFs. This paper targets the common situation where constraints are numerous but sparse: each one involves only a few elements.

The proposed methods change the basis used to represent the problem, separating constrained directions from unconstrained directions into distinct blocks. That separation provides a way to organize computation around which parts of the field the constraints affect. The authors show that their methods substantially reduce computational cost compared with existing alternatives in this setting.

The paper also connects this machinery to Gaussian process regression with linear constraints. By combining the methods with a stochastic partial differential equation approach for Gaussian random fields, the authors formulate that regression problem as a GMRF computation. Two applications using simulated data illustrate the approach. The shared contribution is making sparse constraint structure useful for reducing the cost of constrained probabilistic modeling.
summary.tldr: Separating constrained and unconstrained subspaces makes inference and simulation cheaper for Gaussian Markov random fields with many sparse linear constraints.

title: Efficient methods for Gaussian Markov random fields under sparse linear constraints

abstract: Thompson Sampling is one of the most effective methods for contextual bandits and has been generalized to posterior sampling for certain MDP settings. However, existing posterior sampling methods for reinforcement learning are limited by being model-based or lack worst-case theoretical guarantees beyond linear MDPs. This paper proposes a new model-free formulation of posterior sampling that applies to more general episodic reinforcement learning problems with theoretical guarantees. We introduce novel proof techniques to show that under suitable conditions, the worst-case regret of our posterior sampling method matches the best known results of optimization based methods. In the linear MDP setting with dimension, the regret of our algorithm scales linearly with the dimension as compared to a quadratic dependence of the existing posterior sampling-based exploration algorithms.

We introduce novel proof techniques to show that under suitable conditions, the worst-case regret of our posterior sampling method matches the best known results of optimization based methods. In the linear MDP setting with dimension, the regret of our algorithm scales linearly with the dimension as compared to a quadratic dependence of the existing posterior sampling-based exploration algorithms.

paragraphs: Posterior sampling uses uncertainty to guide exploration: an agent samples from its current beliefs and uses the result to choose how to act. Although this approach has been effective in contextual bandits, extending it to reinforcement learning introduces challenges. Existing approaches either rely on an environment model or lack worst-case guarantees beyond linear Markov decision processes.

This paper introduces a model-free formulation of posterior sampling for more general episodic reinforcement learning problems. Its central contribution combines the algorithmic formulation with new proof techniques. Under suitable conditions, the resulting worst-case regret matches the best known results for optimization-based methods. Regret measures the performance lost while learning, so this comparison concerns the cost of exploration.

For linear Markov decision processes, the algorithm’s regret grows linearly with the model dimension, improving on the quadratic dependence of existing posterior-sampling exploration algorithms. That result gives a specific theoretical advantage as dimension increases. The broader guarantee remains conditional on the paper’s suitable conditions; it is not a claim that posterior sampling attains these bounds in every reinforcement learning environment.
summary.tldr: A model-free posterior-sampling method obtains conditional worst-case regret guarantees and improves dimension dependence in linear reinforcement learning.

title: A Provably Efficient Model-Free Posterior Sampling Method for Episodic Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recent advances in localized implicit functions have enabled neural implicit representation to be scalable to large scenes.However, the regular subdivision of 3D space employed by these approaches fails to take into account the sparsity of the surface occupancy and the varying granularities of geometric details. As a result, its memory footprint grows cubically with the input volume, leading to a prohibitive computational cost even at a moderately dense decomposition. In this work, we present a learnable hierarchical implicit representation for 3D surfaces, coded OctField, that allows high-precision encoding of intricate surfaces with low memory and computational budget. The key to our approach is an adaptive decomposition of 3D scenes that only distributes local implicit functions around the surface of interest. We achieve this goal by introducing a hierarchical octree structure to adaptively subdivide the 3D space according to the surface occupancy and the richness of part geometry. As octree is discrete and non-differentiable, we further propose a novel hierarchical network that models the subdivision of octree cells as a probabilistic process and recursively encodes and decodes both octree structure and surface geometry in a differentiable manner. We demonstrate the value of OctField for a range of shape modeling and reconstruction tasks, showing superiority over alternative approaches.

paragraphs: Local implicit functions can represent large three-dimensional scenes, but regularly dividing all of space allocates resources inefficiently. Much of the volume may contain no surface, while different surface regions need different detail levels. The paper identifies this mismatch as a source of rapidly growing memory and computational costs.

OctField uses an adaptive octree hierarchy to place local implicit functions around relevant surfaces. It subdivides space according to both surface occupancy and geometric complexity. This allows intricate regions to receive finer representation while avoiding the same dense subdivision everywhere, supporting precise surface encoding with a low memory and computation budget.

Learning the hierarchy introduces a difficulty because discrete octree subdivisions are not differentiable. The authors address it with a hierarchical network that treats subdivision probabilistically and recursively encodes and decodes both structure and geometry in a differentiable way. Evaluations across shape modeling and reconstruction tasks show advantages over alternative approaches. The contribution joins adaptive spatial allocation with a learnable representation of the surface itself.
summary.tldr: OctField learns an adaptive octree of local implicit functions to represent detailed 3D surfaces with reduced memory and computation.

title: OctField: Hierarchical Implicit Functions for 3D Modeling

abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a sample-efficient approach to optimizing costly-to-evaluate black-box functions. Most BO methods ignore how evaluation costs may vary over the optimization domain. However, these costs can be highly heterogeneous and are often unknown in advance in many practical settings, such as hyperparameter tuning of machine learning algorithms or physics-based simulation optimization. Moreover, those few existing methods that acknowledge cost heterogeneity do not naturally accommodate a budget constraint on the total evaluation cost. This combination of unknown costs and a budget constraint introduces a new dimension to the exploration-exploitation trade-off, where learning about the cost incurs a cost itself. Existing methods do not reason about the various trade-offs of this problem in a principled way, leading often to poor performance. We formalize this claim by proving that the expected improvement and the expected improvement per unit of cost, arguably the two most widely used acquisition functions in practice, can be arbitrarily inferior with respect to the optimal non-myopic policy. To overcome the shortcomings of existing approaches, we propose the budgeted multi-step expected improvement, a non-myopic acquisition function that generalizes classical expected improvement to the setting of heterogeneous and unknown evaluation costs. We show that our acquisition function outperforms existing methods in a variety of synthetic and real problems.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good inputs to functions that are expensive to evaluate. This paper considers a complication: different inputs can cost different amounts to evaluate, those costs may be unknown, and the total search must respect a budget. Learning which evaluations are affordable therefore consumes some of the same resources needed to improve the objective.

The authors show that expected improvement and expected improvement per unit cost can be arbitrarily worse than an optimal policy that considers future decisions. This is a possibility result about their shortcomings, rather than a claim that they always perform poorly. It motivates an acquisition function that reasons beyond the immediate next evaluation.

The proposed budgeted multi-step expected improvement extends classical expected improvement to unknown, heterogeneous costs under a budget. Its forward-looking structure accounts for how a current evaluation affects later opportunities. Experiments on synthetic and real problems show it outperforming existing methods. The contribution is a way to make evaluation cost, uncertainty about that cost, and remaining search opportunities part of one decision rule.
summary.tldr: Budgeted multi-step expected improvement plans Bayesian-optimization evaluations ahead while accounting for unknown costs and a total budget.

title: Multi-Step Budgeted Bayesian Optimization with Unknown Evaluation Costs

abstract: Diffusion-based generative models have demonstrated a capacity for perceptually impressive synthesis, but can they also be great likelihood-based models? We answer this in the affirmative, and introduce a family of diffusion-based generative models that obtain state-of-the-art likelihoods on standard image density estimation benchmarks. Unlike other diffusion-based models, our method allows for efficient optimization of the noise schedule jointly with the rest of the model. We show that the variational lower bound (VLB) simplifies to a remarkably short expression in terms of the signal-to-noise ratio of the diffused data, thereby improving our theoretical understanding of this model class. Using this insight, we prove an equivalence between several models proposed in the literature. In addition, we show that the continuous-time VLB is invariant to the noise schedule, except for the signal-to-noise ratio at its endpoints. This enables us to learn a noise schedule that minimizes the variance of the resulting VLB estimator, leading to faster optimization. Combining these advances with architectural improvements, we obtain state-of-the-art likelihoods on image density estimation benchmarks, outperforming autoregressive models that have dominated these benchmarks for many years, with often significantly faster optimization. In addition, we show how to use the model as part of a bits-back compression scheme, and demonstrate lossless compression rates close to the theoretical optimum.

title: Variational Diffusion Models

abstract: Mean estimation under differential privacy is a fundamental problem, but worst-case optimal mechanisms do not offer meaningful utility guarantees in practice when the global sensitivity is very large. Instead, various heuristics have been proposed to reduce the error on real-world data that do not resemble the worst-case instance. This paper takes a principled approach, yielding a mechanism that is instance-optimal in a strong sense. In addition to its theoretical optimality, the mechanism is also simple and practical, and adapts to a variety of data characteristics without the need of parameter tuning. It easily extends to the local and shuffle model as well.

paragraphs: Estimating an average while protecting individual data is a fundamental task in differential privacy. A difficulty arises when global sensitivity is very large: mechanisms optimized for the worst case can provide utility guarantees that say little about the particular dataset being analyzed. Real-world data may differ substantially from the instances driving those worst-case guarantees.

The paper develops a principled mechanism with a strong instance-optimality guarantee. Its focus is therefore on accuracy relative to the individual data instance, addressing the motivation behind heuristics that try to reduce error on more favorable datasets. The theoretical contribution gives this adaptation an optimality foundation rather than relying only on a practical rule of thumb.

The authors also describe the mechanism as simple and practical. It adapts to multiple data characteristics without requiring parameter tuning, connecting the theoretical goal to ease of use. The approach extends to local and shuffle privacy models as well. Together, these properties make the contribution about both instance-sensitive accuracy guarantees and a mechanism intended to be usable across privacy settings.
summary.tldr: A practical private mean estimator provides strong instance-optimality guarantees and adapts to data characteristics without parameter tuning.

title: Instance-optimal Mean Estimation Under Differential Privacy

abstract: We study piece-wise constant signals corrupted by additive Gaussian noise over a $d$-dimensional lattice. Data of this form naturally arise in a host of applications, and the tasks of signal detection or testing, de-noising and estimation have been studied extensively in the statistical and signal processing literature. In this paper we consider instead the problem of partition recovery, i.e.~of estimating the partition of the lattice induced by the constancy regions of the unknown signal, using the computationally-efficient dyadic classification and regression tree (DCART) methodology proposed by \citep{donoho1997cart}. We prove that, under appropriate regularity conditions on the shape of the partition elements, a DCART-based procedure consistently estimates the underlying partition at a rate of order $\sigma^2 k^* \log (N)/\kappa^2$, where $k^*$ is the minimal number of rectangular sub-graphs obtained using recursive dyadic partitions supporting the signal partition, $\sigma^2$ is the noise variance, $\kappa$ is the minimal magnitude of the signal difference among contiguous elements of the partition and $N$ is the size of the lattice. Furthermore, under stronger assumptions, our method attains a sharper estimation error of order $\sigma^2\log(N)/\kappa^2$, independent of $k^*$, which we show to be minimax rate optimal. Our theoretical guarantees further extend to the partition estimator based on the optimal regression tree estimator (ORT) of \cite{chatterjee2019adaptive} and to the one obtained through an NP-hard exhaustive search method. We corroborate our theoretical findings and the effectiveness of DCART for partition recovery in simulations.

paragraphs: This paper studies signals that stay constant within regions of a multidimensional grid but are observed with additive Gaussian noise. Its goal is to recover the regions themselves. That makes the task about identifying the underlying partition, beyond estimating a denoised signal value at each grid location.

This means the sharper rate matches the best worst-case rate for the relevant setting. The theoretical guarantees also extend to two other partition estimators. Simulations support both the analysis and the effectiveness of the dyadic-tree procedure for recovering partitions.
summary.tldr: A dyadic-tree procedure recovers constant-valued regions in noisy grids, with minimax-optimal error rates under stronger assumptions.

title: Lattice partition recovery with dyadic CART

abstract: In recent years, several results in the supervised learning setting suggested that classical statistical learning-theoretic measures, such as VC dimension, do not adequately explain the performance of deep learning models which prompted a slew of work in the infinite-width and iteration regimes. However, there is little theoretical explanation for the success of neural networks beyond the supervised setting. In this paper we argue that, under some distributional assumptions, classical learning-theoretic measures can sufficiently explain generalization for graph neural networks in the transductive setting. In particular, we provide a rigorous analysis of the performance of neural networks in the context of transductive inference, specifically by analysing the generalisation properties of graph convolutional networks for the problem of node classification. While VC-dimension does result in trivial generalisation error bounds in this setting as well, we show that transductive Rademacher complexity can explain the generalisation properties of graph convolutional networks for stochastic block models. We further use the generalisation error bounds based on transductive Rademacher complexity to demonstrate the role of graph convolutions and network architectures in achieving smaller generalisation error and provide insights into when the graph structure can help in learning. The findings of this paper could re-new the interest in studying generalisation in neural networks in terms of learning-theoretic measures, albeit in specific problems.

paragraphs: Classical learning theory has often struggled to explain the generalization of deep networks. This paper asks whether those tools can still be informative for graph neural networks in a particular setting: transductive node classification. Here, the analysis concerns predicting labels within the graph under study, rather than only the usual supervised-learning formulation.

The authors analyze graph convolutional networks under distributional assumptions involving stochastic block models. VC dimension still yields trivial error bounds in this setting. However, another classical measure, transductive Rademacher complexity, produces bounds that can explain generalization. The result therefore depends on both the complexity measure chosen and the structure assumed for the graph distribution.

The bounds also reveal how graph convolutions and network architecture can contribute to smaller generalization error. This provides insight into circumstances where graph structure helps learning. The paper’s broader message is qualified: classical measures can sufficiently explain performance for some graph-learning problems, making them useful analytical tools within suitable settings rather than a universal account of neural-network generalization.
summary.tldr: Under stochastic-block-model assumptions, transductive Rademacher complexity can explain aspects of graph convolutional networks’ generalization.

title: Learning Theory Can (Sometimes) Explain Generalisation in Graph Neural Networks

abstract: We propose AdaTS, a Thompson sampling algorithm that adapts sequentially to bandit tasks that it interacts with. The key idea in AdaTS is to adapt to an unknown task prior distribution by maintaining a distribution over its parameters. When solving a bandit task, that uncertainty is marginalized out and properly accounted for. AdaTS is a fully-Bayesian algorithm that can be implemented efficiently in several classes of bandit problems. We derive upper bounds on its Bayes regret that quantify the loss due to not knowing the task prior, and show that it is small. Our theory is supported by experiments, where AdaTS outperforms prior algorithms and works well even in challenging real-world problems.
