paragraphs: A learner facing a sequence of bandit tasks can use experience from earlier tasks to inform later decisions. The difficulty is that the distribution generating those tasks may itself be unknown. This paper introduces AdaTS, a Thompson sampling algorithm that adapts as it interacts with successive tasks while tracking uncertainty about that task distribution.

AdaTS maintains a distribution over the parameters of the unknown task prior. When solving a particular task, it averages over this uncertainty rather than treating one estimated prior as certain. This makes the algorithm fully Bayesian and ensures that uncertainty about the shared prior enters its decisions. The authors describe efficient implementations for several classes of bandit problems.

The theoretical analysis gives upper bounds on Bayes regret that explicitly quantify the cost of not knowing the task prior and show that this cost is small. Experiments support the theory: AdaTS outperforms prior algorithms in the reported comparisons and performs well on challenging real-world problems. The contribution connects learning across tasks with a formal account of the price paid while the shared prior is still uncertain.
summary.tldr: AdaTS learns an unknown bandit-task prior while accounting for its uncertainty, with regret bounds showing a small cost for learning that prior.

title: No Regrets for Learning the Prior in Bandits

abstract: The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture is showing promising results in improving parameter sharing in multi-task learning (MTL) and in scaling high-capacity neural networks. State-of-the-art MoE models use a trainable "sparse gate'" to select a subset of the experts for each input example. While conceptually appealing, existing sparse gates, such as Top-k, are not smooth. The lack of smoothness can lead to convergence and statistical performance issues when training with gradient-based methods. In this paper, we develop DSelect-k: a continuously differentiable and sparse gate for MoE, based on a novel binary encoding formulation. The gate can be trained using first-order methods, such as stochastic gradient descent, and offers explicit control over the number of experts to select. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DSelect-k on both synthetic and real MTL datasets with up to 128 tasks. Our experiments indicate that DSelect-k can achieve statistically significant improvements in prediction and expert selection over popular MoE gates. Notably, on a real-world, large-scale recommender system, DSelect-k achieves over 22% improvement in predictive performance compared to Top-k. We provide an open-source implementation of DSelect-k.

paragraphs: A mixture-of-experts model routes each input to a selection of specialized networks. In multi-task learning, this provides a way to share model capacity across tasks while allowing different inputs to use different experts. The routing rule matters: popular sparse gates such as Top-k are not smooth, which can create difficulties for gradient-based optimization and prediction quality.

DSelect-k replaces that routing rule with a sparse gate that is continuously differentiable. Its binary encoding formulation allows training with first-order methods such as stochastic gradient descent while explicitly controlling how many experts are selected. The approach therefore addresses the interaction between discrete expert selection and the smooth updates used to train the surrounding network.

The authors evaluate the gate on synthetic and real multi-task datasets containing up to 128 tasks. They report statistically significant improvements in prediction and expert selection over popular gates. In a large recommender system, predictive performance improves by more than 22% relative to Top-k. These are empirical findings from the studied settings, supporting differentiable routing as a useful design choice.
summary.tldr: DSelect-k makes sparse expert selection continuously differentiable while controlling the number of selected experts, with reported gains in multi-task learning.

title: DSelect-k: Differentiable Selection in the Mixture of Experts with Applications to Multi-Task Learning

abstract: The unbiased learning to rank (ULTR) problem has been greatly advanced by recent deep learning techniques and well-designed debias algorithms. However, promising results on the existing benchmark datasets may not be extended to the practical scenario due to some limitations of existing datasets. First, their semantic feature extractions are outdated while state-of-the-art large-scale pre-trained language models like BERT cannot be utilized due to the lack of original text. Second, display features are incomplete; thus in-depth study on ULTR is impossible such as the displayed abstract for analyzing the click necessary bias. Third, synthetic user feedback has been adopted by most existing datasets and real-world user feedback is greatly missing. To overcome these disadvantages, we introduce the Baidu-ULTR dataset. It involves randomly sampled 1.2 billion searching sessions and 7,008 expert annotated queries(397,572 query document pairs). Baidu-ULTR is the first billion-level dataset for ULTR. Particularly, it offers: (1)the original semantic features and pre-trained language models of different sizes; (2)sufficient display information such as position, displayed height, and displayed abstract, enabling the comprehensive study of multiple displayed biases; and (3)rich user feedback on search result pages (SERPs) like dwelling time, allowing for user engagement optimization and promoting the exploration of multi-task learning in ULTR. Furthermore, we present the design principle of Baidu-ULTR and the performance of representative ULTR algorithms on Baidu-ULTR. The Baidu-ULTR dataset and corresponding baseline implementations are available at https://github.com/ChuXiaokai/baidu_ultr_dataset. The dataset homepage is available at https://searchscience.baidu.com/dataset.html.

paragraphs: Search rankings influence which results users notice and click, so user feedback can reflect presentation as well as relevance. This paper introduces Baidu-ULTR, a dataset intended to support research on learning rankings from such biased feedback. It addresses three shortcomings of existing benchmarks: missing original text, incomplete information about result presentation, and heavy reliance on simulated user behavior.

The dataset contains 1.2 billion randomly sampled search sessions and expert annotations for 7,008 queries, covering 397,572 query-document pairs. It supplies original semantic information and pretrained language models of different sizes. Researchers can therefore study text representations alongside the ranking problem, rather than relying entirely on previously extracted features.

Its display information includes result position, displayed height, and displayed abstracts. Recorded user behavior includes dwelling time, supporting investigation of engagement beyond clicks. The paper also presents dataset design principles and evaluates representative ranking algorithms. Its central contribution is a large empirical resource for studying several interacting sources of bias using real search feedback.
summary.tldr: Baidu-ULTR provides billion-scale search feedback, original text, and display information for studying unbiased learning to rank.

title: A Large Scale Search Dataset for Unbiased Learning to Rank

abstract: Decentralized optimization are playing an important role in applications such as training large machine learning models, among others. Despite its superior practical performance, there has been some lack of fundamental understanding about its theoretical properties. In this work, we address the following open research question: To train an overparameterized model over a set of distributed nodes, what is the {\it minimum} communication overhead (in terms of the bits got exchanged) that the system needs to sustain, while still achieving (near) zero training loss? We show that for a class of overparameterized models where the number of parameters $D$ is much larger than the total data samples $N$, the best possible communication complexity is ${\Omega}(N)$, which is independent of the problem dimension $D$. Further, for a few specific overparameterized models (i.e., the linear regression, and certain multi-layer neural network with one wide layer), we develop a set of algorithms which uses certain linear compression followed by adaptive quantization, and show that they achieve dimension independent, and sometimes near optimal, communication complexity. To our knowledge, this is the first time that dimension independent communication complexity has been shown for distributed optimization.

paragraphs: Training a large model across distributed machines requires exchanging information, but the number of model parameters may greatly exceed the number of training examples. This paper asks how many communication bits are fundamentally needed to reach zero or nearly zero training loss in such overparameterized problems.

For a class of models with far more parameters D than data samples N, the authors establish a lower bound proportional to N. This lower bound does not depend on D. It identifies a fundamental communication requirement tied to the amount of training data, providing a target for algorithms that avoid costs scaling with every model parameter.

The paper then develops algorithms for linear regression and certain multilayer neural networks containing one wide layer. These methods combine linear compression with adaptive quantization and achieve communication complexity independent of parameter dimension, sometimes approaching the lower bound. The results establish that dimension-independent communication is attainable for the specified models. They do not assert the same algorithmic guarantee for every overparameterized architecture.
summary.tldr: For specified overparameterized models, compression and adaptive quantization enable distributed training with communication costs independent of parameter count.

title: Distributed Optimization for Overparameterized Problems: Achieving Optimal Dimension Independent Communication Complexity

abstract: Social media has become the fulcrum of all forms of communication. Classifying social texts such as fake news, rumour, sarcasm, etc. has gained significant attention. The surface-level signals expressed by a social-text itself may not be adequate for such tasks; therefore, recent methods attempted to incorporate other intrinsic signals such as user behavior and the underlying graph structure. Oftentimes, the public wisdom expressed through the comments/replies to a social-text acts as a surrogate of crowd-sourced view and may provide us with complementary signals. State-of-the-art methods on social-text classification tend to ignore such a rich hierarchical signal. Here, we propose Hyphen, a discourse-aware hyperbolic spectral co-attention network. Hyphen is a fusion of hyperbolic graph representation learning with a novel Fourier co-attention mechanism in an attempt to generalise the social-text classification tasks by incorporating public discourse. We parse public discourse as an Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) graph and use the powerful hyperbolic geometric representation to model graphs with hierarchical structure. Finally, we equip it with a novel Fourier co-attention mechanism to capture the correlation between the source post and public discourse. Extensive experiments on four different social-text classification tasks, namely detecting fake news, hate speech, rumour, and sarcasm, show that Hyphen generalises well, and achieves state-of-the-art results on ten benchmark datasets. We also employ a sentence-level fact-checked and annotated dataset to evaluate how Hyphen is capable of producing explanations as analogous evidence to the final prediction.

summary.tldr: Hyphen combines source posts with structured public discussion to improve classification across four social-text tasks.

title: Public Wisdom Matters! Discourse-Aware Hyperbolic Fourier Co-Attention for Social Text Classification

abstract: A fundamental property of deep learning normalization techniques, such as batch normalization, is making the pre-normalization parameters scale invariant. The intrinsic domain of such parameters is the unit sphere, and therefore their gradient optimization dynamics can be represented via spherical optimization with varying effective learning rate (ELR), which was studied previously. However, the varying ELR may obscure certain characteristics of the intrinsic loss landscape structure. In this work, we investigate the properties of training scale-invariant neural networks directly on the sphere using a fixed ELR. We discover three regimes of such training depending on the ELR value: convergence, chaotic equilibrium, and divergence. We study these regimes in detail both on a theoretical examination of a toy example and on a thorough empirical analysis of real scale-invariant deep learning models. Each regime has unique features and reflects specific properties of the intrinsic loss landscape, some of which have strong parallels with previous research on both regular and scale-invariant neural networks training. Finally, we demonstrate how the discovered regimes are reflected in conventional training of normalized networks and how they can be leveraged to achieve better optima.

Depending on its value, the authors identify three regimes: convergence, chaotic equilibrium, and divergence. They investigate these behaviors through a theoretical toy example and a detailed empirical analysis of real scale-invariant deep learning models.

Each regime exposes different features of the intrinsic loss landscape, with parallels to earlier findings on both ordinary and scale-invariant network training. The authors also show how the regimes appear in conventional training of normalized networks and how knowledge of them can help reach better optima. Fixing the effective learning rate thus serves both as an analytical tool and as a source of insight for training practice.
summary.tldr: Training scale-invariant networks at fixed effective learning rates reveals convergence, chaotic equilibrium, and divergence regimes.

title: Training Scale-Invariant Neural Networks on the Sphere Can Happen in Three Regimes

abstract: We introduce point affiliation into feature upsampling, a notion that describes the affiliation of each upsampled point to a semantic cluster formed by local decoder feature points with semantic similarity. By rethinking point affiliation, we present a generic formulation for generating upsampling kernels. The kernels encourage not only semantic smoothness but also boundary sharpness in the upsampled feature maps. Such properties are particularly useful for some dense prediction tasks such as semantic segmentation. The key idea of our formulation is to generate similarity-aware kernels by comparing the similarity between each encoder feature point and the spatially associated local region of decoder features. In this way, the encoder feature point can function as a cue to inform the semantic cluster of upsampled feature points. To embody the formulation, we further instantiate a lightweight upsampling operator, termed Similarity-Aware Point Affiliation (SAPA), and investigate its variants. SAPA invites consistent performance improvements on a number of dense prediction tasks, including semantic segmentation, object detection, depth estimation, and image matting. Code is available at: https://github.com/poppinace/sapa

paragraphs: Feature upsampling increases spatial resolution inside a prediction model. For dense prediction, the resulting features should remain coherent within semantic regions while preserving sharp boundaries between them. This paper introduces point affiliation: the assignment of an upsampled point to a local cluster of decoder features with similar semantic content.

The method constructs upsampling kernels by comparing an encoder feature at a location with nearby decoder features. That comparison supplies a cue about which semantic cluster the new point should belong to. The resulting similarity-aware kernels are designed to encourage both smooth regions and distinct boundaries in the expanded feature map.

The authors implement this formulation as a lightweight operator called SAPA and investigate variants of it. They report consistent improvements across semantic segmentation, object detection, depth estimation, and image matting. These results support the usefulness of semantic affiliation across several dense prediction tasks. The contribution is a general formulation for upsampling kernels together with a practical operator that instantiates it.
summary.tldr: SAPA uses encoder–decoder feature similarity to upsample coherent semantic regions while preserving boundaries.

title: SAPA: Similarity-Aware Point Affiliation for Feature Upsampling

abstract: The Transformer architecture is ubiquitously used as the building block of largescale autoregressive language models. However, finding architectures with the optimal trade-off between task performance (perplexity) and hardware constraints like peak memory utilization and latency is non-trivial. This is exacerbated by the proliferation of various hardware. We leverage the somewhat surprising empirical observation that the number of decoder parameters in autoregressive Transformers has a high rank correlation with task performance, irrespective of the architecture topology. This observation organically induces a simple Neural Architecture Search (NAS) algorithm that uses decoder parameters as a proxy for perplexity without need for any model training. The search phase of our training-free algorithm, dubbed Lightweight Transformer Search (LTS), can be run directly on target devices since it does not require GPUs. Using on-target device measurements, LTS extracts the Pareto-frontier of perplexity versus any hardware performance cost. We evaluate LTS on diverse devices from ARM CPUs to NVIDIA GPUs and two popular autoregressive Transformer backbones: GPT-2 and Transformer-XL. Results show that the perplexity of 16-layer GPT-2 and Transformer-XL can be achieved with up to 1.5×, 2.5× faster runtime and 1.2×, 2.0× lower peak memory utilization. When evaluated in zero and one-shot settings, LTS Pareto-frontier models achieve higher average accuracy compared to the 350M parameter OPT across 14 tasks, with up to 1.6× lower latency. LTS extracts the Pareto-frontier in under 3 hours while running on a commodity laptop. We effectively remove the carbon footprint of hundreds of GPU hours of training during search, offering a strong simple baseline for future NAS methods in autoregressive language modeling.

title: LiteTransformerSearch: Training-free Neural Architecture Search for Efficient Language Models

abstract: Visual object recognition has been extensively studied in both neuroscience and computer vision. Recently, the most popular class of artificial systems for this task, deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs), has been shown to provide excellent models for its functional analogue in the brain, the ventral stream in visual cortex. This has prompted questions on what, if any, are the common principles underlying the reformatting of visual information as it flows through a CNN or the ventral stream. Here we consider some prominent statistical patterns that are known to exist in the internal representations of either CNNs or the visual cortex and look for them in the other system. We show that intrinsic dimensionality (ID) of object representations along the rat homologue of the ventral stream presents two distinct expansion-contraction phases, as previously shown for CNNs. Conversely, in CNNs, we show that training results in both distillation and active pruning (mirroring the increase in ID) of low- to middle-level image information in single units, as representations gain the ability to support invariant discrimination, in agreement with previous observations in rat visual cortex. Taken together, our findings suggest that CNNs and visual cortex share a similarly tight relationship between dimensionality expansion/reduction of object representations and reformatting of image information.

paragraphs: This paper compares how visual information changes as it passes through convolutional neural networks and the rat visual cortex. Rather than considering only object-recognition performance, the authors investigate statistical patterns in internal representations. They look for patterns previously observed in one system within the other, seeking shared principles of information processing.

In the rat counterpart of the ventral visual stream, object representations show two phases of expansion and contraction in intrinsic dimensionality. This matches a pattern previously found in convolutional networks. They support a similarity in how the two systems transform representations, without establishing that their underlying mechanisms are identical.
summary.tldr: Rat visual cortex and convolutional networks exhibit similar relationships between representational dimensionality and the pruning and distillation of image information.

title: Prune and distill: similar reformatting of image information along rat visual cortex and deep neural networks

abstract: Impactful applications such as materials discovery, hardware design, neural architecture search, or portfolio optimization require optimizing high-dimensional black-box functions with mixed and combinatorial input spaces.While Bayesian optimization has recently made significant progress in solving such problems, an in-depth analysis reveals that the current state-of-the-art methods are not reliable. Their performances degrade substantially when the unknown optima of the function do not have a certain structure. To fill the need for a reliable algorithm for combinatorial and mixed spaces, this paper proposes Bounce that relies on a novel map of various variable types into nested embeddings of increasing dimensionality.Comprehensive experiments show that Bounce reliably achieves and often even improves upon state-of-the-art performance on a variety of high-dimensional problems.

paragraphs: Bounce tackles optimization problems with many input variables, including combinations of discrete choices and other variable types. Such problems arise in applications including materials discovery, hardware design, neural architecture search, and portfolio optimization. The objective is treated as a black box, so the optimizer must search without relying on an explicit formula for its behavior.

The paper first identifies a reliability problem in leading Bayesian optimization methods. Their performance can decline substantially when the unknown best solution lacks a particular structure. This means that strong performance on some problems may depend on properties of the optimum that are unavailable to the optimizer beforehand.

Bounce introduces a mapping of different variable types into nested embeddings whose dimensionality increases. This supplies a common search construction for combinatorial and mixed spaces. Across the reported high-dimensional experiments, Bounce consistently reaches, and often exceeds, state-of-the-art performance. The findings support its empirical reliability across varied problems, addressing the structural sensitivity highlighted by the authors’ analysis.
summary.tldr: Bounce uses nested embeddings of increasing dimensionality to make Bayesian optimization more reliable across high-dimensional combinatorial and mixed-variable problems.

title: Bounce: Reliable High-Dimensional Bayesian Optimization for Combinatorial and Mixed Spaces

abstract: Machine learning provides a valuable tool for analyzing high-dimensional functional neuroimaging data, and is proving effective in predicting various neurological conditions, psychiatric disorders, and cognitive patterns. In functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) research, interactions between brain regions are commonly modeled using graph-based representations. The potency of graph machine learning methods has been established across myriad domains, marking a transformative step in data interpretation and predictive modeling. Yet, despite their promise, the transposition of these techniques to the neuroimaging domain has been challenging due to the expansive number of potential preprocessing pipelines and the large parameter search space for graph-based dataset construction. In this paper, we introduce NeuroGraph, a collection of graph-based neuroimaging datasets, and demonstrated its utility for predicting multiple categories of behavioral and cognitive traits. We delve deeply into the dataset generation search space by crafting 35 datasets that encompass static and dynamic brain connectivity, running in excess of 15 baseline methods for benchmarking. Additionally, we provide generic frameworks for learning on both static and dynamic graphs. Our extensive experiments lead to several key observations. Notably, using correlation vectors as node features, incorporating larger number of regions of interest, and employing sparser graphs lead to improved performance. To foster further advancements in graph-based data driven neuroimaging analysis, we offer a comprehensive open-source Python package that includes the benchmark datasets, baseline implementations, model training, and standard evaluation.

paragraphs: Functional brain imaging can be represented as a graph, with brain regions connected according to their interactions. However, choices about preprocessing and graph construction create a large design space. NeuroGraph provides a benchmark collection for investigating these choices and evaluating graph-based prediction of behavioral and cognitive traits.

The authors construct 35 datasets covering both static connectivity and connectivity that changes over time. They benchmark more than 15 baseline methods and provide general frameworks for learning from static and dynamic graphs. These are empirical findings from the studied settings rather than universal prescriptions for every neuroimaging task. An accompanying Python package brings together datasets, baseline implementations, training, and standardized evaluation, providing a shared basis for subsequent research in graph-based neuroimaging analysis.
summary.tldr: NeuroGraph benchmarks brain-connectivity graph construction and learning methods across 35 datasets for behavioral and cognitive prediction.

title: NeuroGraph: Benchmarks for Graph Machine Learning in Brain Connectomics

abstract: Diffusion-based manifold learning methods have proven useful in representation learning and dimensionality reduction of modern high dimensional, high throughput, noisy datasets. Such datasets are especially present in fields like biology and physics. While it is thought that these methods preserve underlying manifold structure of data by learning a proxy for geodesic distances, no specific theoretical links have been established. Here, we establish such a link via results in Riemannian geometry explicitly connecting heat diffusion to manifold distances. In this process, we also formulate a more general heat kernel based manifold embedding method that we call heat geodesic embeddings. This novel perspective makes clearer the choices available in manifold learning and denoising. Results show that our method outperforms existing state of the art in preserving ground truth manifold distances, and preserving cluster structure in toy datasets. We also showcase our method on single cell RNA-sequencing datasets with both continuum and cluster structure, where our method enables interpolation of withheld timepoints of data. Finally, we show that parameters of our more general method can be configured to give results similar to PHATE (a state-of-the-art diffusion based manifold learning method) as well as SNE (an attraction/repulsion neighborhood based method that forms the basis of t-SNE).

paragraphs: Dimensionality reduction compresses complex data into a smaller representation while trying to retain meaningful relationships. For data organized along a curved manifold, distances along that manifold can matter more than direct distances through the surrounding space. Diffusion-based methods were thought to preserve this geometry, but the abstract identifies a missing theoretical connection between their diffusion calculations and manifold distances.

The paper supplies that connection using results from Riemannian geometry that relate heat diffusion to distance. It also introduces heat geodesic embeddings, a more general embedding method based on heat kernels. This perspective makes the choices involved in representing and denoising data more explicit, grounding the embedding procedure in a relationship between how heat spreads and the geometry it spreads across.

Reported results show improved preservation of known manifold distances and cluster structure in toy datasets. On single-cell RNA-sequencing data containing both continuous variation and clusters, the method supports interpolation of withheld timepoints. Different parameter choices also produce results resembling PHATE and SNE, connecting these established approaches within the broader proposed framework.
summary.tldr: Heat geodesic embeddings connect diffusion to manifold distances and improve geometric preservation in the reported dimensionality-reduction experiments.

title: A Heat Diffusion Perspective on Geodesic Preserving Dimensionality Reduction

abstract: Adaptive methods with non-diagonal preconditioning have shown state-of-the-art results on various tasks. However, their computational complexity and memory requirement makes it challenging to scale these methods to modern neural network architectures. To address this challenge, some previous works have adopted block-diagonal preconditioners. However, the memory cost of storing the block-diagonal matrix remains substantial, leading to the use of smaller block sizes and ultimately resulting in suboptimal performance. To reduce the time and memory complexity without sacrificing performance, we propose approximating each diagonal block of the second moment matrix by low-rank matrices and enforcing the same basis for the blocks within each layer. We provide theoretical justification for such sharing and design an algorithm to efficiently maintain this shared-basis block low-rank approximation during training. Our results on a deep autoencoder and a transformer benchmark demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms first-order methods with slightly more time and memory usage, while also achieving competitive or superior performance compared to other second-order methods with less time and memory usage.

paragraphs: Some adaptive optimization methods improve training by using matrices that account for relationships between parameter updates. However, storing and updating these matrices can consume substantial memory and computation. Dividing them into diagonal blocks reduces the burden, but the remaining storage cost can force small blocks that weaken performance.

The paper proposes representing each block of the second-moment matrix with a low-rank approximation. It also makes blocks within the same layer share a basis: a common set of directions used to represent their information. This adds another way to reduce storage and computation. The authors provide a theoretical justification for sharing and an algorithm that maintains the approximation during training.

Experiments on a deep autoencoder and a transformer benchmark show a favorable performance-resource balance. The method outperforms first-order alternatives while using slightly more time and memory. Compared with other second-order methods, it achieves competitive or better performance with lower resource use. These results support shared representations as a practical way to retain useful preconditioning information more efficiently.
summary.tldr: Sharing a basis across low-rank preconditioner blocks reduces optimization costs while preserving strong performance in the reported benchmarks.

title: Block Low-Rank Preconditioner with Shared Basis for Stochastic Optimization

abstract: Visual Query Localization on long-form egocentric videos requires spatio-temporal search and localization of visually specified objects and is vital to build episodic memory systems. Prior work develops complex multi-stage pipelines that leverage well-established object detection and tracking methods to perform VQL. However, each stage is independently trained and the complexity of the pipeline results in slow inference speeds. We propose VQLoC, a novel single-stage VQL framework that is end-to-end trainable. Our key idea is to first build a holistic understanding of the query-video relationship and then perform spatio-temporal localization in a single shot manner. Specifically, we establish the query-video relationship by jointly considering query-to-frame correspondences between the query and each video frame and frame-to-frame correspondences between nearby video frames. Our experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms prior VQL methods by $20$% accuracy while obtaining a $10\times$ improvement in inference speed. VQLoC is also the top entry on the Ego4D VQ2D challenge leaderboard.

paragraphs: Visual query localization asks where and when a visually specified object appears in a long first-person video. This capability matters for episodic-memory systems that must retrieve past visual experiences. Existing approaches combine several independently trained detection and tracking stages, creating complex pipelines with slow inference.

VQLoC replaces that arrangement with a single-stage framework trained end to end. It first builds a joint understanding of the query and video by considering two kinds of correspondence: matches between the query and individual frames, and relationships between nearby frames. It then uses that combined information to localize the object across space and time in one shot.

The experiments report a 20% accuracy improvement over prior visual-query localization methods alongside a tenfold inference-speed improvement. The abstract also reports VQLoC as the leading entry on the Ego4D VQ2D challenge leaderboard. These results support jointly modeling object appearance and temporal relationships within a unified system, with the evaluated method improving both localization performance and the speed of producing an answer.
summary.tldr: VQLoC jointly models query-to-frame and frame-to-frame relationships, reporting better localization accuracy and tenfold faster inference than prior methods.

title: Single-Stage Visual Query Localization in Egocentric Videos

abstract: We propose a novel framework for analyzing the dynamics of distribution shift in real-world systems that captures the feedback loop between learning algorithms and the distributions on which they are deployed. Prior work largely models feedback-induced distribution shift as adversarial or via an overly simplistic distribution-shift structure. In contrast, we propose a coupled partial differential equation model that captures fine-grained changes in the distribution over time by accounting for complex dynamics that arise due to strategic responses to algorithmic decision-making, non-local endogenous population interactions, and other exogenous sources of distribution shift. We consider two common settings in machine learning: cooperative settings with information asymmetries, and competitive settings where a learner faces strategic users. For both of these settings, when the algorithm retrains via gradient descent, we prove asymptotic convergence of the retraining procedure to a steady-state, both in finite and in infinite dimensions, obtaining explicit rates in terms of the model parameters. To do so we derive new results on the convergence of coupled PDEs that extends what is known on multi-species systems. Empirically, we show that our approach captures well-documented forms of distribution shifts like polarization and disparate impacts that simpler models cannot capture.

paragraphs: A deployed learning algorithm can change the behavior of the population it evaluates, which then changes the data used for retraining. This paper models that feedback using coupled partial differential equations. The framework includes strategic reactions to decisions, interactions across the population, and external sources of distribution shift.

The authors analyze two settings: cooperation with unequal access to information, and competition between a learner and strategic users. For both modeled settings, they prove that gradient-descent retraining converges asymptotically to a steady state. Their results cover finite and infinite dimensions and provide explicit convergence rates expressed through the model parameters.

Establishing these guarantees requires new convergence results for coupled equations, extending existing knowledge about multi-species systems. Empirically, the framework captures documented patterns such as polarization and disparate impacts that simpler models miss. Its contribution is therefore both analytical and descriptive: it characterizes long-run behavior in the studied systems while representing richer changes in population distributions over time.
summary.tldr: Coupled population and learning dynamics model strategic distribution shifts and yield convergence guarantees in the studied cooperative and competitive settings.

title: Strategic Distribution Shift of Interacting Agents via Coupled Gradient Flows

abstract: Various adaptation methods, such as LoRA, prompts, and adapters, have been proposed to enhance the performance of pre-trained vision-language models in specific domains. As test samples in real-world applications usually differ from adaptation data, the robustness of these adaptation methods against distribution shifts are essential. In this study, we assess the robustness of 11 widely-used adaptation methods across 4 vision-language datasets under multimodal corruptions. Concretely, we introduce 7 benchmark datasets, including 96 visual and 87 textual corruptions, to investigate the robustness of different adaptation methods, the impact of available adaptation examples, and the influence of trainable parameter size during adaptation. Our analysis reveals that: 1) Adaptation methods are more sensitive to text corruptions than visual corruptions. 2) Full fine-tuning does not consistently provide the highest robustness; instead, adapters can achieve better robustness with comparable clean performance. 3) Contrary to expectations, our findings indicate that increasing the number of adaptation data and parameters does not guarantee enhanced robustness; instead, it results in even lower robustness. We hope this study could benefit future research in the development of robust multimodal adaptation methods. The benchmark, code, and dataset used in this study can be accessed at https://adarobustness.github.io.

paragraphs: Adapting a pretrained vision-language model to a particular domain can improve its performance, but deployment inputs may differ from the adaptation examples. This paper examines whether commonly used adaptation methods remain reliable when images, text, or both are corrupted. It treats robustness as a separate concern from performance on clean inputs.

The study assesses 11 adaptation methods across four vision-language datasets. It introduces seven benchmark datasets containing 96 visual and 87 textual corruptions. Beyond comparing methods, the evaluation examines how robustness changes with the amount of adaptation data and the number of trainable parameters.

The tested methods are more sensitive to textual corruption than visual corruption. Full fine-tuning does not consistently deliver the strongest robustness; adapters can do better while achieving comparable clean performance. Increasing adaptation data or parameter counts also fails to guarantee improvement and produces lower robustness in the reported findings. These results show why adaptation choices need evaluation under distribution shifts, rather than selection based solely on clean performance or model flexibility.
summary.tldr: A corruption benchmark shows that more adaptation data, more trainable parameters, and full fine-tuning do not reliably improve vision-language robustness.

title: Benchmarking Robustness of Adaptation Methods on Pre-trained Vision-Language Models

This comes at no additional cost in terms of asymptotic computational complexity.

paragraphs: Filtering and smoothing in high-dimensional dynamical systems become expensive when they require full covariance matrices. This paper proposes an approximate Gaussian method that carries low-rank covariance representations through the computation. The aim is to reduce the cost of tracking uncertainty while retaining a controlled connection to the exact Kalman filter.

During prediction, the method projects the relevant Lyapunov equations onto a space of low-rank matrices and solves them with a numerically stable dynamical low-rank integrator. During updates, it exploits the fact that the covariance update transforms the matrix's column space, which is already low-rank. Unlike ensemble approaches, these approximations are deterministic.

As the retained dimension approaches the full problem dimension, the method can reproduce the exact Kalman filter. Its worst-case computational complexity is quadratic in state-space size rather than cubic, and becomes linear when the model satisfies additional criteria. In data-assimilation and spatio-temporal regression experiments, it consistently produces smaller mean and covariance errors relative to the exact filter than ensemble methods, without increasing asymptotic computational complexity.
summary.tldr: A deterministic low-rank Kalman approximation reduces computational cost and improves reported accuracy over ensemble methods.

title: The Rank-Reduced Kalman Filter: Approximate Dynamical-Low-Rank Filtering In High Dimensions

abstract: Many methods of semantic image segmentation have borrowed the success of open compound domain adaptation. They minimize the style gap between the images of source and target domains, more easily predicting the accurate pseudo annotations for target domain's images that train segmentation network. The existing methods globally adapt the scene style of the images, whereas the object styles of different categories or instances are adapted improperly. This paper proposes the Object Style Compensation, where we construct the Object-Level Discrepancy Memory with multiple sets of discrepancy features. The discrepancy features in a set capture the style changes of the same category's object instances adapted from target to source domains. We learn the discrepancy features from the images of source and target domains, storing the discrepancy features in memory. With this memory, we select appropriate discrepancy features for compensating the style information of the object instances of various categories, adapting the object styles to a unified style of source domain. Our method enables a more accurate computation of the pseudo annotations for target domain's images, thus yielding state-of-the-art results on different datasets.

Existing approaches reduce differences in overall scene style, but the paper argues that this can leave individual object categories or instances improperly adapted. A scene-level adjustment may therefore fail to address the style differences most relevant to an object.

Object Style Compensation introduces a memory containing sets of discrepancy features. Each set describes style changes for instances of the same category when adapting from the target domain toward the source domain. These features are learned from source and target images and stored for later use. The method selects suitable features from memory to compensate the style of individual objects.

This object-specific compensation aligns instances from different categories with the source domain’s style and improves the computation of target pseudo annotations. Those annotations then support segmentation training. The authors report state-of-the-art results across different datasets. The contribution is a more targeted adaptation mechanism: it represents and corrects category-specific style discrepancies that a global scene transformation can leave unresolved.
summary.tldr: Object Style Compensation uses a category-aware discrepancy memory to improve target-domain pseudo annotations and semantic segmentation.

title: Open Compound Domain Adaptation with Object Style Compensation for Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Automatic coding of International Classification of Diseases (ICD) is a multi-label text categorization task that involves extracting disease or procedure codes from clinical notes. Despite the application of state-of-the-art natural language processing (NLP) techniques, there are still challenges including limited availability of data due to privacy constraints and the high variability of clinical notes caused by different writing habits of medical professionals and various pathological features of patients. In this work, we investigate the semi-structured nature of clinical notes and propose an automatic algorithm to segment them into sections. To address the variability issues in existing ICD coding models with limited data, we introduce a contrastive pre-training approach on sections using a soft multi-label similarity metric based on tree edit distance. Additionally, we design a masked section training strategy to enable ICD coding models to locate sections related to ICD codes. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that our proposed training strategies effectively enhance the performance of existing ICD coding methods.

This paper uses the semi-structured organization of notes to help models handle that variation.

The authors first propose an algorithm that automatically divides notes into sections. They then pretrain on those sections using contrastive learning, with a soft multi-label similarity measure based on tree edit distance. This provides a structured way to compare training examples while accounting for their multiple labels, rather than treating every comparison as simply identical or unrelated.

A masked-section training strategy further helps coding models locate sections relevant to particular codes. Extensive experiments show that these training strategies improve existing ICD coding methods. The contribution is a way to make note structure useful throughout training: section-level comparisons support representation learning, and section masking encourages the model to identify the evidence associated with its coding decisions.
summary.tldr: Section-based contrastive pretraining and masked-section training improve automatic ICD coding from variable clinical notes.

title: Towards Semi-Structured Automatic ICD Coding via Tree-based Contrastive Learning

abstract: Specifying reward signals that allow agents to learn complex behaviors is a long-standing challenge in reinforcement learning.A promising approach is to extract preferences for behaviors from unlabeled videos, which are widely available on the internet. We present Video Prediction Rewards (VIPER), an algorithm that leverages pretrained video prediction models as action-free reward signals for reinforcement learning. Specifically, we first train an autoregressive transformer on expert videos and then use the video prediction likelihoods as reward signals for a reinforcement learning agent. VIPER enables expert-level control without programmatic task rewards across a wide range of DMC, Atari, and RLBench tasks. Moreover, generalization of the video prediction model allows us to derive rewards for an out-of-distribution environment where no expert data is available, enabling cross-embodiment generalization for tabletop manipulation. We see our work as starting point for scalable reward specification from unlabeled videos that will benefit from the rapid advances in generative modeling. Source code and datasets are available on the project website: https://ViperRL.com

paragraphs: VIPER addresses the difficulty of specifying rewards for complex behavior. It uses expert videos to learn a reward signal without requiring action labels in those videos. The central idea is to turn a model of how expert video sequences unfold into feedback that a reinforcement-learning agent can use while learning control.

The method first trains an autoregressive transformer to predict expert videos. It then uses the likelihoods supplied by that video prediction model as rewards. This connects generative modeling directly to reward specification: the learned model supplies the training signal instead of requiring a programmatic task reward for each behavior.

The authors report expert-level control across a range of DMC, Atari, and RLBench tasks. They also show that a video model’s generalization can provide rewards in an out-of-distribution environment without expert data from that environment, enabling cross-embodiment transfer for tabletop manipulation. The findings support video prediction as a useful source of rewards, including a demonstrated case where the reward model transfers beyond its expert-data setting.
summary.tldr: VIPER turns expert-video prediction likelihoods into reinforcement-learning rewards, enabling expert-level control and demonstrated cross-embodiment transfer.

title: Video Prediction Models as Rewards for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Generalization remains a central challenge in machine learning. In this work, we propose *Learning from Teaching* (**LoT**), a novel regularization technique for deep neural networks to enhance generalization. Inspired by the human ability to capture concise and abstract patterns, we hypothesize that generalizable correlations are expected to be easier to imitate. LoT operationalizes this concept to improve the generalization of the main model with auxiliary student learners. The student learners are trained by the main model and, in turn, provide feedback to help the main model capture more generalizable and imitable correlations. Our experimental results across several domains, including Computer Vision, Natural Language Processing, and methodologies like Reinforcement Learning, demonstrate that the introduction of LoT brings significant benefits compared to training models on the original dataset. The results suggest the effectiveness and efficiency of LoT in identifying generalizable information at the right scales while discarding spurious data correlations, thus making LoT a valuable addition to current machine learning. Code is available at https://github.com/jincan333/LoT.

paragraphs: Learning from Teaching, or LoT, is a regularization method intended to help neural networks generalize beyond their training data. Its starting hypothesis is that useful, generalizable relationships should be relatively easy for another learner to imitate. This turns teachability into a possible signal for improving the model being trained.

The method introduces auxiliary student learners that learn from the main model. Their learning then provides feedback to that model, encouraging it to capture relationships that are both imitable and generalizable. Teaching is therefore part of the main model's training process, with students serving as a source of feedback about the information it has learned.

Experiments in computer vision, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning report significant benefits over training on the original dataset alone. The authors interpret the results as evidence that LoT can retain useful information at appropriate scales while discarding spurious correlations. The findings support the approach across the tested settings, while the connection between ease of imitation and generalization remains the method's motivating hypothesis.
summary.tldr: LoT uses feedback from auxiliary students to encourage a main model to learn relationships that are easier to imitate and generalize.

title: Learning from Teaching Regularization: Generalizable Correlations Should be Easy to Imitate

abstract: We present the first algorithm for testing equivalence between two continuous distributions using differential privacy (DP). Our algorithm is a private version of the algorithm of Diakonikolas et al. The algorithm of Diakonikolas et al uses the data itself to repeatedly discretize the real line so that --- when the two distributions are far apart in ${\cal A}_k$-norm --- one of the discretized distributions exhibits large $L_2$-norm difference; and upon repeated sampling such large gap would be detected. Designing its private analogue poses two difficulties. First, our DP algorithm can not resample new datapoints as a change to a single datapoint may lead to a very large change in the descretization of the real line. In contrast, the (sorted) index of the discretization point changes only by $1$ between neighboring instances, and so we use a novel algorithm that set the discretization points using random Bernoulli noise, resulting in only a few buckets being affected under the right coupling. Second, our algorithm, which doesn't resample data, requires we also revisit the utility analysis of the original algorithm and prove its correctness w.r.t. the original sorted data; a problem we tackle using sampling a subset of Poisson-drawn size from each discretized bin. Lastly, since any distribution can be reduced to a continuous distribution, our algorithm is successfully carried to multiple other families of distributions and thus has numerous applications.

paragraphs: This paper develops an algorithm for testing whether two continuous distributions are equivalent while protecting individual data points through differential privacy. It builds on a method that repeatedly partitions the real line using observed data. When distributions differ sufficiently in the specified A_k norm, a suitable partition exposes a detectable difference between the resulting discrete distributions.

Privatizing that procedure is difficult because changing one observation can substantially shift a partition boundary in value. The authors instead use the observation's position in sorted order, which changes by only one between neighboring datasets. A new mechanism adds Bernoulli randomness when choosing partition points, allowing only a few buckets to be affected under an appropriate coupling.

The private procedure also avoids resampling, so the original correctness argument must be rebuilt around the already sorted data. The authors handle this using subsets whose sizes are drawn from a Poisson distribution within each bin. They further carry the method to other distribution families through reductions to continuous distributions, extending the reach of the private testing construction.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces a differentially private test for continuous-distribution equivalence using randomized partitions based on sorted data positions.

title: Differentially Private Equivalence Testing for Continuous Distributions and Applications

abstract: As the volume of data invested in statistical learning increases and concerns regarding privacy grow, the privacy leakage issue has drawn significant attention. Differential privacy has emerged as a widely accepted concept capable of mitigating privacy concerns, and numerous differentially private (DP) versions of machine learning algorithms have been developed. However, existing works on DP kernel learning algorithms have exhibited practical limitations, including scalability, restricted choice of kernels, or dependence on test data availability. We propose DP scalable kernel empirical risk minimization (ERM) algorithms and a DP kernel mean embedding (KME) release algorithm suitable for general kernels. Our approaches address the shortcomings of previous algorithms by employing Nyström methods, classical techniques in non-private scalable kernel learning. These methods provide data-dependent low-rank approximations of the kernel matrix for general kernels in a DP manner. We present excess empirical risk bounds and computational complexities for the scalable kernel DP ERM, KME algorithms, contrasting them with established methodologies. Furthermore, we develop a private data-generating algorithm capable of learning diverse kernel models. We conduct experiments to demonstrate the performance of our algorithms, comparing them with existing methods to highlight their superiority.

paragraphs: Kernel methods offer a way to learn from similarities between data points, but privacy-preserving versions can face practical obstacles. The paper identifies scalability problems, restrictions on which kernels can be used, and requirements that test data already be available. It develops differentially private approaches intended to address these obstacles for general kernels.

The central technique is a private use of Nyström approximation. This constructs a data-dependent, low-rank approximation to the kernel matrix, making kernel computations more manageable while preserving differential privacy. The authors use it to build algorithms for empirical risk minimization and for releasing a kernel mean embedding. These cover both learning predictive models and releasing a kernel-based representation of data.

It also develops a private data-generating algorithm capable of supporting diverse kernel models. Experiments report advantages over existing methods. The contribution combines privacy guarantees, scalable approximation, and broader kernel applicability within a shared approach.
summary.tldr: Private Nyström approximations support scalable learning and data representations for general kernels with theoretical and experimental evaluation.

title: Differential Privacy in Scalable General Kernel Learning via $K$-means Nystr{\"o}m Random Features

abstract: Models for inferring monocular shape of surfaces with diffuse reflection---shape from shading---ought to produce distributions of outputs, because there are fundamental mathematical ambiguities of both continuous (e.g., bas-relief) and discrete (e.g., convex/concave) types that are also experienced by humans. Yet, the outputs of current models are limited to point estimates or tight distributions around single modes, which prevent them from capturing these effects. We introduce a model that reconstructs a multimodal distribution of shapes from a single shading image, which aligns with the human experience of multistable perception. We train a small denoising diffusion process to generate surface normal fields from $16\times 16$ patches of synthetic images of everyday 3D objects. We deploy this model patch-wise at multiple scales, with guidance from inter-patch shape consistency constraints. Despite its relatively small parameter count and predominantly bottom-up structure, we show that multistable shape explanations emerge from this model for ambiguous test images that humans experience as being multistable. At the same time, the model produces veridical shape estimates for object-like images that include distinctive occluding contours and appear less ambiguous. This may inspire new architectures for stochastic 3D shape perception that are more efficient and better aligned with human experience.

paragraphs: A single shaded image can support multiple three-dimensional interpretations, including convex and concave shapes. Humans can experience these alternatives as perception switches between them. Models that produce only one shape, or a narrow distribution around it, cannot represent the full ambiguity. This paper develops a model that instead reconstructs a multimodal distribution of possible shapes.

The authors train a small denoising diffusion process to generate surface-normal fields from 16-by-16 patches of synthetic images of everyday objects. They apply this learned process across patches at several scales. Constraints encouraging consistent shapes between patches guide the local predictions toward coherent interpretations of the complete image.

For ambiguous test images that people experience as multistable, the model produces multiple shape explanations despite its small parameter count and predominantly bottom-up design. For less ambiguous, object-like images with distinctive occluding contours, it produces accurate shape estimates. These results suggest that local generative modeling combined with consistency constraints can capture meaningful perceptual ambiguity, and may inform more efficient stochastic models of three-dimensional perception.
summary.tldr: A small patch-based diffusion model produces multiple plausible 3D shapes from ambiguous shading while recovering accurate shapes from clearer images.

title: Multistable Shape from Shading Emerges from Patch Diffusion

abstract: While multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) have shown significant progress across popular visual reasoning benchmarks, whether they possess abstract visual reasoning abilities remains an open question. Similar to the Sudoku puzzles, abstract visual reasoning (AVR) problems require finding high-level patterns (e.g., repetition constraints on numbers) that control the input shapes (e.g., digits) in a specific task configuration (e.g., matrix). However, existing AVR benchmarks only consider a limited set of patterns (addition, conjunction), input shapes (rectangle, square), and task configurations (3 × 3 matrices). And they fail to capture all abstract reasoning patterns in human cognition necessary for addressing real-world tasks, such as geometric properties and object boundary understanding in real-world navigation. To evaluate MLLMs’ AVR abilities systematically, we introduce MARVEL founded on the core knowledge system in human cognition, a multi-dimensional AVR benchmark with 770 puzzles composed of six core knowledge patterns, geometric and abstract shapes, and five different task configurations. To inspect whether the model performance is grounded in perception or reasoning, MARVEL complements the standard AVR question with perception questions in a hierarchical evaluation framework. We conduct comprehensive experiments on MARVEL with ten representative MLLMs in zero-shot and few-shot settings. Our experiments reveal that all MLLMs show near-random performance on MARVEL, with significant performance gaps (40%) compared to humans across all patterns and task configurations. Further analysis of perception questions reveals that MLLMs struggle to comprehend the visual features (near-random performance). Although closed-source MLLMs, such as GPT-4V, show a promising understanding of reasoning patterns (on par with humans) after adding textual descriptions, this advantage is hindered by their weak perception abilities. We release our entirecode and dataset at https://github.com/1171-jpg/MARVEL_AVR.

The benchmark also separates questions about visual perception from the main reasoning questions. summary.tldr: MARVEL finds near-random visual puzzle performance in tested multimodal models and identifies weak perception as an obstacle to their reasoning abilities.

title: MARVEL: Multidimensional Abstraction and Reasoning through Visual Evaluation and Learning

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has proven highly effective in addressing complex decision-making and control tasks. However, in most traditional RL algorithms, the policy is typically parameterized as a diagonal Gaussian distribution with learned mean and variance, which constrains their capability to acquire complex policies. In response to this problem, we propose an online RL algorithm termed diffusion actor-critic with entropy regulator (DACER). This algorithm conceptualizes the reverse process of the diffusion model as a novel policy function and leverages the capability of the diffusion model to fit multimodal distributions, thereby enhancing the representational capacity of the policy. Since the distribution of the diffusion policy lacks an analytical expression, its entropy cannot be determined analytically. To mitigate this, we propose a method to estimate the entropy of the diffusion policy utilizing Gaussian mixture model. Building on the estimated entropy, we can learn a parameter $\alpha$ that modulates the degree of exploration and exploitation. Parameter $\alpha$ will be employed to adaptively regulate the variance of the added noise, which is applied to the action output by the diffusion model. Experimental trials on MuJoCo benchmarks and a multimodal task demonstrate that the DACER algorithm achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in most MuJoCo control tasks while exhibiting a stronger representational capacity of the diffusion policy.

DACER replaces that policy representation with the reverse process of a diffusion model, using its ability to represent multimodal distributions.

The algorithm also addresses how to regulate exploration with this more expressive policy. Its probability distribution has no available analytical expression, so the policy's entropy cannot be calculated analytically. DACER instead estimates entropy using a Gaussian mixture model. That estimate supports learning a parameter that controls the variance of noise added to the diffusion model's output action.

This links exploration to an estimate of the policy's uncertainty while retaining the diffusion model's representational capacity. Experiments on MuJoCo benchmarks and a multimodal task report state-of-the-art performance on most of the tested MuJoCo control tasks, alongside stronger policy representation. The stated result is therefore both an expressive action model and an adaptive mechanism for balancing exploration with exploitation during online learning.
summary.tldr: DACER combines a diffusion policy with estimated-entropy control to adapt exploration and improve online reinforcement learning.

title: Diffusion Actor-Critic with Entropy Regulator

abstract: Fair-range clustering extends classical clustering formulations by associating each data point with one or more demographic labels. It imposes lower and upper bound constraints on the number of facilities opened for each label, ensuring fair representation of all demographic groups by the selected facilities. In this paper we focus on the fair-range $k$-median and $k$-means problems in Euclidean spaces. We give $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithms with fixed-parameter tractable running times for both problems, parameterized by the numbers of opened facilities and demographic labels. For Euclidean metrics, these are the first parameterized approximation schemes for the problems, improving upon the previously known $O(1)$-approximation ratios given by Thejaswi et al. (KDD 2022).

The fairness requirement therefore concerns which facilities are opened and how their labels are represented, alongside the usual clustering objective.

It provides approximation algorithms with a factor of one plus epsilon, meaning their objective values can approach the optimum according to the chosen approximation tolerance. Their running times are fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the number of opened facilities and the number of demographic labels.

The contribution is a theoretical improvement in achievable solution quality under demographic representation constraints, with computational tractability expressed through the two specified parameters. This framing ties the guarantee to the structure of the clustering problem rather than claiming unrestricted computational efficiency.
summary.tldr: The paper gives the first parameterized approximation schemes for Euclidean fair-range k-median and k-means under demographic facility-selection constraints.

title: Parameterized Approximation Schemes for Fair-Range Clustering

abstract: The diffusion model, a new generative modeling paradigm, has achieved significant success in generating images, audio, video, and text. It has been adapted for sequence-to-sequence text generation (Seq2Seq) through DiffuSeq, termed the S2S-Diffusion model. Existing S2S-Diffusion models predominantly rely on fixed or hand-crafted rules to schedule noise during the diffusion and denoising processes. However, these models are limited by non-contextualized noise, which fails to fully consider the characteristics of Seq2Seq tasks. In this paper, we propose the Meta-Diffu$B$ framework—a novel scheduler-exploiter S2S-Diffusion paradigm designed to overcome the limitations of existing S2S-Diffusion models. We employ Meta-Exploration to train an additional scheduler model dedicated to scheduling contextualized noise for each sentence. Our exploiter model, an S2S-Diffusion model, leverages the noise scheduled by our scheduler model for updating and generation. Meta-Diffu$B$ achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to previous S2S-Diffusion models and fine-tuned pre-trained language models (PLMs) across four Seq2Seq benchmark datasets. We further investigate and visualize the impact of Meta-Diffu$B$'s noise scheduling on the generation of sentences with varying difficulties. Additionally, our scheduler model can function as a "plug-and-play" model to enhance DiffuSeq without the need for fine-tuning during the inference stage.

title: Meta-Diffu$B$: A Contextualized Sequence-to-Sequence Text Diffusion Model with Meta-Exploration

abstract: Despite the effectiveness of data selection for pretraining and instruction fine-tuninglarge language models (LLMs), improving data efficiency in supervised fine-tuning(SFT) for specialized domains poses significant challenges due to the complexityof fine-tuning data. To bridge this gap, we introduce an effective and scalabledata selection method for SFT, SmallToLarge (S2L), which trains a smallmodel, clusters loss trajectories of the examples, and samples from these clusters toguide data selection for larger models. We prove that during fine-tuning, sampleswithin the same loss trajectory cluster exhibit similar gradients. Then, we showthat S2L subsets have a bounded gradient error w.r.t. the full data, hence guaranteeconvergence to the neighborhood of the optimal solution. We demonstrate throughextensive experiments that S2L significantly improves data efficiency in SFT formathematical problem-solving, reducing the training data requirement to just $11$%of the original MathInstruct dataset to match full dataset performance whileoutperforming state-of-the-art data selection algorithms by an average of $4.7$%across $6$ in- and out-domain evaluation datasets. Remarkably, selecting only 50Kdata for SFT, S2L achieves a $32.7$% accuracy on the challenging MATHbenchmark, improving Phi-2 by $16.6$%. In clinical text summarization on theMIMIC-III dataset, S2L again outperforms training on the full dataset usingonly $50$% of the data. Notably, S2L can perform scalable data selection using areference model $100\times$ smaller than the target model, proportionally reducing thecomputational cost.

paragraphs: Selecting useful supervised fine-tuning data can reduce training costs, but specialized examples differ in how they influence learning. SmallToLarge uses a small reference model to study that behavior. It records how each example’s loss changes during training, groups examples with similar loss trajectories, and samples from those groups to select data for a larger model.

The theoretical argument connects similar loss trajectories to similar gradients during fine-tuning. The authors show that the selected subset has bounded gradient error relative to the full dataset, supporting convergence to a neighborhood of the optimum. This gives trajectory clustering a learning-based justification beyond grouping examples by their content.

On mathematical problem-solving, S2L matches full-data performance using 11% of MathInstruct and outperforms leading selection methods by an average of 4.7% across six evaluations. Using 50,000 examples, it reaches 32.7% accuracy on MATH. On MIMIC-III clinical summarization, half the data outperforms full-data training. The method also supports a reference model 100 times smaller than the target, reducing the computation needed for selection. These findings demonstrate data savings in the evaluated domains.
summary.tldr: S2L selects fine-tuning examples by clustering their learning trajectories in a small model, achieving strong results with substantially less data.

title: SmallToLarge (S2L): Scalable Data Selection for Fine-tuning Large Language Models by Summarizing Training Trajectories of Small Models

abstract: In this paper, we point out that suboptimal noise-data mapping leads to slow training of diffusion models. During diffusion training, current methods diffuse each image across the entire noise space, resulting in a mixture of all images at every point in the noise layer. We emphasize that this random mixture of noise-data mapping complicates the optimization of the denoising function in diffusion models. Drawing inspiration from the immiscibility phenomenon in physics, we propose *Immiscible Diffusion*, a simple and effective method to improve the random mixture of noise-data mapping. In physics, miscibility can vary according to various intermolecular forces. Thus, immiscibility means that the mixing of molecular sources is distinguishable. Inspired by this concept, we propose an assignment-then-diffusion training strategy to achieve *Immiscible Diffusion*. As one example, prior to diffusing the image data into noise, we assign diffusion target noise for the image data by minimizing the total image-noise pair distance in a mini-batch. The assignment functions analogously to external forces to expel the diffuse-able areas of images, thus mitigating the inherent difficulties in diffusion training. Our approach is remarkably simple, requiring only *one line of code* to restrict the diffuse-able area for each image while preserving the Gaussian distribution of noise. In this way, each image is preferably projected to nearby noise. To address the high complexity of the assignment algorithm, we employ a quantized assignment strategy, which significantly reduces the computational overhead to a negligible level (e.g. 22.8ms for a large batch size of 1024 on an A6000). Experiments demonstrate that our method can achieve up to 3x faster training for unconditional Consistency Models on the CIFAR dataset, as well as for DDIM and Stable Diffusion on CelebA and ImageNet dataset, and in class-conditional training and fine-tuning. In addition, we conducted a thorough analysis that sheds light on how it improves diffusion training speed while improving fidelity. The code is available at https://yhli123.github.io/immiscible-diffusion

title: Immiscible Diffusion: Accelerating Diffusion Training with Noise Assignment

abstract: Novel View Synthesis (NVS) and 3D generation have recently achieved prominent improvements. However, these works mainly focus on confined categories or synthetic 3D assets, which are discouraged from generalizing to challenging in-the-wild scenes and fail to be employed with 2D synthesis directly. Moreover, these methods heavily depended on camera poses, limiting their real-world applications. To overcome these issues, we propose MVInpainter, re-formulating the 3D editing as a multi-view 2D inpainting task. Specifically, MVInpainter partially inpaints multi-view images with the reference guidance rather than intractably generating an entirely novel view from scratch, which largely simplifies the difficulty of in-the-wild NVS and leverages unmasked clues instead of explicit pose conditions. To ensure cross-view consistency, MVInpainter is enhanced by video priors from motion components and appearance guidance from concatenated reference key\&value attention. Furthermore, MVInpainter incorporates slot attention to aggregate high-level optical flow features from unmasked regions to control the camera movement with pose-free training and inference. Sufficient scene-level experiments on both object-centric and forward-facing datasets verify the effectiveness of MVInpainter, including diverse tasks, such as multi-view object removal, synthesis, insertion, and replacement. The project page is https://ewrfcas.github.io/MVInpainter/.

The unmasked parts of the images provide clues about the scene, reducing the generation problem and allowing the method to operate without explicit camera-pose conditions.

To keep edited views consistent, the method combines video-derived motion priors with reference-based appearance guidance through attention. It also uses slot attention to aggregate high-level optical-flow features from unmasked regions. These features provide information for controlling camera movement, enabling both training and inference without supplied poses. The design uses the visible scene as a source of motion and appearance constraints.

Experiments on object-centric and forward-facing scene datasets demonstrate applications including object removal, synthesis, insertion, and replacement across views. The findings support multi-view inpainting as a bridge between 2D image editing and 3D scene editing. Its central advantage is making use of existing image content and shared reference guidance to coordinate edits in challenging scenes.
summary.tldr: MVInpainter coordinates reference-guided edits across multiple images, using unmasked scene information to support consistent 3D editing without explicit camera poses.

title: MVInpainter: Learning Multi-View Consistent Inpainting to Bridge 2D and 3D Editing

abstract: Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. developed influential scaling laws for the optimal model size as a function of the compute budget, but these laws yield substantially different predictions. We explain the discrepancy by reproducing the Kaplan scaling law on two datasets (OpenWebText2 and RefinedWeb) and identifying three factors causing the difference: last layer computational cost, warmup duration, and scale-dependent optimizer tuning. With these factors corrected, we obtain excellent agreement with the Hoffmann et al. (i.e., "Chinchilla") scaling law. Counter to a hypothesis of Hoffmann et al., we find that careful learning rate decay is not essential for the validity of their scaling law. As a secondary result, we derive scaling laws for the optimal learning rate and batch size, finding that tuning the AdamW $\beta_2$ parameter is essential at lower batch sizes.
