paragraphs: Influential language-model scaling laws disagree about the model size that best uses a fixed compute budget. This paper investigates why the predictions associated with Kaplan and Hoffmann differ. The authors first reproduce the Kaplan scaling law on OpenWebText2 and RefinedWeb, giving them a basis for examining the source of the discrepancy.

They identify three contributing factors: the computational cost of the last layer, the duration of learning-rate warmup, and optimizer tuning that depends on scale. Correcting these factors produces close agreement with the Hoffmann, or Chinchilla, scaling law. The result connects the disagreement to how computation and training choices are handled.

The study also finds that carefully designed learning-rate decay is not essential for the Chinchilla law to hold, contrary to a proposed explanation. As a secondary contribution, it derives scaling laws for the optimal learning rate and batch size. It further finds that tuning AdamW’s beta-two parameter is essential at lower batch sizes, reinforcing the importance of optimizer choices when comparing training scales.
summary.tldr: Compute accounting, warmup duration, and scale-dependent optimizer tuning explain the studied discrepancy between Kaplan and Chinchilla scaling laws.

title: Resolving Discrepancies in Compute-Optimal Scaling of Language Models

abstract: Semantic segmentation suffers from significant performance degradation when the trained network is applied to a different domain. To address this issue, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) has been extensively studied. Despite the effectiveness of selftraining techniques in UDA, they still overlook the explicit modeling of domain-shared feature extraction. In this paper, we propose DiDA, an unsupervised domain bridging approach for semantic segmentation. DiDA consists of two key modules: (1) Degradation-based Intermediate Domain Construction, which creates continuous intermediate domains through simple image degradation operations to encourage learning domain-invariant features as domain differences gradually diminish; (2) Semantic Shift Compensation, which leverages a diffusion encoder to disentangle and compensate for semantic shift information with degraded time-steps, preserving discriminative representations in the intermediate domains. As a plug-and-play solution, DiDA supports various degradation operations and seamlessly integrates with existing UDA methods. Extensive experiments on multiple domain adaptive semantic segmentation benchmarks demonstrate that DiDA consistently achieves significant performance improvements across all settings. Code is available at https://github.com/Woof6/DiDA.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation can lose accuracy when a model encounters images from a different domain. Unsupervised domain adaptation addresses this transfer problem, but the authors argue that existing self-training methods insufficiently model how to extract shared features. DiDA creates intermediate domains intended to encourage features that remain useful across the original domain differences.

Its first component applies simple image-degradation operations to construct a continuous progression of intermediate domains. As domain differences diminish along that progression, the model is encouraged to learn invariant features. Its second component uses a diffusion encoder to separate and compensate for semantic shifts associated with degradation timesteps, preserving information needed to distinguish image content.

The two components address a linked problem: degradation can bring domains closer while also altering useful semantics. DiDA combines that bridge with explicit semantic compensation and can integrate into existing adaptation methods using different degradation operations. Experiments across multiple segmentation benchmarks report significant, consistent improvements in every tested setting, supporting this combination as a useful addition to existing adaptation pipelines.
summary.tldr: DiDA bridges image domains through progressive degradation while compensating for semantic shifts to improve segmentation adaptation.

title: Towards Unsupervised Domain Bridging via Image Degradation in Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Current text-to-image diffusion generation typically employs complete-text conditioning. Due to the intricate syntax, diffusion transformers (DiTs) inherently suffer from a comprehension defect of complete-text captions. One-fly complete-text input either overlooks critical semantic details or causes semantic confusion by simultaneously modeling diverse semantic primitive types. To mitigate this defect of DiTs, we propose a novel split-text conditioning framework named DiT-ST. This framework converts a complete-text caption into a split-text caption, a collection of simplified sentences, to explicitly express various semantic primitives and their interconnections. The split-text caption is then injected into different denoising stages of DiT-ST in a hierarchical and incremental manner. Specifically, DiT-ST leverages Large Language Models to parse captions, extracting diverse primitives and hierarchically sorting out and constructing these primitives into a split-text input. Moreover, we partition the diffusion denoising process according to its differential sensitivities to diverse semantic primitive types and determine the appropriate timesteps to incrementally inject tokens of diverse semantic primitive types into input tokens via cross-attention. In this way, DiT-ST enhances the representation learning of specific semantic primitive types across different stages. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of our proposed DiT-ST in mitigating the complete-text comprehension defect. Datasets and models are available.

paragraphs: A detailed image caption can combine many semantic components and relationships in complicated syntax. The authors argue that presenting this information all at once can cause diffusion transformers to miss details or confuse meanings. DiT-ST addresses this problem by changing both the form of the caption and when its components reach the image generator.

A language model first parses the caption into semantic primitives and their connections, then organizes them hierarchically into simpler sentences. The resulting split caption is introduced incrementally during denoising. The authors divide that process according to how sensitive different stages are to different kinds of semantic information, using cross-attention to introduce the corresponding tokens at selected timesteps.

This design gives particular semantic components attention during stages suited to learning their representations. Experiments support its effectiveness in reducing the complete-caption comprehension problem identified by the authors. The contribution is therefore a coordinated treatment of language structure and generation timing: simplifying the input works together with staged conditioning to improve how the transformer uses textual instructions.
summary.tldr: DiT-ST breaks captions into simpler semantic components and introduces them at selected stages of image denoising.

title: Enhancing Text-to-Image Diffusion Transformer via Split-Text Conditioning

abstract: Correct model interpretation in high-stakes settings is critical, yet both post-hoc feature attribution methods and so-called intrinsically interpretable models can systematically attribute false-positive importance to non-informative features such as suppressor variables. Specifically, both linear models and their powerful non-linear generalisation such as General Additive Models (GAMs) are susceptible to spurious attributions to suppressors. We present a principled generalisation of activation patterns - originally developed to make linear models interpretable - to additive models, correctly rejecting suppressor effects for non-linear features. This yields PatternGAM, an importance attribution method based on univariate generative surrogate models for the broad family of additive models, and PatternQLR for polynomial models. Empirical evaluations on the XAI-TRIS benchmark with a novel false-negative invariant formulation of the earth mover's distance accuracy metric demonstrates significant improvements over popular feature attribution methods and the traditional interpretation of additive models. Finally, real-world case studies on the COMPAS and MIMIC-IV datasets provide new insights into the role of specific features by disentangling genuine target-related information from suppression effects that would mislead conventional GAM interpretations.

paragraphs: A model can look easy to interpret while still giving misleading impressions of which inputs carry information about its target. This paper examines suppressor variables: non-informative features that can receive false-positive importance attributions. The problem affects both explanations applied after training and direct interpretations of linear models and generalized additive models.

The authors generalize activation patterns, an approach originally developed for interpreting linear models, to the broader family of additive models. The resulting method, PatternGAM, uses univariate generative surrogate models to distinguish target-related information from suppression effects involving nonlinear features. They also introduce PatternQLR for polynomial models. The aim is to correct feature importance rather than assume that an additive structure makes its interpretation reliable.

Evaluations on XAI-TRIS use a new false-negative-invariant version of an earth mover’s distance accuracy metric and show significant improvements over popular attribution methods and conventional additive-model interpretation. Case studies on COMPAS and MIMIC-IV further illustrate how separating genuine information from suppression changes the interpretation of particular features.
summary.tldr: PatternGAM and PatternQLR correct misleading feature importance caused by suppressor variables in additive and polynomial models.

title: Correcting misinterpretations of additive models

abstract: Modifying well-trained models for purposes such as pruning or unlearning, without access to training data or the original loss function, is a challenging problem. While techniques exist for such modification, they often require training data, are computationally expensive, or are architecture-specific. To address this, we investigate the fundamental question of identifying components that are critical to the model’s predictive performance, without access to either gradients or the loss function, and with only distributional access such as synthetic data. We theoretically demonstrate that the global reconstruction error is linearly bounded by local reconstruction errors for Lipschitz-continuous networks such as CNNs and well-trained Transformers (which, contrary to existing literature, we find exhibit Lipschitz continuity). This motivates using the locally reconstructive behavior of component subsets to quantify their global importance, via a metric that we term *Subset Fidelity*. In the uncorrelated features setting, selecting individual components via their Subset Fidelity scores is optimal, which we use to propose **ModHiFi**, an algorithm for model modification that requires no training data or loss function access. **ModHiFi-P**, for structured pruning, achieves an 11% speedup over the current state of the art on ImageNet models and competitive performance on language models. **ModHiFi-U**, for classwise unlearning, achieves complete unlearning on CIFAR-10 without fine-tuning and demonstrates competitive performance on Swin Transformers.

title: ModHiFi: Identifying High Fidelity predictive components for Model Modification

abstract: The imbalance (or long-tail) is the nature of many real-world data distributions, which often induces the undesirable bias of deep classification models toward frequent classes, resulting in poor performance for tail classes. In this paper, we propose a novel two-stage learning approach to mitigate such a majority-biased tendency while preserving valuable information within datasets. Specifically, the first stage proposes a new representation learning technique from the information theory perspective. This approach is theoretically equivalent to minimizing intra-class distance, yielding an effective and well-separated feature space. The second stage develops a novel sampling strategy that selects mathematically informative instances, able to rectify majority-biased decision boundaries without compromising a model’s overall performance. As a result, our approach achieves the state-of-the-art performance across various long-tailed benchmark datasets, validated via extensive experiments. Our code is available at https://github.com/fudong03/BNS_IPDPP.

paragraphs: Long-tailed recognition involves datasets where some classes have many examples and others have few. Models trained on these distributions often favor common classes, hurting recognition of rare ones. This paper proposes a two-stage method designed to reduce that bias while preserving useful information in the training data.

The first stage learns representations using an information-theoretic approach. The authors show that its objective is theoretically equivalent to reducing distances between examples from the same class, and report an effective, well-separated feature space. The second stage introduces a sampling strategy that selects mathematically informative examples to adjust decision boundaries biased toward the majority classes.

Separating representation learning from informative sample selection gives the approach two distinct ways to address imbalance: organizing features and improving the decisions built on those features. The authors report that the sampling stage corrects majority bias without sacrificing overall performance. Extensive experiments achieve state-of-the-art results across several long-tailed benchmarks, supporting the combination as a way to improve recognition under uneven class frequencies.
summary.tldr: A two-stage method combines information-theoretic representation learning with informative sampling to reduce majority-class bias in long-tailed recognition.

title: Long-Tailed Recognition via Information-Preservable Two-Stage Learning

abstract: Graph transfer learning, especially in unsupervised domain adaptation, aims to transfer knowledge from a label-abundant source graph to an unlabeled target graph. However, most existing approaches overlook the common issue of label imbalance in the source domain, typically assuming a balanced label distribution that rarely holds in practice. Moreover, they face challenges arising from biased knowledge in the source graph and substantial domain distribution shifts. To remedy the above challenges, we propose a dual-branch prototype-enhanced contrastive framework for class-imbalanced graph domain adaptation in this paper. Specifically, we introduce a dual-branch graph encoder to capture both local and global information, generating class-specific prototypes from a distilled anchor set. Then, a prototype-enhanced contrastive learning framework is introduced. On the one hand, we encourage class alignment between the two branches based on constructed prototypes to alleviate the bias introduced by class imbalance. On the other hand, we infer the pseudo-labels for the target domain and align sample pairs across domains that share similar semantics to reduce domain discrepancies. Experimental results show that our ImGDA outperforms the state-of-the-art methods across multiple datasets and settings. The code is available at: https://github.com/maxin88scu/ImGDA.

paragraphs: Transferring a model from a labeled graph to an unlabeled graph requires handling differences between the two domains. This paper addresses an additional difficulty: the labeled source graph may contain uneven numbers of examples from different classes. Such imbalance can bias the knowledge being transferred, compounding the challenge of adapting to a different target distribution.

The proposed ImGDA framework uses two graph-encoder branches to capture local and global information. It constructs class-specific prototypes from a distilled set of anchors, giving the learning process reference representations for each class. A contrastive objective encourages the branches to agree at the class level through these prototypes, aiming to reduce the bias associated with uneven class representation.

A second alignment process addresses the gap between source and target graphs. The method infers target pseudo-labels and aligns cross-domain sample pairs with similar semantics. These two mechanisms tackle class imbalance and domain discrepancy within one framework. Across the reported datasets and settings, ImGDA outperforms state-of-the-art methods, supporting the usefulness of jointly addressing both problems when transferring graph representations.
summary.tldr: ImGDA combines class prototypes and cross-domain contrastive alignment to improve graph adaptation when source labels are imbalanced.

title: Dual Prototype-Enhanced Contrastive Framework for Class-Imbalanced Graph Domain Adaptation

abstract: With the rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC) technologies, synthetic images have become increasingly prevalent in everyday life, posing new challenges for authenticity assessment and detection. Despite the effectiveness of existing methods in evaluating image authenticity and locating forgeries, these approaches often lack human interpretability and do not fully address the growing complexity of synthetic data. To tackle these challenges, we introduce FakeVLM, a specialized large multimodal model designed for both general synthetic image and DeepFake detection tasks. FakeVLM not only excels in distinguishing real from fake images but also provides clear, natural language explanations for image artifacts, enhancing interpretability. Additionally, we present FakeClue, a comprehensive dataset containing over 100,000 images across seven categories, annotated with fine-grained artifact clues in natural language. FakeVLM demonstrates performance comparable to expert models while eliminating the need for additional classifiers, making it a robust solution for synthetic data detection. Extensive evaluations across multiple datasets confirm the superiority of FakeVLM in both authenticity classification and artifact explanation tasks, setting a new benchmark for synthetic image detection. The code, model weights, and dataset can be found here: https://github.com/opendatalab/FakeVLM.

paragraphs: Determining whether an image is synthetic is more useful when the system can also explain the visual evidence behind its judgment. This paper introduces FakeVLM, a large multimodal model for both general synthetic-image detection and DeepFake detection. Its intended output combines an authenticity decision with a natural-language account of image artifacts.

To support this task, the authors create FakeClue, a dataset containing more than 100,000 images across seven categories. The images include detailed artifact clues expressed in natural language. These annotations provide material for connecting authenticity judgments with descriptions of the visual features that motivate them, rather than supplying only real-or-fake labels.

Evaluations across multiple datasets report strong results in both authenticity classification and artifact explanation. FakeVLM performs comparably to expert models without requiring additional classifiers, and the authors report superiority in their broader evaluations. The contribution brings detection and explanation into a single multimodal model, making interpretable descriptions part of the task being trained and evaluated.
summary.tldr: FakeVLM detects synthetic images and explains their artifacts, supported by a dataset of over 100,000 images with natural-language clues.

title: Spot the Fake: Large Multimodal Model-Based Synthetic Image Detection with Artifact Explanation

abstract: Model customization necessitates high-quality and diverse datasets, but acquiring such data remains time-consuming and labor-intensive. Despite the great potential of large language models (LLMs) for data synthesis, current approaches are constrained by limited seed data, model biases and low-variation prompts, resulting in limited diversity and biased distribution with the increase of data scales. To tackle this challenge, we introduce TreeSynth, a tree-guided subspace-based data synthesis approach inspired by decision trees. It constructs a spatial partitioning tree to recursively divide a task-specific full data space (i.e., root node) into numerous atomic subspaces (i.e., leaf nodes) with mutually exclusive and exhaustive attributes to ensure both distinctiveness and comprehensiveness, before synthesizing samples within each atomic subspace. This globally divide-and-synthesize method finally collects subspace samples into a comprehensive dataset, effectively circumventing repetition and space collapse to ensure the diversity of large-scale data synthesis. Furthermore, the spatial partitioning tree enables sample allocation into atomic subspaces, allowing the re-balancing of existing datasets for more balanced and comprehensive distributions. Empirically, extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks consistently validates the superior data diversity, model performance, and robust scalability of TreeSynth compared to both human-crafted datasets and peer data synthesis methods, with the average performance gain reaching 10%. Besides, the consistent improvements of TreeSynth-balanced datasets highlight its efficacious application to redistribute existing datasets for more comprehensive coverage and the induced performance enhancement. The code is available at https://github.com/cpa2001/TreeSynth.

paragraphs: Generating more examples with a language model does not automatically produce a more diverse dataset. Limited seed data, model biases, and repetitive prompts can concentrate output in a narrow part of the intended task space. TreeSynth addresses this by organizing coverage before generating individual samples.

It constructs a tree that repeatedly divides a task-specific data space into smaller regions. The leaf regions use mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive attributes, aiming to make their coverage both distinct and comprehensive. Samples are generated within these regions and then assembled into a dataset. The same tree can also allocate samples to rebalance an existing dataset.

Experiments across diverse benchmarks report stronger data diversity, downstream model performance, and scaling behavior than human-crafted datasets and competing synthesis methods, with an average performance gain of 10%. Rebalanced datasets also show consistent improvements. These findings support explicit control over where generated examples come from: the tree provides an organizing structure for both expanding a dataset and correcting uneven coverage in one that already exists.
summary.tldr: TreeSynth partitions a task’s data space before generating examples, improving dataset diversity and enabling systematic rebalancing.

title: TreeSynth: Synthesizing Diverse Data from Scratch via Tree-Guided Subspace Partitioning

abstract: Humans exhibit diverse and expressive whole-body movements. However, attaining human-like whole-body coordination in humanoid robots remains challenging, as conventional approaches that mimic whole-body motions often neglect the distinct roles of upper and lower body. This oversight leads to computationally intensive policy learning and frequently causes robot instability and falls during real-world execution. To address these issues, we propose Adversarial Locomotion and Motion Imitation (ALMI), a novel framework that enables adversarial policy learning between upper and lower body. Specifically, the lower body aims to provide robust locomotion capabilities to follow velocity commands while the upper body tracks various motions. Conversely, the upper-body policy ensures effective motion tracking when the robot executes velocity-based movements. Through iterative updates, these policies achieve coordinated whole-body control, which can be extended to loco-manipulation tasks with teleoperation systems. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves robust locomotion and precise motion tracking in both simulation and on the full-size Unitree H1-2 robot. Additionally, we release a large-scale whole-body motion control dataset featuring high-quality episodic trajectories from MuJoCo simulations. The project page is https://almi-humanoid.github.io.

paragraphs: Humanoid robots need to balance locomotion with expressive movements of the rest of the body. The paper argues that whole-body imitation methods often overlook the different roles of the upper and lower body, making policy learning expensive and contributing to instability during execution. ALMI addresses this by explicitly separating those roles while learning their coordination.

The lower-body policy learns to follow velocity commands robustly while the upper body performs different motions. The upper-body policy, in turn, learns to track its target motions while the robot moves according to those commands. An adversarial learning setup and iterative policy updates make each part adapt to the demands imposed by the other, producing coordinated whole-body control.

Experiments demonstrate robust locomotion and precise motion tracking in simulation and on a full-size Unitree H1-2 robot. The framework can also extend to locomotion combined with manipulation through teleoperation systems. Alongside the method, the authors release a large collection of whole-body motion-control trajectories from MuJoCo simulations, providing data associated with the control setting they study.
summary.tldr: ALMI jointly develops upper- and lower-body policies to combine robust humanoid locomotion with precise motion imitation.

title: Adversarial Locomotion and Motion Imitation for Humanoid Policy Learning

abstract: Owing to their reasoning capabilities, large language models (LLMs) have been evaluated on planning tasks described in natural language. However, LLMs have largely been tested on planning domains without constraints. In order to deploy them in real-world settings where adherence to constraints, in particular safety constraints, is critical, we need to evaluate their performance on constrained planning tasks. We introduce LexiCon—a natural language-based (Lexi) constrained (Con) planning benchmark, consisting of a suite of environments, that can be used to evaluate the planning capabilities of LLMs in a principled fashion. The core idea behind LexiCon is to take existing planning environments and impose temporal constraints on the states. These constrained problems are then translated into natural language and given to an LLM to solve. A key feature of LexiCon is its extensibility. That is, the set of supported environments can be extended with new (unconstrained) environment generators, for which temporal constraints are constructed automatically. This renders LexiCon future-proof: the hardness of the generated planning problems can be increased as the planning capabilities of LLMs improve. Our experiments reveal that the performance of state-of-the-art LLMs, including reasoning models like GPT-5, o3, and R1, deteriorates as the degree of constrainedness of the planning tasks increases.

paragraphs: A plan can reach its goal yet violate requirements along the way. LexiCon evaluates this aspect of language-model planning by introducing temporal constraints into planning problems described in natural language. The motivation is that unconstrained planning benchmarks do not adequately test adherence to requirements that matter in real-world settings, including safety constraints.

The benchmark starts with existing planning environments, adds temporal constraints on their states, and translates the resulting problems into natural language for a model to solve. Its extensible design accepts new unconstrained environment generators and constructs constraints automatically. This provides a way to expand the environment collection and increase problem difficulty as model capabilities improve.

Experiments show that evaluated state-of-the-art models, including GPT-5, o3, and R1, perform worse as tasks become more constrained. The result highlights a gap between general planning ability and producing plans that satisfy additional requirements. LexiCon makes that gap measurable through a systematic family of constrained problems.
summary.tldr: LexiCon tests natural-language planning with temporal constraints and finds that model performance declines as constraints increase.

title: LexiCon: a Benchmark for Planning under Temporal Constraints in Natural Language

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer promising capabilities for tackling complex reasoning tasks, including optimization problems. However, existing methods either rely on prompt engineering, which leads to poor generalization across problem types, or require costly supervised training. We introduce SolverLLM, a training-free framework that leverages test-time scaling to solve diverse optimization problems. Rather than solving directly, SolverLLM generates mathematical formulations and translates them into solver-ready code, guided by a novel Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) strategy. To enhance the search process, we modify classical MCTS with (1) dynamic expansion for adaptive formulation generation, (2) prompt backpropagation to guide exploration via outcome-driven feedback, and (3) uncertainty backpropagation to incorporate reward reliability into decision-making. Experiments on six standard benchmark datasets demonstrate that SolverLLM outperforms both prompt-based and learning-based baselines, achieving strong generalization without additional training.

paragraphs: Using language models for optimization involves translating a problem into a form that can be solved reliably. SolverLLM addresses this by spending additional computation at inference time without further model training. It searches over mathematical formulations and translates them into solver-ready code, making formulation quality a central part of the solution process.

The search builds on Monte Carlo Tree Search with three changes. Dynamic expansion adapts the generation of candidate formulations. Prompt backpropagation carries outcome-based feedback into further exploration. Uncertainty backpropagation accounts for how reliable the reward information is when making search decisions. Together, these mechanisms guide the model's exploration of possible formulations.

Across six standard benchmark datasets, SolverLLM outperforms both prompt-based and learning-based baselines and shows strong generalization without additional training. The findings support investing inference-time effort in guided formulation search. They also connect successful optimization assistance to the model's ability to construct useful mathematical representations and executable solver inputs, rather than only generating a final answer.
summary.tldr: SolverLLM uses inference-time tree search to generate mathematical formulations and solver-ready code, improving optimization results without additional training.

title: SolverLLM: Leveraging Test-Time Scaling for Optimization Problem via LLM-Guided Search

abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) have been remarkably successful at synthesizing novel views of 3D scenes by optimizing a volumetric scene function. This scene function models how optical rays bring color information from a 3D object to the camera pixels. Radio frequency (RF) or audio signals can also be viewed as a vehicle for delivering information about the environment to a sensor. However, unlike camera pixels, an RF/audio sensor receives a mixture of signals that contain many environmental reflections (also called “multipath”). Is it still possible to infer the environment using such multipath signals? We show that with redesign, NeRFs can be taught to learn from multipath signals, and thereby “see” the environment. As a grounding application, we aim to infer the indoor floorplan of a home from sparse WiFi measurements made at multiple locations inside the home. Although a difficult inverse problem, our implicitly learnt floorplans look promising, and enables forward applications, such as indoor signal prediction and basic ray tracing.

paragraphs: Neural Radiance Fields usually learn a three-dimensional scene from camera observations, modeling how light traveling through the scene produces pixel colors. This paper asks whether a related representation can recover environmental structure from other signals. Radio and audio also carry information about their surroundings, even though their sensors do not produce ordinary images.

The main obstacle is multipath: a sensor receives a mixture of signals that have undergone different environmental reflections. Inferring the scene therefore requires interpreting that mixture. The authors redesign the NeRF approach so it can learn from multipath measurements, extending the scene-learning idea beyond the optical relationship between objects and camera pixels.

Their concrete application is recovering an indoor floorplan from sparse WiFi measurements collected at multiple locations in a home. The learned floorplans are described as promising, preserving the exploratory strength of the result. They also support forward uses, including predicting indoor signals and basic ray tracing. Together, these outcomes suggest that a learned scene representation can connect wireless measurements with useful information about indoor structure.
summary.tldr: A redesigned NeRF learns promising indoor floorplans from sparse WiFi multipath measurements and supports signal prediction and basic ray tracing.

title: Can NeRFs "See" without Cameras?

abstract: Recent work analyzing in-context learning (ICL) has identified a broad set of strategies that describe model behavior in different experimental conditions. We aim to unify these findings by asking why a model learns these disparate strategies in the first place. Specifically, we start with the observation that when trained to learn a mixture of tasks, as is popular in the literature, the strategies learned by a model for performing ICL can be captured by a family of Bayesian predictors: a memorizing predictor, which assumes a discrete prior on the set of seen tasks, and a generalizing predictor, where the prior matches the underlying task distribution. Adopting the normative lens of rational analysis, where a learner’s behavior is explained as an optimal adaptation to data given computational constraints, we develop a hierarchical Bayesian framework that almost perfectly predicts Transformer next- token predictions throughout training—without assuming access to its weights. Under this framework, pretraining is viewed as a process of updating the posterior probability of different strategies, and inference-time behavior as a posterior- weighted average over these strategies’ predictions. Our framework draws on common assumptions about neural network learning dynamics, which make explicit a tradeoff between loss and complexity among candidate strategies: beyond how well it explains the data, a model’s preference towards implementing a strategy is dictated by its complexity. This helps explain well-known ICL phenomena, while offering novel predictions: e.g., we show a superlinear trend in the timescale for transitioning from generalization to memorization as task diversity increases. Overall, our work advances an explanatory and predictive account of ICL grounded in tradeoffs between strategy loss and complexity.

These correspond to memorizing and generalizing approaches to interpreting examples in context.

The authors place these strategies inside a hierarchical Bayesian framework. Pretraining updates the relative probabilities of the strategies, and inference combines their predictions using those probabilities. Under assumptions about neural learning dynamics, strategy preference reflects both predictive loss and implementation complexity. This makes the explanation sensitive to computational constraints as well as fit to the training data.

The framework almost perfectly predicts Transformer next-token outputs throughout the studied training process without accessing model weights. It also predicts a superlinear increase in the time required to shift from generalization to memorization as task diversity grows. The contribution is an explanatory account in which changing behavior follows from competition among strategies with different losses and complexities.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian account explains changing in-context learning strategies through tradeoffs between predictive loss and strategy complexity.

title: In-Context Learning Strategies Emerge Rationally

abstract: This paper investigates convex-concave minimax optimization problems where only the function value access is allowed. We introduce a class of Hessian-aware quantum zeroth-order methods that can find the $\epsilon$-saddle point within $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d^{2/3}\epsilon^{-2/3})$ function value oracle calls. This represents an improvement of $d^{1/3}\epsilon^{-1/3}$ over the $\mathcal{O}(d\epsilon^{-1})$ upper bound of classical zeroth-order methods, where $d$ denotes the problem dimension. We extend these results to $\mu$-strongly-convex $\mu$-strongly-concave minimax problems using a restart strategy, and show a speedup of $d^{1/3}\mu^{-1/3}$ compared to classical zeroth-order methods. The acceleration achieved by our methods stems from the construction of efficient quantum estimators for the Hessian and the subsequent design of efficient Hessian-aware algorithms. In addition, we apply such ideas to non-convex optimization, leading to a reduction in the query complexity compared to classical methods.

The objective is to find an approximate saddle point while reducing the number of function-value queries. The proposed quantum methods use estimated curvature information, represented by the Hessian, to guide optimization.

For dimension d and target accuracy epsilon, the stated query bound scales as d to the two-thirds power times epsilon to the minus two-thirds power, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Relative to the cited classical upper bound of d times epsilon to the minus one, this yields the reported improvement in query complexity.

summary.tldr: Quantum Hessian estimation enables improved function-query bounds for minimax optimization, with extensions to strongly convex–concave and non-convex settings.

title: Quantum Speedups for Minimax Optimization and Beyond

abstract: Neural fields have emerged as a powerful representation for 3D geometry, enabling compact and continuous modeling of complex shapes. Despite their expressive power, manipulating neural fields in a controlled and accurate manner -- particularly under spatial constraints -- remains an open challenge, as existing approaches struggle to balance surface quality, robustness, and efficiency. We address this by introducing a novel method for handle-guided neural field deformation, which leverages discrete local surface representations to optimize the As-Rigid-As-Possible deformation energy. To this end, we propose the local patch mesh representation, which discretizes level sets of a neural signed distance field by projecting and deforming flat mesh patches guided solely by the SDF and its gradient. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation showing that our method consistently outperforms baselines in deformation quality, robustness, and computational efficiency. We also present experiments that motivate our choice of discretization over marching cubes. By bridging classical geometry processing and neural representations through local patch meshing, our work enables scalable, high-quality deformation of neural fields and paves the way for extending other geometric tasks to neural domains.

paragraphs: Implicit-ARAP addresses controlled editing of shapes represented by neural fields. These representations describe geometry continuously and compactly, but deforming them under spatial constraints presents a difficult balance between surface quality, robustness, and speed. The paper uses handle-guided deformation, where selected spatial controls guide the change in shape.

Its central construction is a local patch mesh that supplies discrete surface geometry for optimizing an As-Rigid-As-Possible deformation objective. The patches are built by projecting and deforming initially flat meshes onto level sets of a neural signed distance field. This process uses only the field and its gradient. It connects a continuous neural representation to a classical geometric objective through local surface discretization.

The evaluation reports consistent improvements over baselines in deformation quality, robustness, and computational efficiency. Additional experiments motivate the chosen discretization compared with marching cubes. The broader contribution is a practical connection between neural shape representations and established geometry-processing methods. The demonstrated task is deformation, while extending the same connection to other geometric tasks is presented as a future possibility.
summary.tldr: Implicit-ARAP uses local surface meshes to deform neural fields with improved reported quality, robustness, and efficiency.

title: Implicit-ARAP: Efficient Handle-Guided Neural Field Deformation via Local Patch Meshing

abstract: The ability to reason lies at the core of artificial intelligence (AI), and challenging problems usually call for deeper and longer reasoning to tackle. A crucial question about AI reasoning is whether models can extrapolate learned reasoning patterns to solve harder tasks that require longer chain-of-thoughts (CoT). In this work, we present a theoretical analysis of transformers trained via gradient descent on synthetic data for various state tracking tasks, revealing how length-generalizable reasoning can emerge. Specifically, we prove that: (i) for tasks with simple algebraic structure such as cyclic-group composition, transformers trained on short, constant-length chains learn a solution pattern that extrapolates to much longer chains; and (ii) for more complex tasks such as symmetric-group composition, a recursive self-training curriculum bootstraps longer reasoning and generalizes well beyond the training horizon, up to the natural limit of our setting. Our results demonstrate that transformers can learn sequential reasoning skills that scale with problem complexity. Moreover, we provide the first optimization-based guarantee demonstrating that constant-depth transformers can learn the state tracking problems in $\mathsf{NC}^1$, which exceeds the prior barrier limited to $\mathsf{TC}^0$, unless the famous conjecture $\mathsf{TC}^0 \neq \mathsf{NC}^1$ is false.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether transformers can learn reasoning patterns that remain useful when a problem requires longer chains than those encountered during training. It studies synthetic state-tracking tasks with gradient-descent training, allowing the authors to prove how length generalization can emerge in specific mathematical settings.

summary.tldr: The paper proves length-generalizable transformer reasoning on synthetic state-tracking tasks, using short-chain training or recursive self-training depending on task structure.

title: Transformers Provably Learn Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Length Generalization

abstract: Existing video steganography methods primarily embed secret information by modifying video content in the spatial or compressed domains. However, such methods are prone to distortion drift and are easily detected by steganalysis. Generative steganography, which avoids direct modification of the cover data, offers a promising alternative. Despite recent advances, most generative steganography studies focus on images and are difficult to extend to videos because of compression-induced distortions and the unique architecture of video generation models. To address these challenges, we propose LD-RoViS, a training-free and robust video steganography framework for the deterministic latent diffusion model. By modulating implicit conditional parameters during the diffusion process, LD-RoViS constructs a dedicated steganographic channel. Additionally, we introduce a novel multi-mask mechanism to mitigate errors caused by video compression and post-processing. The experimental results demonstrate that LD-RoViS can embed approximately 12,000 bits of data into a 5-second video with an extraction accuracy exceeding 99\%. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/xiangkun1999/LD-RoViS.

paragraphs: Video steganography hides information inside video. LD-RoViS instead places information into the video-generation process itself, using a deterministic latent diffusion model without additional training.

The method adjusts implicit conditioning parameters during diffusion to create a channel for carrying secret data. This shifts the embedding mechanism away from direct alterations to an existing cover video. Those robustness measures address a central difficulty in extending generative steganography from images to videos.

This demonstrates a combination of capacity and extraction reliability in the evaluated setting. The contribution is a training-free framework that couples generation-time embedding with explicit protection against errors introduced by video compression and post-processing.
summary.tldr: LD-RoViS embeds data during diffusion video generation without training, reporting roughly 12,000 bits per five-second video with over 99% extraction accuracy.

title: LD-RoViS: Training-free Robust Video Steganography for Deterministic Latent Diffusion Model

abstract: There is growing concern over the safety of powerful diffusion models, as they are often misused to produce inappropriate, not-safe-for-work content or generate copyrighted material or data of individuals who wish to be forgotten. Many existing methods tackle these issues by heavily relying on text-based negative prompts or retraining the model to eliminate certain features or samples. In this paper, we take a radically different approach, directly modifying the sampling trajectory by leveraging a negation set (e.g., unsafe images, copyrighted data, or private data) to avoid specific regions of data distribution, without needing to retrain or fine-tune the model. We formally derive the relationship between the expected denoised samples that are safe and those that are unsafe, leading to our *safe* denoiser, which ensures its final samples are away from the area to be negated. We achieve state-of-the-art safety performance in large-scale datasets such as the CoPro dataset while also enabling significantly more cost-effective sampling than existing methodologies.

paragraphs: Diffusion models may generate content that users want excluded, including inappropriate images, copyrighted material, or data associated with people requesting removal. This paper introduces a sampling-time method that uses a negation set of such examples to steer generation away from specified regions of the data distribution.

The approach directly modifies the sampling trajectory without retraining or fine-tuning the model. The authors derive a relationship between expected denoised samples associated with safe and unsafe regions, then use that relationship to construct a safe denoiser. On large-scale datasets including CoPro, the method achieves reported state-of-the-art safety performance and substantially more cost-effective sampling than existing approaches. The contribution is therefore both a formal denoiser construction and a practical way to apply exclusions during generation. It makes the supplied negation set an actionable part of the sampling process while leaving the underlying model’s training untouched.
summary.tldr: A training-free denoiser uses a negation set to steer diffusion sampling away from specified unwanted regions.

title: Training-Free Safe Denoisers for Safe Use of Diffusion Models

abstract: Class imbalance in graph data presents a significant challenge for effective node classification, particularly in semi-supervised scenarios. In this work, we formally introduce the concept of geometric imbalance, which captures how message passing on class-imbalanced graphs leads to geometric ambiguity among minority-class nodes in the riemannian manifold embedding space. We provide a rigorous theoretical analysis of geometric imbalance on the riemannian manifold and propose a unified framework that explicitly mitigates it through pseudo-label alignment, node reordering, and ambiguity filtering. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks show that our approach consistently outperforms existing methods, especially under severe class imbalance. Our findings offer new theoretical insights and practical tools for robust semi-supervised node classification.

paragraphs: When graph classes have very different numbers of nodes, learning to classify the minority classes becomes difficult. This paper examines that problem in semi-supervised classification, where labels are available for only part of the graph. Its focus is how passing information between connected nodes affects the geometry of the learned representations.

The authors introduce geometric imbalance to describe the ambiguity that message passing creates among minority-class nodes in a Riemannian manifold embedding space. This connects unequal class representation to the structure of the space in which nodes are represented. They provide a theoretical analysis of the phenomenon and design a framework intended to mitigate it explicitly.

The framework combines pseudo-label alignment, node reordering, and ambiguity filtering. Across diverse benchmark experiments, it consistently outperforms existing methods, with particularly strong results under severe class imbalance. The contribution is both explanatory and practical: it identifies a geometric consequence of imbalance and uses that analysis to guide a method for more robust node classification.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes geometric ambiguity affecting minority graph classes and introduces a framework that improves classification under imbalance.

title: Geometric Imbalance in Semi-Supervised Node Classification

abstract: Video inpainting and editing have long been challenging tasks in the video generation community, requiring extensive computational resources and large datasets to train models with satisfactory performance. Recent breakthroughs in large-scale video foundation models have greatly enhanced text-to-video generation capabilities. This naturally leads to the idea of leveraging the prior knowledge from these powerful generators to facilitate video inpainting and editing. In this work, we investigate the feasibility of employing pre-trained text-to-video foundation models for high-quality video inpainting and editing without additional training. Specifically, we introduce a model-agnostic denoising sampler that optimizes the trajectory by maximizing the log-likelihood expectation conditioned on the known video segments. To enable efficient dynamic object removal and replacement, we propose a latent mask fuser that performs accurate video masking directly in latent space, eliminating the need for explicit VAE decoding and encoding. We implement our approach in widely-used foundation generators such as CogVideoX and HunyuanVideo, demonstrating the model-agnostic nature of our sampler. Comprehensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations confirm that our method achieves outstanding video inpainting and editing performance in a plug-and-play fashion.

paragraphs: Video inpainting and editing often require substantial training resources and large datasets. ZeroPatcher investigates whether pretrained text-to-video generators already contain enough useful knowledge to perform these tasks without additional training. Its approach changes the sampling process used with the generator so that known parts of a video guide the generated result.

The proposed denoising sampler optimizes the generation trajectory by maximizing an expected log-likelihood conditioned on known video segments. This makes the available video content part of the objective guiding the trajectory. For removing or replacing moving objects, a latent mask fuser performs video masking directly in the model’s latent space, avoiding explicit decoding and re-encoding through the variational autoencoder.

The authors implement the method with CogVideoX and HunyuanVideo, providing evidence that the sampler can work across different foundation generators. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations report strong inpainting and editing performance in a plug-and-play setting. The contribution is a reusable sampling and masking procedure that applies pretrained video-generation capabilities to editing without further model training.
summary.tldr: ZeroPatcher enables video inpainting and editing without additional training by guiding pretrained generators with a new sampler and latent-space masking.

title: ZeroPatcher: Training-free Sampler for Video Inpainting and Editing

abstract: We study agnostic online learning from continuous-time data streams, a setting that naturally arises in applications such as environmental monitoring, personalized recommendation, and high-frequency trading. Unlike classical discrete-time models, learners in this setting must interact with a continually evolving data stream while making queries and updating models only at sparse, strategically selected times. We develop a general theoretical framework for learning from both *oblivious* and *adaptive* data streams, which may be noisy and non-stationary. For oblivious streams, we present a black-box reduction to classical online learning that yields a regret bound of $T \cdot R(S)/S$ for any class with discrete-time regret $R(S)$, where $T$ is the time horizon and $S$ is the *query budget*. For adaptive streams, which can evolve in response to learner actions, we design a dynamic query strategy in conjunction with a novel importance weighting scheme that enables unbiased loss estimation. In particular, for hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}$ with a finite Littlestone dimension, we establish a tight regret bound of $\tilde{\Theta}(T \cdot \sqrt{\mathsf{Ldim}(\mathcal{H})/S})$ that holds in both settings. Our results provide the first *quantitative* characterization of agnostic learning in continuous-time online environments with limited interaction.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning from a continuously changing stream when the learner can query it and update only at selected moments. The data may be noisy or non-stationary. The central question is how much performance is lost when interaction is limited, rather than assuming that the learner observes a new labeled example at every discrete step.

For streams that do not react to the learner, the authors give a reduction to classical online learning. If a discrete-time method has regret R(S) after S interactions, their construction yields regret T times R(S) divided by S over a time horizon T. For streams that respond to learner actions, they combine dynamic query timing with importance weighting to estimate losses without bias.

For hypothesis classes with finite Littlestone dimension, the paper establishes matching regret bounds up to logarithmic factors in both settings. Regret scales with the time horizon and with the square root of class complexity divided by query budget. This quantifies how additional observations can improve learning and how a more complex hypothesis class increases the difficulty of sparse interaction.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes how query budgets and hypothesis complexity govern regret when learning from continuous-time streams.

title: Agnostic Continuous-Time Online Learning

abstract: Large language models often possess latent capabilities that lie dormant unless explicitly elicited, or surfaced, through fine-tuning or prompt engineering. Predicting, assessing, and understanding these latent capabilities pose significant challenges in the development of effective, safe AI systems. In this work, we recast elicitation as an information-constrained fine-tuning problem and empirically characterize upper bounds on the minimal number of parameters needed to achieve specific task performances. We find that training as few as 10–100 randomly chosen parameters—several orders of magnitude fewer than state-of-the-art parameter-efficient methods—can recover up to 50\% of the performance gap between pretrained-only and full fine-tuned models, and 1,000s to 10,000s of parameters can recover 95\% of this performance gap. We show that a logistic curve fits the relationship between the number of trained parameters and model performance gap recovery. This scaling generalizes across task formats and domains, as well as model sizes and families, extending to reasoning models and remaining robust to increases in inference compute. To help explain this behavior, we consider a simplified picture of elicitation via fine-tuning where each trainable parameter serves as an encoding mechanism for accessing task-specific knowledge. We observe a relationship between the number of trained parameters and how efficiently relevant model capabilities can be accessed and elicited, offering a potential route to distinguish elicitation from teaching.

paragraphs: A pretrained language model may possess useful capabilities that its ordinary responses do not reveal. This paper studies how much fine-tuning is sufficient to surface those capabilities. It treats elicitation as an information-constrained problem and uses successful training configurations to establish empirical upper bounds on the number of parameters needed for particular performance levels.

Training only 10–100 randomly selected parameters can recover up to half the performance gap between a pretrained model and a fully fine-tuned one. Training thousands to tens of thousands can recover 95% of that gap. The authors find that a logistic curve describes gap recovery as the number of trained parameters increases, with the pattern extending across tested tasks, model families, sizes, reasoning models, and increased inference compute.

To interpret this pattern, the paper considers a simplified account in which trainable parameters encode ways to access task-relevant knowledge. The observed relationship suggests that relatively small changes can substantially improve access to existing capabilities. This offers a possible route toward distinguishing elicitation from teaching, without establishing that every measured improvement comes exclusively from previously dormant knowledge.
summary.tldr: Fine-tuning very few parameters can recover substantial performance, providing an empirical way to study latent capability elicitation.

title: Quantifying Elicitation of Latent Capabilities in Language Models

abstract: Manipulation in cluttered environments is challenging due to spatial dependencies among objects, where an improper manipulation order can cause collisions or blocked access. Existing approaches often overlook these spatial relationships, limiting their flexibility and scalability. To address these limitations, we propose OrderMind, a unified spatial-aware manipulation ordering framework that directly learns object manipulation priorities based on spatial context. Our architecture integrates a spatial context encoder with a temporal priority structuring module. We construct a spatial graph using k-Nearest Neighbors to aggregate geometric information from the local layout and encode both object-object and object-manipulator interactions to support accurate manipulation ordering in real-time. To generate physically and semantically plausible supervision signals, we introduce a spatial prior labeling method that guides a vision-language model to produce reasonable manipulation orders for distillation. We evaluate OrderMind on our Manipulation Ordering Benchmark, comprising 163,222 samples of varying difficulty. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world environments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms prior approaches in effectiveness and efficiency, enabling robust manipulation in cluttered scenes.

paragraphs: In cluttered environments, the order in which a robot manipulates objects can determine whether it collides with something or blocks access to another object. OrderMind learns manipulation priorities from the spatial arrangement of the scene. The focus is on deciding a workable order while accounting for relationships that approaches overlooking spatial dependencies may miss.

summary.tldr: OrderMind learns object manipulation priorities from spatial relationships, improving ordering effectiveness and efficiency in simulated and real cluttered environments.

title: Learning Spatial-Aware Manipulation Ordering

abstract: Scaling models has led to significant advancements in deep learning, but training these models in decentralized settings remains challenging due to communication bottlenecks. While existing compression techniques are effective in data-parallel, they do not extend to model parallelism. Unlike data-parallel training, where weight gradients are exchanged, model-parallel requires compressing activations and activation gradients as they propagate through layers, accumulating compression errors. We propose a novel compression algorithm that compresses both forward and backward passes, enabling up to 99% compression with no convergence degradation with negligible memory/compute overhead. By leveraging a recursive structure in transformer networks, we predefine a low-dimensional subspace to confine the activations and gradients, allowing full reconstruction in subsequent layers. Our method achieves up to 100x improvement in communication efficiency and enables training billion-parameter-scale models over low-end GPUs connected via consumer-grade internet speeds as low as 80Mbps, matching the convergence of centralized datacenter systems with 100Gbps connections with model parallel.

Unlike data-parallel training, where weight gradients are exchanged, model-parallel requires compressing activations and activation gradients as they propagate through layers, accumulating compression errors. By leveraging a recursive structure in transformer networks, we predefine a low-dimensional subspace to confine the activations and gradients, allowing full reconstruction in subsequent layers. These are stated maximum gains, showing how substantially the method can reduce communication requirements.

title: Subspace Networks: Scaling Decentralized Training with Communication-Efficient Model Parallelism

abstract: This paper presents a latent variable structured prediction model for discriminative supervised clustering of items called the Latent Left-linking Model (L3M). We present an online clustering algorithm for L3M based on a feature-based item similarity function. We provide a learning framework for estimating the similarity function and present a fast stochastic gradient-based learning technique. In our experiments on coreference resolution and document clustering, L3 M outperforms several existing online as well as batch supervised clustering techniques.

In our experiments on coreference resolution and document clustering, L3 M outperforms several existing online as well as batch supervised clustering techniques.

paragraphs: The paper studies supervised clustering, where training information helps determine how items should be grouped. It introduces the Latent Left-linking Model, abbreviated L3M, as a discriminative structured-prediction model with latent variables. This formulation treats the grouping of items as the prediction problem to be learned.

The authors provide an online clustering algorithm driven by a feature-based similarity function between items. They also give a framework for learning that function, together with a fast stochastic-gradient training method. The similarity used to make clustering decisions is therefore estimated through learning, linking the representation of item relationships to the supervised clustering task.

Experiments cover coreference resolution and document clustering. L3M outperforms several existing supervised clustering methods, including both online and batch approaches, in these evaluations. The contribution brings together a latent-variable formulation, an online grouping procedure, and an efficient learning technique. The reported results show that this combination can compete favorably with methods using either style of clustering.
summary.tldr: L3M learns feature-based similarities for online supervised clustering and outperforms several online and batch methods in two applications.

title: A Discriminative Latent Variable Model for Online Clustering

abstract: This paper presents new consistent algorithms for multiclass learning with complex performance measures, defined by arbitrary functions of the confusion matrix. This setting includes as a special case all loss-based performance measures, which are simply linear functions of the confusion matrix, but also includes more complex performance measures such as the multiclass G-mean and micro F_1 measures. We give a general framework for designing consistent algorithms for such performance measures by viewing the learning problem as an optimization problem over the set of feasible confusion matrices, and give two specific instantiations based on the Frank-Wolfe method for concave performance measures and on the bisection method for ratio-of-linear performance measures. The resulting algorithms are provably consistent and outperform a multiclass version of the state-of-the-art SVMperf method in experiments; for large multiclass problems, the algorithms are also orders of magnitude faster than SVMperf.

paragraphs: Multiclass classifiers may be judged by measures that combine several kinds of correct and incorrect predictions. A confusion matrix records those outcomes, but a performance measure can depend on its entries nonlinearly. This paper develops a framework for learning with such objectives, including multiclass G-mean and micro F1 as well as ordinary loss-based measures.

The main idea is to optimize over the set of confusion matrices that classifiers can achieve. This moves the performance measure into the center of the learning problem. The authors develop two concrete algorithms: one uses Frank-Wolfe optimization for concave measures, and the other uses bisection for measures expressed as ratios of linear functions.

The resulting algorithms are provably consistent, connecting their learning behavior to the intended performance objective. In experiments, they outperform a multiclass adaptation of SVMperf; on large multiclass problems, they are also orders of magnitude faster. The work therefore offers both a general way to organize complex objectives and specific algorithms with theoretical and empirical support for the covered measure families.
summary.tldr: Optimizing over feasible confusion matrices yields consistent multiclass algorithms for complex measures with strong reported performance and speed.

title: Consistent Multiclass Algorithms for Complex Performance Measures

abstract: Given two sets of variables, derived from a common set of samples, sparse Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) seeks linear combinations of a small number of variables in each set, such that the induced \emphcanonical variables are maximally correlated. Sparse CCA is NP-hard. We propose a novel combinatorial algorithm for sparse diagonal CCA, \textiti.e., sparse CCA under the additional assumption that variables within each set are standardized and uncorrelated. Our algorithm operates on a low rank approximation of the input data and its computational complexity scales linearly with the number of input variables. It is simple to implement, and parallelizable. In contrast to most existing approaches, our algorithm administers precise control on the sparsity of the extracted canonical vectors, and comes with theoretical data-dependent global approximation guarantees, that hinge on the spectrum of the input data. Finally, it can be straightforwardly adapted to other constrained variants of CCA enforcing structure beyond sparsity. We empirically evaluate the proposed scheme and apply it on a real neuroimaging dataset to investigate associations between brain activity and behavior measurements.

paragraphs: Sparse canonical correlation analysis looks for two small groups of variables whose weighted combinations are strongly correlated across shared samples. Finding the best sparse combinations is computationally hard. This paper addresses the diagonal version of the problem, which assumes that variables within each group have been standardized and are mutually uncorrelated.

The proposed combinatorial algorithm works with a low-rank approximation of the input. Its computational cost grows linearly with the number of variables, and the authors describe it as straightforward to implement and parallelize. It also provides precise control over how many variables appear in the resulting combinations, making sparsity an explicit part of the solution.

The theoretical contribution is a global approximation guarantee whose strength depends on the input data’s spectrum. Thus, the guarantee is sensitive to the data rather than a claim of exact recovery for every input. The authors evaluate the method empirically, including a neuroimaging application connecting brain activity with behavior, and describe adaptations to constraints beyond sparsity.
summary.tldr: A combinatorial algorithm efficiently approximates sparse diagonal CCA with explicit sparsity control and data-dependent guarantees.

title: A Simple and Provable Algorithm for Sparse Diagonal CCA

abstract: The Gumbel trick is a method to sample from a discrete probability distribution, or to estimate its normalizing partition function. The method relies on repeatedly applying a random perturbation to the distribution in a particular way, each time solving for the most likely configuration. We derive an entire family of related methods, of which the Gumbel trick is one member, and show that the new methods have superior properties in several settings with minimal additional computational cost. In particular, for the Gumbel trick to yield computational benefits for discrete graphical models, Gumbel perturbations on all configurations are typically replaced with so-called low-rank perturbations. We show how a subfamily of our new methods adapts to this setting, proving new upper and lower bounds on the log partition function and deriving a family of sequential samplers for the Gibbs distribution. Finally, we balance the discussion by showing how the simpler analytical form of the Gumbel trick enables additional theoretical results.

paragraphs: The Gumbel trick uses random perturbations and repeated most-likely-configuration searches to sample discrete distributions or estimate their normalizing partition functions. This paper shows that the trick belongs to a broader family of related methods. Several members have better properties in particular settings while adding little computational cost.

For discrete graphical models, perturbing every possible configuration can undermine the computational benefits of this approach. A common alternative uses low-rank perturbations. The authors show how a subfamily of their methods works in this setting, deriving new upper and lower bounds on the log partition function. They also construct a family of sequential samplers for the Gibbs distribution, extending the framework from normalization estimates to sampling.

The comparison remains qualified: the new methods improve on the Gumbel trick in several settings, while the original method retains advantages. In particular, its simpler analytical form enables additional theoretical results. The contribution broadens the set of perturbation-based tools and clarifies that their benefits depend on both computational and analytical considerations.
summary.tldr: A broader family of Gumbel-related methods improves some sampling and normalization tasks while preserving useful tradeoffs with the original trick.

title: Lost Relatives of the Gumbel Trick

abstract: We investigate, theoretically and empirically, the effectiveness of kernel K-means++ samples as landmarks in the Nyström method for low-rank approximation of kernel matrices. Previous empirical studies (Zhang et al., 2008; Kumar et al.,2012) observe that the landmarks obtained using (kernel) K-means clustering define a good low-rank approximation of kernel matrices. However, the existing work does not provide a theoretical guarantee on the approximation error for this approach to landmark selection. We close this gap and provide the first bound on the approximation error of the Nyström method with kernel K-means++ samples as landmarks. Moreover, for the frequently used Gaussian kernel we provide a theoretically sound motivation for performing Lloyd refinements of kernel K-means++ landmarks in the instance space. We substantiate our theoretical results empirically by comparing the approach to several state-of-the-art algorithms.

paragraphs: The Nyström method constructs a low-rank approximation of a kernel matrix using selected landmarks. Which landmarks are chosen affects the quality of that approximation. Earlier empirical work suggested that landmarks derived from kernel clustering work well, but the approach lacked a theoretical guarantee on its approximation error.

This paper supplies the first such bound for landmarks selected through kernel K-means++ sampling. The result gives a mathematical basis for a choice that had previously been supported empirically. It connects a specific landmark-selection procedure to control of the error in the resulting matrix approximation.

For the Gaussian kernel, the authors also provide theoretical motivation for refining the selected landmarks through Lloyd updates in the original instance space. This addresses both initial landmark selection and subsequent refinement. Comparisons with several state-of-the-art algorithms substantiate the theoretical results empirically. The contribution is therefore an explanation of why these clustering-based landmarks can be effective, together with evidence about their use in practical approximation procedures.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes an approximation-error bound for Nyström landmarks chosen by kernel K-means++ and motivates refinements for Gaussian kernels.

title: Nyström Method with Kernel K-means++ Samples as Landmarks

abstract: This work studies the robustness certification problem of neural network models, which aims to find certified adversary-free regions as large as possible around data points. In contrast to the existing approaches that seek regions bounded uniformly along all input features, we consider non-uniform bounds and use it to study the decision boundary of neural network models. We formulate our target as an optimization problem with nonlinear constraints. Then, a framework applicable for general feedforward neural networks is proposed to bound the output logits so that the relaxed problem can be solved by the augmented Lagrangian method. Our experiments show the non-uniform bounds have larger volumes than uniform ones. Compared with normal models, the robust models have even larger non-uniform bounds and better interpretability. Further, the geometric similarity of the non-uniform bounds gives a quantitative, data-agnostic metric of input features’ robustness.

Then, a framework applicable for general feedforward neural networks is proposed to bound the output logits so that the relaxed problem can be solved by the augmented Lagrangian method. paragraphs: Robustness certification seeks a region around an input within which adversarial changes cannot alter the model’s decision. This paper studies regions whose permitted changes differ across input features. Such non-uniform bounds can describe the local decision boundary more flexibly than bounds that impose the same allowance on every feature.

The authors formulate the search for these regions as an optimization problem with nonlinear constraints. They propose a framework for general feedforward networks that bounds the output logits, the scores used to make predictions. These bounds allow a relaxed version of the optimization problem to be solved using an augmented Lagrangian method.

In experiments, the non-uniform certified regions have greater volume than uniform ones. Robust models produce still larger non-uniform bounds than normal models and offer better interpretability in the reported comparisons. The authors also use geometric similarity among the bounds to define a quantitative, data-agnostic measure of feature robustness. The contribution thus connects certification with a more detailed description of how robustness varies across features.
summary.tldr: Feature-specific robustness bounds certify larger regions in experiments and reveal more detailed geometry of neural-network decision boundaries.

title: On Certifying Non-Uniform Bounds against Adversarial Attacks

abstract: Tractable probabilistic models obviate the need for unreliable approximate inference approaches and as a result often yield accurate query answers in practice. However, most tractable models that achieve state-of-the-art generalization performance (measured using test set likelihood score) use latent variables. Such models admit poly-time marginal (MAR) inference but do not admit poly-time (full) maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) inference. To address this problem, in this paper, we propose a novel approach for inducing cutset networks, a well-known tractable, highly interpretable representation that does not use latent variables and admits linear time MAR as well as MAP inference. Our approach addresses a major limitation of existing techniques that learn cutset networks from data in that their accuracy is quite low as compared to latent variable models such as ensembles of cutset networks and sum-product networks. The key idea in our approach is to construct deep cutset networks by not only learning them from data but also compiling them from a more accurate latent tractable model. We show experimentally that our new approach yields more accurate MAP estimates as compared with existing approaches and significantly improves the test set log-likelihood score of cutset networks bringing them closer in terms of generalization performance to latent variable models.
