paragraphs: Tractable probabilistic models aim to answer probability queries without relying on approximate inference. Yet efficient answers to one kind of query do not ensure efficient answers to another. The paper notes that many accurate models with latent variables allow polynomial-time marginal inference but lack polynomial-time full maximum-a-posteriori inference, which seeks the most probable complete assignment.

Cutset networks avoid latent variables and support both forms of inference in linear time. Their difficulty has been predictive accuracy: existing learning methods lag behind latent-variable alternatives. The authors propose constructing deep cutset networks using both learning from data and compilation from a more accurate tractable model that contains latent variables.

Compilation allows the final representation to draw on the stronger source model while retaining the inference properties of a cutset network. Experiments show more accurate maximum-a-posteriori estimates than existing approaches and substantial improvements in test log-likelihood. The latter brings cutset networks closer to latent-variable models in generalization performance. The result improves the balance between efficient inference, interpretability, and probabilistic accuracy without claiming to eliminate the accuracy gap.
summary.tldr: Compiling stronger latent-variable models into cutset networks improves accuracy while retaining linear-time marginal and full MAP inference.

title: Look Ma, No Latent Variables: Accurate Cutset Networks via Compilation

abstract: We build new test sets for the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets. Both benchmarks have been the focus of intense research for almost a decade, raising the danger of overfitting to excessively re-used test sets. By closely following the original dataset creation processes, we test to what extent current classification models generalize to new data. We evaluate a broad range of models and find accuracy drops of 3% - 15% on CIFAR-10 and 11% - 14% on ImageNet. However, accuracy gains on the original test sets translate to larger gains on the new test sets. Our results suggest that the accuracy drops are not caused by adaptivity, but by the models’ inability to generalize to slightly "harder" images than those found in the original test sets.

paragraphs: Repeatedly evaluating models on the same benchmark raises a concern: progress might partly reflect adaptation to that particular test set. This paper examines the issue by building new CIFAR-10 and ImageNet test sets while closely following the original dataset creation procedures. It then evaluates a broad range of classifiers on the fresh images.

Accuracy falls by the reported 3%–15% on CIFAR-10 and 11%–14% on ImageNet. These drops show that performance on an established test set can overstate performance on newly collected data, even when the collection process closely follows the original. The new evaluations therefore probe how well benchmark results transfer beyond the familiar test examples.

However, models with accuracy gains on the original test sets achieve even larger gains on the new sets. This preserves evidence of meaningful progress despite the lower absolute scores. The authors interpret the pattern as suggesting difficulty generalizing to slightly harder images, rather than adaptivity to reused tests, as the explanation for the drops. That causal interpretation is presented as a suggestion supported by their results.
summary.tldr: Fresh CIFAR-10 and ImageNet test sets lower accuracy, while preserving model progress and suggesting sensitivity to slightly harder images.

title: Do ImageNet Classifiers Generalize to ImageNet?

abstract: Learning distances that operate directly on multi-dimensional sequences is challenging because such distances are structural by nature and the vectors in sequences are not independent. Generally, distances for sequences heavily depend on the ground metric between the vectors in sequences. We propose to learn the distance for sequences through learning a ground Mahalanobis metric for the vectors in sequences. The learning samples are sequences of vectors for which how the ground metric between vectors induces the overall distance is given, and the objective is that the distance induced by the learned ground metric produces large values for sequences from different classes and small values for those from the same class. We formulate the metric as a parameter of the distance, bring closer each sequence to an associated virtual sequence w.r.t. the distance to reduce the number of constraints, and develop a general iterative solution for any ground-metric-based sequence distance. Experiments on several sequence datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our method.

paragraphs: Comparing sequences of multidimensional vectors requires accounting for their structure and the dependence among their elements. The paper focuses on the ground metric, the rule used to compare individual vectors within those sequences. Because this rule influences the overall sequence distance, learning it offers a way to improve sequence comparisons.

The method learns a Mahalanobis ground metric from labeled sequences. It assumes that the way vector-level comparisons induce the full sequence distance is given. Its objective encourages sequences from the same class to have small distances and sequences from different classes to have large distances, linking the learned metric to the desired discrimination.

To reduce the number of constraints, the authors associate each sequence with a virtual sequence and bring the pair closer under the chosen distance. They develop an iterative solution applicable to sequence distances based on a ground metric. Experiments on several sequence datasets demonstrate effectiveness and efficiency, supporting adaptation of the underlying vector comparison as a general strategy for learning structured sequence distances.
summary.tldr: The method learns sequence distances by adapting a Mahalanobis metric for their component vectors and reducing optimization constraints with virtual sequences.

title: Learning Distance for Sequences by Learning a Ground Metric

abstract: Probabilistic clustering models (or equivalently, mixture models) are basic building blocks in countless statistical models and involve latent random variables over discrete spaces. For these models, posterior inference methods can be inaccurate and/or very slow. In this work we introduce deep network architectures trained with labeled samples from any generative model of clustered datasets. At test time, the networks generate approximate posterior samples of cluster labels for any new dataset of arbitrary size. We develop two complementary approaches to this task, requiring either O(N) or O(K) network forward passes per dataset, where N is the dataset size and K the number of clusters. Unlike previous approaches, our methods sample the labels of all the data points from a well-defined posterior, and can learn nonparametric Bayesian posteriors since they do not limit the number of mixture components. As a scientific application, we present a novel approach to neural spike sorting for high-density multielectrode arrays.

paragraphs: Probabilistic clustering describes uncertainty over which cluster each observation belongs to. Computing that uncertainty can be slow or inaccurate because cluster assignments are discrete latent variables. This paper trains neural networks to generate approximate posterior samples of assignments, using labeled datasets sampled from a generative clustering model.

At test time, the networks handle new datasets of arbitrary size. The authors develop two complementary approaches: one needs a number of forward passes proportional to the number of observations, while the other needs passes proportional to the number of clusters. These counts describe how network evaluations scale with the dataset or its clustering.

Both approaches sample labels for all observations from a well-defined posterior. They also avoid fixing an upper limit on the number of mixture components, allowing them to learn nonparametric Bayesian posteriors. The paper presents neural spike sorting for high-density multielectrode arrays as a scientific application. Its contribution is a learned route to approximate clustering inference that accommodates variable dataset sizes and an unrestricted number of clusters.
summary.tldr: Neural Clustering Processes learn to sample approximate cluster-label posteriors for variable-size datasets without imposing a fixed limit on cluster count.

title: Neural Clustering Processes

abstract: Sharing parameters in multi-agent deep reinforcement learning has played an essential role in allowing algorithms to scale to a large number of agents. Parameter sharing between agents significantly decreases the number of trainable parameters, shortening training times to tractable levels, and has been linked to more efficient learning. However, having all agents share the same parameters can also have a detrimental effect on learning. We demonstrate the impact of parameter sharing methods on training speed and converged returns, establishing that when applied indiscriminately, their effectiveness is highly dependent on the environment. We propose a novel method to automatically identify agents which may benefit from sharing parameters by partitioning them based on their abilities and goals. Our approach combines the increased sample efficiency of parameter sharing with the representational capacity of multiple independent networks to reduce training time and increase final returns.

However, having all agents share the same parameters can also have a detrimental effect on learning. We demonstrate the impact of parameter sharing methods on training speed and converged returns, establishing that when applied indiscriminately, their effectiveness is highly dependent on the environment. We propose a novel method to automatically identify agents which may benefit from sharing parameters by partitioning them based on their abilities and goals. paragraphs: Sharing network parameters across reinforcement-learning agents reduces the number of trainable parameters and can make large populations tractable to train. It can also improve learning efficiency. However, using the same parameters for every agent can hurt learning. This paper examines how the value of sharing depends on the environment and the agents involved.

The authors study effects on both training speed and final returns, finding that indiscriminate sharing has strongly environment-dependent effectiveness. They propose automatically partitioning agents according to their abilities and goals, identifying groups that may benefit from common parameters. This makes the sharing decision responsive to differences among agents rather than applying a single arrangement to the entire population.

The approach combines the sample-efficiency benefits of sharing with the representational capacity of multiple independent networks. The reported outcome is reduced training time and increased final returns. The contribution treats parameter sharing as a choice about which agents can usefully learn together, providing a way to retain computational benefits while accommodating distinct capabilities and objectives.
summary.tldr: Automatically grouping agents by abilities and goals enables selective parameter sharing that reduces training time and improves final returns.

title: Scaling Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Selective Parameter Sharing

abstract: Recent findings have shown multiple graph learning models, such as graph classification and graph matching, are highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks, i.e. small input perturbations in graph structures and node attributes can cause the model failures. Existing defense techniques often defend specific attacks on particular multiple graph learning tasks. This paper proposes an attack-agnostic graph-adaptive 1-Lipschitz neural network, ERNN, for improving the robustness of deep multiple graph learning while achieving remarkable expressive power. A K_l-Lipschitz Weibull activation function is designed to enforce the gradient norm as K_l at layer l. The nearest matrix orthogonalization and polar decomposition techniques are utilized to constraint the weight norm as 1/K_l and make the norm-constrained weight close to the original weight. The theoretical analysis is conducted to derive lower and upper bounds of feasible K_l under the 1-Lipschitz constraint. The combination of norm-constrained weight and activation function leads to the 1-Lipschitz neural network for expressive and robust multiple graph learning.
originalAbstract: Recent findings have shown multiple graph learning models, such as graph classification and graph matching, are highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks, i.e. small input perturbations in graph structures and node attributes can cause the model failures. Existing defense techniques often defend specific attacks on particular multiple graph learning tasks. This paper proposes an attack-agnostic graph-adaptive 1-Lipschitz neural network, ERNN, for improving the robustness of deep multiple graph learning while achieving remarkable expressive power. A K_l-Lipschitz Weibull activation function is designed to enforce the gradient norm as K_l at layer l. The nearest matrix orthogonalization and polar decomposition techniques are utilized to constraint the weight norm as 1/K_l and make the norm-constrained weight close to the original weight. The theoretical analysis is conducted to derive lower and upper bounds of feasible K_l under the 1-Lipschitz constraint. The combination of norm-constrained weight and activation function leads to the 1-Lipschitz neural network for expressive and robust multiple graph learning.

This paper proposes ERNN, a graph-adaptive network intended to improve robustness across multiple-graph learning without tailoring the defense to a specific attack.

The design combines a Weibull activation function with constraints on the layer weights. At layer l, the activation enforces a gradient norm of K_l, while the weight norm is constrained to its reciprocal. Nearest matrix orthogonalization and polar decomposition impose the weight constraint while keeping the constrained weights close to their original values.

Together, these components produce a 1-Lipschitz network, controlling how strongly the network can amplify input changes while seeking to retain expressive power. The paper derives lower and upper bounds on feasible values of K_l under that constraint. Its central contribution is this coordinated activation-and-weight construction and its theoretical analysis for robust multiple-graph learning.
summary.tldr: ERNN combines constrained weights and a Weibull activation to build expressive 1-Lipschitz networks for robust multiple-graph learning.

title: Expressive 1-Lipschitz Neural Networks for Robust Multiple Graph Learning against Adversarial Attacks

abstract: Ranking problems based on pairwise comparisons, such as those arising in online gaming, often involve a large pool of items to order. In these situations, the gap in performance between any two items can be significant, and the smallest and largest winning probabilities can be very close to zero or one. Furthermore, each item may be compared only to a subset of all the items, so that not all pairwise comparisons are observed. In this paper, we study the performance of the Bradley-Terry-Luce model for ranking from pairwise comparison data under more realistic settings than those considered in the literature so far. In particular, we allow for near-degenerate winning probabilities and arbitrary comparison designs. We obtain novel results about the existence of the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) and the corresponding $\ell_2$ estimation error without the bounded winning probability assumption commonly used in the literature and for arbitrary comparison graph topologies. Central to our approach is the reliance on the Fisher information matrix to express the dependence on the graph topologies and the impact of the values of the winning probabilities on the estimation risk and on the conditions for the existence of the MLE. Our bounds recover existing results as special cases but are more broadly applicable.

paragraphs: Ranking from pairwise comparisons becomes difficult when competitors differ greatly and only some pairs are observed. Winning probabilities may approach zero or one, while the pattern of available comparisons can be irregular. This paper analyzes the Bradley-Terry-Luce ranking model under these conditions, broadening settings commonly used in earlier theory.

The authors derive results about whether the maximum likelihood estimator exists and how large its estimation error can be. Their analysis allows arbitrary comparison graph structures and removes the usual requirement that winning probabilities stay bounded away from zero and one. Allowing these cases does not assert that an estimator always exists; the work characterizes conditions for its existence.

The Fisher information matrix is central to the analysis. It expresses how the comparison graph and winning probabilities jointly influence estimation risk and existence conditions. The resulting bounds recover previous results as special cases while applying more broadly. This gives a unified way to account for both uneven competition and incomplete comparisons in ranking guarantees.
summary.tldr: New Bradley-Terry-Luce estimation guarantees accommodate arbitrary comparison graphs and winning probabilities close to zero or one.

title: Generalized Results for the Existence and Consistency of the MLE in the Bradley-Terry-Luce Model

abstract: We propose a model-agnostic randomized learning framework based on Random Hypothesis Subspace Sampling (RHSS). Given any hypothesis class, it randomly samples $k$ hypotheses and learns a near-optimal model from their span by simply solving a linear least square problem in $O(n k^2)$ time, where $n$ is the number of training instances. On the theory side, we derive the performance guarantee of RHSS from a generic subspace approximation perspective, leveraging properties of metric entropy and random matrices. On the practical side, we apply the RHSS framework to learn kernel, network and tree based models. Experimental results show they converge efficiently as $k$ increases and outperform their model-specific counterparts including random Fourier feature, random vector functional link and extra tree on real-world data sets.

paragraphs: Learning methods often use optimization procedures tailored to a particular model family. This paper proposes Random Hypothesis Subspace Sampling, or RHSS, as a shared alternative. It begins with a hypothesis class, randomly selects k candidate hypotheses, and learns a model from their span: the collection of their linear combinations.

Once those candidates are selected, learning reduces to a linear least-squares problem. The stated computational cost is O(n k²), where n is the number of training examples. The theoretical analysis studies how well the sampled subspace can approximate the desired solution, using metric entropy and random-matrix properties to derive performance guarantees.

The authors apply the framework to kernel, network, and tree models. In their experiments, performance converges efficiently as k increases, and RHSS outperforms the tested model-specific alternatives: random Fourier features, random vector functional links, and extra trees. The contribution is a common sampling-and-fitting approach across several model families, backed by approximation theory and empirical results, rather than a separate learning procedure for each family.
summary.tldr: RHSS learns combinations of randomly sampled hypotheses through least squares, providing one framework for kernel, network, and tree models.

title: A Model-Agnostic Randomized Learning Framework based on Random Hypothesis Subspace Sampling

abstract: The recent focus on the efficiency of deep neural networks (DNNs) has led to significant work on model compression approaches, of which weight pruning is one of the most popular. At the same time, there is rapidly-growing computational support for efficiently executing the unstructured-sparse models obtained via pruning. Yet, most existing pruning methods minimize just the number of remaining weights, i.e. the size of the model, rather than optimizing for inference time. We address this gap by introducing SPDY, a new compression method which automatically determines layer-wise sparsity targets achieving a desired inference speedup on a given system, while minimizing accuracy loss. SPDY is the composition of two new techniques. The first is an efficient and general dynamic programming algorithm for solving constrained layer-wise compression problems, given a set of layer-wise error scores. The second technique is a local search procedure for automatically determining such scores in an accurate and robust manner. Experiments across popular vision and language models show that SPDY guarantees speedups while recovering higher accuracy relative to existing strategies, both for one-shot and gradual pruning scenarios, and is compatible with most existing pruning approaches. We also extend our approach to the recently-proposed task of pruning with very little data, where we achieve the best known accuracy recovery when pruning to the GPU-supported 2:4 sparsity pattern.

paragraphs: Weight pruning often targets the number of parameters remaining in a neural network, but a smaller model is not automatically faster on a particular system. SPDY instead chooses sparsity levels for individual layers to reach a requested inference speedup while minimizing accuracy loss. Its optimization target therefore includes actual execution efficiency.

The method combines two components. A dynamic programming algorithm solves a constrained layer-wise compression problem when given error scores for the layers. A local search procedure determines those scores accurately and robustly. Together, they automate how the pruning budget is distributed across the network.

Experiments on vision and language models report guaranteed speedups with higher recovered accuracy than existing strategies, covering both one-shot and gradual pruning. SPDY is also compatible with most existing pruning approaches. In an extension to pruning with very little data, the authors report the best known accuracy recovery for the GPU-supported 2:4 sparsity pattern. The results connect compression choices directly to the speed target on a given system.
summary.tldr: SPDY automatically allocates layer sparsity to meet system-specific inference speedups while limiting accuracy loss.

title: SPDY: Accurate Pruning with Speedup Guarantees

abstract: Building generalizable goal-conditioned agents from rich observations is a key to reinforcement learning (RL) solving real world problems. Traditionally in goal-conditioned RL, an agent is provided with the exact goal they intend to reach. However, it is often not realistic to know the configuration of the goal before performing a task. A more scalable framework would allow us to provide the agent with an example of an analogous task, and have the agent then infer what the goal should be for its current state. We propose a new form of state abstraction called goal-conditioned bisimulation that captures functional equivariance, allowing for the reuse of skills to achieve new goals. We learn this representation using a metric form of this abstraction, and show its ability to generalize to new goals in real world manipulation tasks. Further, we prove that this learned representation is sufficient not only for goal-conditioned tasks, but is amenable to any downstream task described by a state-only reward function.

paragraphs: Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning usually assumes that an agent receives an exact description of the state it should reach. This paper addresses situations where that configuration is unavailable before acting. Instead, the intended framework lets an agent receive an example of an analogous task and infer a suitable goal for its own current situation.

The authors introduce goal-conditioned bisimulation, a form of state abstraction that captures functional equivariance. The purpose is to represent relationships that let a skill remain useful when the particular state and goal change. They learn the representation through a metric version of the abstraction, connecting the formal notion of task similarity to a representation that an agent can use.

The learned representation generalizes to new goals in real-world manipulation tasks. The paper also proves a broader sufficiency result: the representation supports goal-conditioned tasks and downstream tasks whose rewards depend only on state. That reward restriction defines the stated scope of the broader result. Together, the findings connect learning by analogy with a formal account of reusable representations.
summary.tldr: Goal-conditioned bisimulation learns representations that support skill reuse and generalization to new goals through task analogies.

title: Bisimulation Makes Analogies in Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Transferability estimation has been an essential tool in selecting a pre-trained model and the layers in it for transfer learning, to transfer, so as to maximize the performance on a target task and prevent negative transfer. Existing estimation algorithms either require intensive training on target tasks or have difficulties in evaluating the transferability between layers. To this end, we propose a simple, efficient, and effective transferability measure named TransRate. Through a single pass over examples of a target task, TransRate measures the transferability as the mutual information between features of target examples extracted by a pre-trained model and their labels. We overcome the challenge of efficient mutual information estimation by resorting to coding rate that serves as an effective alternative to entropy. From the perspective of feature representation, the resulting TransRate evaluates both completeness (whether features contain sufficient information of a target task) and compactness (whether features of each class are compact enough for good generalization) of pre-trained features. Theoretically, we have analyzed the close connection of TransRate to the performance after transfer learning. Despite its extraordinary simplicity in 10 lines of codes, TransRate performs remarkably well in extensive evaluations on 35 pre-trained models and 16 downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Choosing a pretrained model, and deciding which layers to transfer, requires estimating how useful its features will be for a new task. Training every candidate extensively can make that selection expensive. TransRate provides a transferability score from a single pass over labeled examples of the target task.

The score estimates the mutual information between extracted features and target labels, using coding rate as an efficient substitute for entropy. Its interpretation combines completeness and compactness: whether the features retain enough task-relevant information, and whether examples from each class form sufficiently compact feature groups. These two properties connect the score to both information preservation and generalization.

The authors provide theoretical analysis linking TransRate to performance after transfer learning. They also evaluate it across 35 pretrained models and 16 downstream tasks, reporting strong performance despite an implementation of only ten lines. The practical contribution is an inexpensive basis for comparing models and layers before committing to transfer training, supported by both analysis and broad empirical evaluation.
summary.tldr: TransRate estimates the transferability of pretrained features in one pass using an efficient information-based score.

title: Frustratingly Easy Transferability Estimation

abstract: Task-free continual learning (CL) aims to learn a non-stationary data stream without explicit task definitions and not forget previous knowledge. The widely adopted memory replay approach could gradually become less effective for long data streams, as the model may memorize the stored examples and overfit the memory buffer. Second, existing methods overlook the high uncertainty in the memory data distribution since there is a big gap between the memory data distribution and the distribution of all the previous data examples. To address these problems, for the first time, we propose a principled memory evolution framework to dynamically evolve the memory data distribution by making the memory buffer gradually harder to be memorized with distributionally robust optimization (DRO). We then derive a family of methods to evolve the memory buffer data in the continuous probability measure space with Wasserstein gradient flow (WGF). The proposed DRO is w.r.t the worst-case evolved memory data distribution, thus guarantees the model performance and learns significantly more robust features than existing memory-replay-based methods. Extensive experiments on existing benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods for alleviating forgetting. As a by-product of the proposed framework, our method is more robust to adversarial examples than existing task-free CL methods.

paragraphs: Task-free continual learning handles changing data streams without explicit task boundaries while trying to preserve earlier knowledge. Replaying stored examples is a common strategy, but a model can eventually memorize its buffer. The buffer also gives an uncertain picture of past data because it differs substantially from the full history.

This paper proposes evolving the memory distribution to make its contents progressively harder to memorize. It formulates the process through distributionally robust optimization, training against a worst-case evolved memory distribution. Wasserstein gradient flow supplies a way to derive a family of methods that change the buffer’s data distribution within a continuous space of probability measures.

The framework ties its performance guarantee to that worst-case evolved distribution and reports more robust learned features than existing replay methods. Benchmark experiments demonstrate reduced forgetting. The method also shows greater robustness to adversarial examples than the compared task-free continual-learning approaches, suggesting that challenging the model through memory evolution can help both retention and resistance to perturbations.
summary.tldr: Evolving replay memory through distributionally robust optimization reduces forgetting and improves reported adversarial robustness in task-free continual learning.

title: Improving Task-free Continual Learning by Distributionally Robust Memory Evolution

abstract: The use of deep neural networks for modelling system dynamics is increasingly popular, but long-term prediction accuracy and out-of-distribution generalization still present challenges. In this study, we address these challenges by considering the parameters of dynamical systems as factors of variation of the data and leverage their ground-truth values to disentangle the representations learned by generative models. Our experimental results in phase-space and observation-space dynamics, demonstrate the effectiveness of latent-space supervision in producing disentangled representations, leading to improved long-term prediction accuracy and out-of-distribution robustness.
originalAbstract: The use of deep neural networks for modelling system dynamics is increasingly popular, but long-term prediction accuracy and out-of-distribution generalization still present challenges. In this study, we address these challenges by considering the parameters of dynamical systems as factors of variation of the data and leverage their ground-truth values to disentangle the representations learned by generative models. Our experimental results in phase-space and observation-space dynamics, demonstrate the effectiveness of latent-space supervision in producing disentangled representations, leading to improved long-term prediction accuracy and out-of-distribution robustness.

paragraphs: Neural models of dynamical systems face two connected difficulties: predictions can become inaccurate over long horizons, and performance can deteriorate outside the training distribution. This paper investigates whether the internal representation learned by a generative model can help address both problems. It focuses on how the model represents the parameters governing a system's dynamics.

The method treats those parameters as distinct factors responsible for variation in the data. It uses their ground-truth values to supervise the model's latent space, encouraging a disentangled representation. The supervision therefore concerns how the model organizes its internal description of the system, alongside the broader task of modeling dynamics. Availability of the true parameter values is part of the stated approach.

Experiments cover both phase-space dynamics and dynamics expressed in observation space. The reported findings associate latent-space supervision with more disentangled representations, better long-term predictions, and stronger robustness outside the training distribution. The contribution is empirical evidence that organizing representations around known system parameters can improve the evaluated dynamics models.
summary.tldr: Supervising generative models with true system parameters improves representation disentanglement, long-term prediction, and out-of-distribution robustness in the reported experiments.

title: Disentangled Generative Models for Robust Prediction of System Dynamics

abstract: We demonstrate the potential of few-shot translation systems, trained with unpaired language data, for both high and low-resource language pairs. We show that with only 5 examples of high-quality translation data shown at inference, a transformer decoder-only model trained solely with self-supervised learning, is able to match specialized supervised state-of-the-art models as well as more general commercial translation systems. In particular, we outperform the best performing system on the WMT’21 English-Chinese news translation task by only using five examples of English-Chinese parallel data at inference. Furthermore, the resulting models are two orders of magnitude smaller than state-of-the-art language models. We then analyze the factors which impact the performance of few-shot translation systems, and highlight that the quality of the few-shot demonstrations heavily determines the quality of the translations generated by our models. Finally, we show that the few-shot paradigm also provides a way to control certain attributes of the translation — we show that we are able to control for regional varieties and formality using only a five examples at inference, paving the way towards controllable machine translation systems.

paragraphs: This paper studies translation with a decoder-only transformer trained through self-supervision on unpaired language data. At inference time, the model receives a small set of high-quality translation examples. The authors demonstrate the potential of this approach for both high-resource and low-resource language pairs, separating general language training from the examples used to guide translation.

With five translation demonstrations, the models can match specialized supervised state-of-the-art systems and general commercial translation systems in the reported evaluations. On the WMT'21 English-Chinese news translation task, the approach outperforms the best-performing system using only five parallel examples at inference. The resulting models are also two orders of magnitude smaller than state-of-the-art language models.

The quality of the demonstrations strongly influences translation quality, making example selection central to the approach. Demonstrations can also guide particular output attributes: the authors show control over regional varieties and formality with five examples. The findings therefore concern both translation performance and a practical mechanism for steering how a translation is expressed through the examples supplied.
summary.tldr: Five high-quality translation examples can guide self-supervised models to strong translation performance and control regional variety or formality.

title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Few-shot Learning for Machine Translation

abstract: We present an online post-hoc calibration method, called Online Platt Scaling (OPS), which combines the Platt scaling technique with online logistic regression. We demonstrate that OPS smoothly adapts between i.i.d. and non-i.i.d. settings with distribution drift. Further, in scenarios where the best Platt scaling model is itself miscalibrated, we enhance OPS by incorporating a recently developed technique called calibeating to make it more robust. Theoretically, our resulting OPS+calibeating method is guaranteed to be calibrated for adversarial outcome sequences. Empirically, it is effective on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets, with and without distribution drifts, achieving superior performance without hyperparameter tuning. Finally, we extend all OPS ideas to the beta scaling method.

paragraphs: Calibration concerns whether predicted probabilities agree with how often outcomes occur. This paper introduces Online Platt Scaling, or OPS, to adjust a model’s outputs as observations arrive. It combines Platt scaling with online logistic regression, making post-processing responsive to incoming data rather than relying entirely on one fixed calibration fit.

The authors demonstrate that OPS adapts between independent, identically distributed data and settings with distribution drift. They also address a further problem: even the best available Platt scaling model may remain miscalibrated. Adding a technique called calibeating makes the procedure more robust to that situation, and the combined method has a calibration guarantee for adversarial outcome sequences.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, both with and without drift, show superior performance without hyperparameter tuning. The authors also extend the approach to beta scaling. Together, the contributions provide an adaptive calibration procedure, a theoretical guarantee for its strengthened version, and evidence that the approach works across several evaluated data conditions.
summary.tldr: Online Platt Scaling adapts probability calibration to incoming data, while calibeating adds a guarantee for adversarial outcome sequences.

title: Online Platt Scaling with Calibeating

abstract: Diffusion-based graph generative models have recently obtained promising results for graph generation. However, existing diffusion-based graph generative models are mostly one-shot generative models that apply Gaussian diffusion in the dequantized adjacency matrix space. Such a strategy can suffer from difficulty in model training, slow sampling speed, and incapability of incorporating constraints. We propose an autoregressive diffusion model for graph generation. Unlike existing methods, we define a node-absorbing diffusion process that operates directly in the discrete graph space. For forward diffusion, we design a diffusion ordering network , which learns a data-dependent node absorbing ordering from graph topology. For reverse generation, we design a denoising network that uses the reverse node ordering to efficiently reconstruct the graph by predicting the node type of the new node and its edges with previously denoised nodes at a time. Based on the permutation invariance of graph, we show that the two networks can be jointly trained by optimizing a simple lower bound of data likelihood. Our experiments on six diverse generic graph datasets and two molecule datasets show that our model achieves better or comparable generation performance with previous state-of-the-art, and meanwhile enjoys fast generation speed.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to generate graphs through diffusion while respecting their discrete structure. Earlier approaches often add Gaussian noise to a continuous version of the adjacency matrix and generate the graph in one shot. The authors identify potential difficulties with training, sampling speed, and incorporating constraints in that strategy.

Their model instead uses a process that absorbs nodes directly in discrete graph space. A learned ordering network decides the absorption order from the graph’s topology. Generation reverses that order: a denoising network reconstructs one node at a time, predicting its type and its connections to nodes already reconstructed. This makes graph construction a sequence of structured decisions.

The authors use the fact that relabeling nodes does not change the underlying graph to derive a simple likelihood lower bound for jointly training both networks. Across six general graph datasets and two molecular datasets, they report generation quality that matches or improves on previous leading methods, together with fast generation. These results support sequential discrete diffusion as a practical graph-generation approach.
summary.tldr: A diffusion model generates graphs node by node in discrete space, achieving competitive or better generation quality with fast sampling.

title: Autoregressive Diffusion Model for Graph Generation

abstract: We introduce DS-1000, a code generation benchmark with a thousand data science problems spanning seven Python libraries, such as Numpy and Pandas. Compared to prior works, DS-1000 incorporates three core features. First, our problems reflect diverse, realistic, and practical use cases since we collected them from StackOverflow. Second, our automatic evaluation is highly specific (reliable) – across all Codex-002-predicted solutions that our evaluation accepts, only 1.8% of them are incorrect; we achieve this with multi-criteria metrics, checking both functional correctness by running test cases and surface-form constraints by restricting API usages or keywords. Finally, we proactively defend against memorization by slightly modifying our problems to be different from the original StackOverflow source; consequently, models cannot answer them correctly by memorizing the solutions from pre-training. The current best public system (Codex-002) achieves 43.3% accuracy, leaving ample room for improvement. We release our benchmark at https://ds1000-code-gen.github.io.
originalAbstract: We introduce DS-1000, a code generation benchmark with a thousand data science problems spanning seven Python libraries, such as Numpy and Pandas. Compared to prior works, DS-1000 incorporates three core features. First, our problems reflect diverse, realistic, and practical use cases since we collected them from StackOverflow. Second, our automatic evaluation is highly specific (reliable) – across all Codex-002-predicted solutions that our evaluation accepts, only 1.8% of them are incorrect; we achieve this with multi-criteria metrics, checking both functional correctness by running test cases and surface-form constraints by restricting API usages or keywords. Finally, we proactively defend against memorization by slightly modifying our problems to be different from the original StackOverflow source; consequently, models cannot answer them correctly by memorizing the solutions from pre-training. The current best public system (Codex-002) achieves 43.3% accuracy, leaving ample room for improvement. We release our benchmark at https://ds1000-code-gen.github.io.

paragraphs: DS-1000 evaluates whether code-generation systems can solve practical data-science problems. It contains one thousand problems across seven Python libraries, including NumPy and pandas. Drawing the tasks from StackOverflow gives the benchmark a basis in varied questions that arise during real programming work.

Evaluation combines running test cases with checking constraints on API use or keywords. This allows the benchmark to assess both what a solution does and whether it follows requirements about how to do it. Among the Codex-002 solutions accepted by this evaluation, only 1.8% are incorrect. That figure describes incorrect acceptances for those evaluated outputs, rather than every possible aspect of evaluation accuracy.

The authors also slightly modify source problems so that memorizing the original posted solutions is insufficient to answer them correctly. Codex-002, the best public system reported in the abstract, achieves 43.3% accuracy. Together, realistic tasks, multiple evaluation criteria, and changes that resist direct memorization make the benchmark a focused test of data-science coding ability with substantial room for improvement.
summary.tldr: DS-1000 tests data-science code generation on realistic, modified programming problems with execution checks and constraints on solution form.

title: DS-1000: A Natural and Reliable Benchmark for Data Science Code Generation

abstract: Early stopping based on hold-out data is a popular regularization technique designed to mitigate overfitting and increase the predictive accuracy of neural networks. Models trained with early stopping often provide relatively accurate predictions, but they generally still lack precise statistical guarantees unless they are further calibrated using independent hold-out data. This paper addresses the above limitation with conformalized early stopping: a novel method that combines early stopping with conformal calibration while efficiently recycling the same hold-out data. This leads to models that are both accurate and able to provide exact predictive inferences without multiple data splits nor overly conservative adjustments. Practical implementations are developed for different learning tasks—outlier detection, multi-class classification, regression—and their competitive performance is demonstrated on real data.

paragraphs: Early stopping uses held-out data to decide when a neural network should stop training, helping reduce overfitting. Although this can improve prediction accuracy, accurate predictions alone do not supply precise statistical guarantees. Conformal calibration can provide predictive inference, but ordinarily requires independent held-out data beyond the examples already used to select a stopping point.

This paper introduces conformalized early stopping, which combines stopping decisions and conformal calibration while reusing the same held-out data. The contribution is a method for making that reuse statistically valid. It avoids requiring multiple data splits or relying on overly conservative adjustments to account for the shared use of data.

The authors develop practical versions for outlier detection, multiclass classification, and regression, and demonstrate competitive performance on real data. The stated outcome combines accurate models with exact predictive inference. Its practical importance lies in connecting a familiar training procedure to statistical calibration while making more efficient use of the held-out examples that the procedure already requires.
summary.tldr: Conformalized early stopping reuses held-out data for both stopping and calibration while providing exact predictive inference.

title: Conformal Inference is (almost) Free for Neural Networks Trained with Early Stopping

abstract: Domain randomization (DR) is widely used in reinforcement learning (RL) to bridge the gap between simulation and reality by maximizing its average returns under the perturbation of environmental parameters. However, even the most complex simulators cannot capture all details in reality due to finite domain parameters and simplified physical models. Additionally, the existing methods often assume that the distribution of domain parameters belongs to a specific family of probability functions, such as normal distributions, which may not be correct. To overcome these limitations, we propose a new approach to DR by rethinking it from the perspective of adversarial state perturbation, without the need for reconfiguring the simulator or relying on prior knowledge about the environment. We also address the issue of over-conservatism that can occur when perturbing agents to the worst states during training by introducing a Relaxed State-Adversarial Algorithm that simultaneously maximizes the average-case and worst-case returns. We evaluate our method by comparing it to state-of-the-art methods, providing experimental results and theoretical proofs to verify its effectiveness. Our source code and appendix are available at https://github.com/sophialien/RAPPO.

paragraphs: Domain randomization trains reinforcement learning agents across varied simulator parameters to improve transfer to reality. Its reach is restricted by the details a simulator can represent and by assumptions about how those parameters are distributed. Even a complex simulator has a finite parameterization and simplified physical models.

This paper reinterprets domain randomization through adversarial perturbations of states. The proposed approach does not require reconfiguring the simulator or supplying prior knowledge of the environment. It also addresses a drawback of purely worst-case perturbations: training against the worst states can make an agent overly conservative.

The Relaxed State-Adversarial Algorithm therefore simultaneously maximizes average-case and worst-case returns. This objective incorporates both ordinary performance and performance under difficult perturbations into training. The authors provide theoretical proofs and experimental comparisons with state-of-the-art methods to support its effectiveness. The contribution is a different route to robustness, built around state perturbations and a relaxed adversarial objective rather than relying exclusively on distributions over simulator parameters.
summary.tldr: Relaxed adversarial state perturbations combine average-case and worst-case objectives to address limitations of simulator-based domain randomization.

title: Revisiting Domain Randomization via Relaxed State-Adversarial Policy Optimization

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) is a powerful approach for solving optimal control problems. However, RL-trained policies often suffer from the action fluctuation problem, where the consecutive actions significantly differ despite only slight state variations. This problem results in mechanical components’ wear and tear and poses safety hazards. The action fluctuation is caused by the high Lipschitz constant of actor networks. To address this problem, we propose a neural network named LipsNet. We propose the Multi-dimensional Gradient Normalization (MGN) method, to constrain the Lipschitz constant of networks with multi-dimensional input and output. Benefiting from MGN, LipsNet achieves Lipschitz continuity, allowing smooth actions while preserving control performance by adjusting Lipschitz constant. LipsNet addresses the action fluctuation problem at network level rather than algorithm level, which can serve as actor networks in most RL algorithms, making it more flexible and user-friendly than previous works. Experiments demonstrate that LipsNet has good landscape smoothness and noise robustness, resulting in significantly smoother action compared to the Multilayer Perceptron.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning controller can produce sharply different consecutive actions even when its observed state changes only slightly. Such fluctuations can cause mechanical wear and create safety hazards. This paper attributes the problem to high Lipschitz constants in actor networks, meaning that small input changes can produce large changes in the network’s output.

LipsNet addresses that sensitivity through the network architecture. Its Multi-dimensional Gradient Normalization method constrains the Lipschitz constant for networks with multiple input and output dimensions. Adjusting the constant allows the network to produce smoother actions while preserving control performance, making smoothness an explicit property of the actor’s mapping from states to actions.

Because the intervention operates at the network level, LipsNet can serve as the actor in most reinforcement learning algorithms. Experiments report smooth network landscapes, robustness to noise, and significantly smoother actions than a multilayer perceptron. These findings support controlling network sensitivity as a way to reduce action fluctuations while retaining flexibility in the surrounding learning algorithm.
summary.tldr: LipsNet controls actor-network sensitivity to produce smoother, noise-robust actions while preserving control performance.

title: LipsNet: A Smooth and Robust Neural Network with Adaptive Lipschitz Constant for High Accuracy Optimal Control

abstract: This paper tackles the memory hurdle of of processing long context sequences in Large Language Models (LLMs), by presenting a novel approach, Dropping In Convolutions for Long Context Compression (LoCoCo). LoCoCo employs only a fixed-size Key-Value (KV) cache, and can enhance efficiency in both inference and fine-tuning stages. Diverging from prior methods that selectively drop KV pairs based on heuristics, LoCoCo leverages a data-driven adaptive fusion technique, blending previous KV pairs with incoming tokens to minimize the loss of contextual information and ensure accurate attention modeling. This token integration is achieved through injecting one-dimensional convolutional kernels that dynamically calculate mixing weights for each KV cache slot. Designed for broad compatibility with existing LLM frameworks, LoCoCo allows for straightforward "drop-in" integration without needing architectural modifications, while incurring minimal tuning overhead. Experiments demonstrate that LoCoCo maintains consistently outstanding performance across various context lengths and can achieve a high context compression rate during both inference and fine-tuning phases. During inference, we successfully compressed up to $3482$ tokens into a $128$-size KV cache, while retaining comparable performance to the full sequence - an accuracy improvement of up to $0.2791$ compared to baselines at the same cache size. During post-training tuning, we also effectively extended the context length from 4K to 32K using a KV cache of fixed size 512, achieving performance similar to fine-tuning with entire sequences.

paragraphs: Long contexts increase the memory needed to store a language model's attention keys and values. LoCoCo keeps this KV cache at a fixed size by learning how to combine older information with incoming tokens. Its goal is to preserve useful context through adaptive fusion, rather than deciding which stored pairs to discard using heuristics.

It reports accuracy gains of up to 0.2791 over baselines with the same cache size. During post-training tuning, it extends context length from 4K to 32K with a fixed cache of 512, achieving performance similar to full-sequence fine-tuning. These are demonstrated compression outcomes in the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: LoCoCo learns convolutional mixing weights to compress long contexts into a fixed-size KV cache during inference and fine-tuning.

title: LoCoCo: Dropping In Convolutions for Long Context Compression

abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has recently revolutionized the field of neural rendering with its high fidelity and efficiency. However, 3DGS heavily depends on the initialized point cloud produced by Structure-from-Motion (SfM) techniques. When tackling large-scale scenes that unavoidably contain texture-less surfaces, SfM techniques fail to produce enough points in these surfaces and cannot provide good initialization for 3DGS. As a result, 3DGS suffers from difficult optimization and low-quality renderings. In this paper, inspired by classic multi-view stereo (MVS) techniques, we propose GaussianPro, a novel method that applies a progressive propagation strategy to guide the densification of the 3D Gaussians. Compared to the simple split and clone strategies used in 3DGS, our method leverages the priors of the existing reconstructed geometries of the scene and utilizes patch matching to produce new Gaussians with accurate positions and orientations. Experiments on both large-scale and small-scale scenes validate the effectiveness of our method. Our method significantly surpasses 3DGS on the Waymo dataset, exhibiting an improvement of 1.15dB in terms of PSNR. Codes and data are available at https://github.com/kcheng1021/GaussianPro.

paragraphs: GaussianPro addresses a weakness in 3D Gaussian Splatting: its dependence on the initial point cloud used to reconstruct a scene. Structure-from-Motion techniques can provide too few points on surfaces with little texture, especially in large scenes. That sparse starting representation makes optimization harder and can reduce the quality of rendered images.

The method progressively guides where additional 3D Gaussians should be created. Drawing inspiration from multi-view stereo, it uses already reconstructed scene geometry and patch matching to place and orient new Gaussians accurately. This gives the expansion process geometric guidance beyond the simple splitting and cloning strategies used in the original method.

Experiments on both large and small scenes support the approach. On the Waymo dataset, GaussianPro improves PSNR by 1.15 dB over 3D Gaussian Splatting. The result indicates that better-guided scene densification can improve rendering quality when the initial reconstruction is inadequate. Its central contribution is to use existing geometry to help repair weaknesses in how the scene representation grows.
summary.tldr: GaussianPro improves Gaussian-splatting reconstruction by using existing geometry and patch matching to guide the creation of new Gaussians.

title: GaussianPro: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Progressive Propagation

abstract: Speculative decoding is a relatively new decoding framework that leverages small and efficient draft models to reduce the latency of LLMs. In this study, we introduce GliDe and CaPE, two low-hassle modifications to vanilla speculative decoding to further improve the decoding speed of a frozen LLM. Specifically, GliDe is a modified draft model architecture that reuses the cached keys and values from the target LLM, while CaPE is a proposal expansion method that uses the draft model’s confidence scores to help select additional candidate tokens for verification. Extensive experiments on different benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed GliDe draft model significantly reduces the expected decoding latency. Additional evaluation using walltime reveals that GliDe can accelerate Vicuna models up to 2.17x and further extend the improvement to 2.61x with CaPE. We will release our code, data, and the trained draft models.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding uses a smaller draft model to propose text that a larger language model then verifies. This can reduce generation latency, but the draft model’s design and the choice of proposals affect how much speed is gained. This paper introduces two modifications intended to improve decoding speed while keeping the target language model frozen.

GliDe changes the draft model so it can reuse the target model’s cached keys and values. CaPE changes proposal expansion: it uses the draft model’s confidence scores to select additional candidate tokens for verification. The two contributions act on different parts of the process, improving how the draft is produced and how the set of candidates is assembled.

Experiments across different benchmarks show that GliDe substantially reduces expected decoding latency. Measurements of actual elapsed time report speedups of up to 2.17 times for Vicuna models, increasing to 2.61 times with CaPE. These are reported maxima from the evaluations. Together, the results show that modifying the drafting and proposal stages can accelerate a fixed target model.
summary.tldr: GliDe reuses target-model caches and CaPE expands proposals using confidence, achieving reported Vicuna decoding speedups of up to 2.61 times together.

title: GliDe with a CaPE: A Low-Hassle Method to Accelerate Speculative Decoding

abstract: Counterfactuals, or modified inputs that lead to a different outcome, are an important tool for understanding the logic used by machine learning classifiers and how to change an undesirable classification. Even if a counterfactual changes a classifier’s decision, however, it may not affect the true underlying class probabilities, i.e. the counterfactual may act like an adversarial attack and “fool” the classifier. We propose a new framework for creating modified inputs that change the true underlying probabilities in a beneficial way which we call Trustworthy Actionable Perturbations (TAP). This includes a novel verification procedure to ensure that TAP change the true class probabilities instead of acting adversarially. Our framework also includes new cost, reward, and goal definitions that are better suited to effectuating change in the real world. We present PAC-learnability results for our verification procedure and theoretically analyze our new method for measuring reward. We also develop a methodology for creating TAP and compare our results to those achieved by previous counterfactual methods.

paragraphs: A counterfactual explanation changes an input so that a classifier produces a different decision. This paper highlights that the changed decision may leave the true underlying class probabilities unaffected. In that case, the modification can resemble an adversarial attack: it changes the classifier’s response without delivering the underlying improvement that the user seeks.

The authors introduce Trustworthy Actionable Perturbations, a framework aimed at beneficial changes in true class probabilities. A new verification procedure is designed to distinguish such changes from adversarial behavior. The framework also revises the definitions of cost, reward, and goals to better reflect the objective of producing meaningful changes in the real world.

The paper provides PAC-learnability results for the verification procedure and a theoretical analysis of its reward measure. It also develops a method for creating these perturbations and compares it with earlier counterfactual approaches. The contribution connects generating a proposed modification with verifying the kind of probabilistic improvement it is meant to achieve, making the underlying target of a changed decision explicit.
summary.tldr: Trustworthy Actionable Perturbations pair input modifications with verification aimed at improving true class probabilities rather than merely changing classifier outputs.

title: Trustworthy Actionable Perturbations

abstract: This paper tackles the emerging challenge of training generative models within a self-consuming loop, wherein successive generations of models are recursively trained on mixtures of real and synthetic data from previous generations. We construct a theoretical framework to rigorously evaluate how this training procedure impacts the data distributions learned by future models, including parametric and non-parametric models. Specifically, we derive bounds on the total variation (TV) distance between the synthetic data distributions produced by future models and the original real data distribution under various mixed training scenarios for diffusion models with a one-hidden-layer neural network score function. Our analysis demonstrates that this distance can be effectively controlled under the condition that mixed training dataset sizes or proportions of real data are large enough. Interestingly, we further unveil a phase transition induced by expanding synthetic data amounts, proving theoretically that while the TV distance exhibits an initial ascent, it declines beyond a threshold point. Finally, we present results for kernel density estimation, delivering nuanced insights such as the impact of mixed data training on error propagation.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes generative models trained in a recursive loop, where each generation learns from real data mixed with synthetic data produced by earlier models. The central question is how the generated distribution changes across generations relative to the original real-data distribution. The framework considers both parametric and nonparametric models.

For diffusion models with a one-hidden-layer neural network score function, the authors bound this discrepancy using total variation distance under several mixed-training scenarios. They show that the distance can be controlled when the mixed datasets are sufficiently large or the proportion of real data is sufficiently high. These are sufficient conditions within the analyzed settings.

The theory also identifies a phase transition as synthetic-data quantities increase: the distance initially grows, then decreases beyond a threshold. This makes the relationship between synthetic-data volume and distributional error nonmonotonic in the analysis. Additional results for kernel density estimation examine how mixed-data training affects error propagation, extending the investigation beyond the specified diffusion-model formulation.
summary.tldr: Theoretical bounds show conditions under which recursively mixing real and synthetic training data can control generative distribution drift.

title: Towards Theoretical Understandings of Self-Consuming Generative Models

abstract: Important applications such as fraud or spam detection or churn prediction involve binary classification problems where the datasets are imbalanced and the cost of false positives greatly differs from the cost of false negatives. We focus on classification trees, in particular oblique trees, which subsume both the traditional axis-aligned trees and logistic regression, but are more accurate than both while providing interpretable models. Rather than using ROC curves, we advocate a loss based on minimizing the false negatives subject to a maximum false positive rate, which we prove to be equivalent to minimizing a weighted 0/1 loss. This yields a curve of classifiers that provably dominates the ROC curve, but is hard to optimize due to the 0/1 loss. We give the first algorithm that can iteratively update the tree parameters globally so that the weighted 0/1 loss decreases monotonically. Experiments on various datasets with class imbalance or class costs show this indeed dominates ROC-based classifiers and significantly improves over previous approaches to learn trees based on weighted purity criteria or over- or undersampling.

paragraphs: In binary classification, the two kinds of mistakes can have very different consequences. Fraud, spam, and churn prediction also often involve uneven class frequencies. This paper focuses on learning classification trees for those conditions, especially oblique trees, whose decision rules can combine input features and encompass both conventional axis-aligned trees and logistic regression.

The authors formulate the objective as reducing false negatives while respecting a maximum false-positive rate. They prove an equivalence to a weighted loss that counts classification mistakes, producing a curve of classifiers that provably dominates the ROC curve in their formulation. Directly optimizing this discrete mistake-counting objective is the main computational obstacle.

Their algorithm updates tree parameters globally and guarantees that the weighted loss decreases monotonically during iteration. This links the training procedure directly to the intended error tradeoff. Experiments on datasets with class imbalance or unequal error costs show improvements over ROC-based classifiers and earlier tree-learning approaches using weighted purity measures or changes to class sampling.
summary.tldr: A tree-learning algorithm directly reduces cost-weighted classification errors and produces improved false-positive versus false-negative tradeoffs.

title: Beyond the ROC Curve: Classification Trees Using Cost-Optimal Curves, with Application to Imbalanced Datasets

abstract: AI-based frameworks for protein engineering use self-supervised learning (SSL) to obtain representations for downstream mutation effect predictions. The most common training objective for these methods is wildtype accuracy: given a sequence or structure where a wildtype residue has been masked, predict the missing amino acid. Wildtype accuracy, however, does not align with the primary goal of protein engineering, which is to suggest a mutation rather than to identify what already appears in nature. Here we present Evolutionary Ranking (EvoRank), a training objective that incorporates evolutionary information derived from multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) to learn more diverse protein representations. EvoRank corresponds to ranking amino-acid likelihoods in the probability distribution induced by an MSA. This objective forces models to learn the underlying evolutionary dynamics of a protein. Across a variety of phenotypes and datasets, we demonstrate that EvoRank leads to dramatic improvements in zero-shot performance and can compete with models fine-tuned on experimental data. This is particularly important in protein engineering, where it is expensive to obtain data for fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Protein representation models commonly learn by reconstructing a masked amino acid from a naturally occurring protein. That objective rewards identifying the existing residue, while protein engineering often aims to suggest a useful replacement. This paper addresses that mismatch by changing what the model is trained to predict.

Evolutionary Ranking, or EvoRank, uses evolutionary information from multiple sequence alignments. Its objective ranks amino-acid likelihoods according to the probability distribution induced by an alignment. Training therefore incorporates information about alternatives represented across related sequences, encouraging more diverse protein representations and learning about the protein's evolutionary dynamics.

Across several phenotypes and datasets, the authors report large improvements in zero-shot mutation-effect prediction. They also find that EvoRank can compete with models fine-tuned on experimental data. This matters because obtaining such data is expensive in protein engineering. The results support aligning the self-supervised objective more closely with mutation selection, while the comparison with fine-tuned models remains a reported empirical finding across the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: EvoRank trains protein models to rank evolution-informed amino-acid alternatives, improving zero-shot mutation-effect prediction.

title: Evolution-Inspired Loss Functions for Protein Representation Learning

abstract: Fast convolution algorithms, including Winograd and FFT, can efficiently accelerate convolution operations in deep models. However, these algorithms depend on high-precision arithmetic to maintain inference accuracy, which conflicts with the model quantization. To resolve this conflict and further improve the efficiency of quantized convolution, we proposes SFC, a new algebra transform for fast convolution by extending the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) with symbolic computing, in which only additions are required to perform the transformation at specific transform points, avoiding the calculation of irrational number and reducing the requirement for precision. Additionally, we enhance convolution efficiency by introducing correction terms to convert invalid circular convolution outputs of the Fourier method into effective ones. The numerical error analysis is presented for the first time in this type of work and proves that our algorithms can provide a 3.68× multiplication reduction for 3×3 convolution, while the Winograd algorithm only achieves a 2.25× reduction with similarly low numerical errors. Experiments carried out on benchmarks and FPGA show that our new algorithms can further improve the computation efficiency of quantized models while maintaining accuracy, surpassing both the quantization-alone method and existing works on fast convolution quantization.
originalAbstract: Fast convolution algorithms, including Winograd and FFT, can efficiently accelerate convolution operations in deep models. However, these algorithms depend on high-precision arithmetic to maintain inference accuracy, which conflicts with the model quantization. To resolve this conflict and further improve the efficiency of quantized convolution, we proposes SFC, a new algebra transform for fast convolution by extending the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) with symbolic computing, in which only additions are required to perform the transformation at specific transform points, avoiding the calculation of irrational number and reducing the requirement for precision. Additionally, we enhance convolution efficiency by introducing correction terms to convert invalid circular convolution outputs of the Fourier method into effective ones. The numerical error analysis is presented for the first time in this type of work and proves that our algorithms can provide a 3.68× multiplication reduction for 3×3 convolution, while the Winograd algorithm only achieves a 2.25× reduction with similarly low numerical errors. Experiments carried out on benchmarks and FPGA show that our new algorithms can further improve the computation efficiency of quantized models while maintaining accuracy, surpassing both the quantization-alone method and existing works on fast convolution quantization.

SFC addresses this tension with an algebraic transform that extends the discrete Fourier transform using symbolic computation. At selected transform points, the transformation requires only additions, avoiding irrational-number calculations and lowering the precision requirement.

The method also introduces correction terms that turn otherwise invalid circular-convolution outputs into usable results. This improves how much useful computation the Fourier approach delivers. Numerical error analysis connects these algorithmic changes to the balance between reducing multiplication counts and keeping errors small, which is central when arithmetic uses limited precision.

For 3×3 convolution, the paper establishes a 3.68-fold multiplication reduction, compared with a 2.25-fold reduction for Winograd at similarly low numerical error. These figures concern multiplication counts. Benchmark and FPGA experiments additionally report improved computational efficiency while maintaining accuracy, surpassing quantization alone and existing fast-convolution quantization approaches. The findings support designing the transform itself around low-precision arithmetic.
summary.tldr: SFC redesigns Fourier-based convolution for low precision, reducing multiplication counts and improving reported efficiency while maintaining accuracy.

title: SFC: Achieve Accurate Fast Convolution under Low-precision Arithmetic

abstract: Many existing two-phase kernel-based hypothesis transfer learning algorithms employ the same kernel regularization across phases and rely on the known smoothness of functions to obtain optimality. Therefore, they fail to adapt to the varying and unknown smoothness between the target/source and their offset. This paper introduces Smoothness Adaptive Transfer Learning (SATL), a two-phase kernel ridge regression (KRR)-based algorithm to address these limitations. We first demonstrate that employing a misspecified fixed bandwidth Gaussian kernel in target-only KRR learning can achieve minimax optimality when the true function resides in Sobolev spaces. Leveraging this result, SATL enables the estimators to provably and universally adapt to the varying and unknown Sobolev smoothness of the source and offset functions. We derive the minimax lower bound of the learning problem in excess risk and show that SATL achieves a matching upper bound up to logarithmic factors. The optimal statistical rate reveals the factors influencing the transfer dynamics and efficacy, including the source sample size and the relative strength between domains. The theoretical findings and the effectiveness of SATL are confirmed by several experiments.

title: Smoothness Adaptive Hypothesis Transfer Learning

abstract: Diffusion-based re-ranking is a common method used for retrieving instances by performing similarity propagation in a nearest neighbor graph. However, existing techniques that construct the affinity graph based on pairwise instances can lead to the propagation of misinformation from outliers and other manifolds, resulting in inaccurate results. To overcome this issue, we propose a novel Cluster-Aware Similarity (CAS) diffusion for instance retrieval. The primary concept of CAS is to conduct similarity diffusion within local clusters, which can reduce the influence from other manifolds explicitly. To obtain a symmetrical and smooth similarity matrix, our Bidirectional Similarity Diffusion strategy introduces an inverse constraint term to the optimization objective of local cluster diffusion. Additionally, we have optimized a Neighbor-guided Similarity Smoothing approach to ensure similarity consistency among the local neighbors of each instance. Evaluations in instance retrieval and object re-identification validate the effectiveness of the proposed CAS, our code is publicly available.
