paragraphs: Instance retrieval often improves an initial ranking by propagating similarity through a nearest-neighbor graph. The idea is that nearby examples can reinforce useful matches. However, connections based only on pairs of instances can also spread misleading information from outliers or from different underlying groups, reducing retrieval accuracy.

Cluster-Aware Similarity diffusion changes where this propagation occurs. It diffuses similarity within local clusters, explicitly reducing influence from other groups. The method also introduces Bidirectional Similarity Diffusion, which adds an inverse constraint to the optimization objective to obtain a symmetric, smooth similarity matrix. A further neighbor-guided smoothing step encourages agreement among each instance's local neighbors.

These components address related aspects of the same problem: controlling which examples exchange similarity information and making the resulting relationships consistent. Evaluations on instance retrieval and object re-identification support the effectiveness of the approach. The findings suggest that the structure used to propagate similarity matters alongside the initial pairwise scores, because a poorly organized graph can amplify misleading relationships.
summary.tldr: Cluster-Aware Similarity diffusion improves retrieval by restricting similarity propagation to local clusters and smoothing neighboring relationships.

title: Cluster-Aware Similarity Diffusion for Instance Retrieval

abstract: Multimodal alignment between language and vision is the fundamental topic in current vision-language model research. Contrastive Captioners (CoCa), as a representative method, integrates Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) and Image Caption (IC) into a unified framework, resulting in impressive results. CLIP imposes a bidirectional constraints on global representations of entire images and sentences. Although IC conducts an unidirectional image-to-text generation on local representation, it lacks any constraint on local text-to-image reconstruction, which limits the ability to understand images at a fine-grained level when aligned with texts. To achieve multimodal alignment from both global and local perspectives, this paper proposes Symmetrizing Contrastive Captioners (SyCoCa), which introduces bidirectional interactions on images and texts across the global and local representation levels. Specifically, we expand a Text-Guided Masked Image Modeling (TG-MIM) head based on ITC and IC heads. The improved SyCoCa further leverages textual cues to reconstruct contextual images and visual cues to predict textual contents. When implementing bidirectional local interactions, the local contents of images tend to be cluttered or unrelated to their textual descriptions. Thus, we employ an attentive masking strategy to select effective image patches for interaction. Extensive experiments on five vision-language tasks, including image-text retrieval, image-captioning, visual question answering, and zero-shot/finetuned image classification, validate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

Contrastive Captioners combine global image-text matching with image-to-text generation. This paper identifies an asymmetry at the local level: generating text from visual features does not also impose a corresponding text-to-image reconstruction task.

SyCoCa adds text-guided masked image modeling to establish local interactions in both directions. Text helps reconstruct image content, while visual information helps predict text. Together with global alignment, these objectives encourage connections between the modalities at more than one level of detail.

Not every image region is useful for this interaction, because local content can be cluttered or unrelated to its description. An attentive masking strategy selects effective image patches for the task. Experiments support the approach across image-text retrieval, captioning, visual question answering, and zero-shot and fine-tuned classification. The contribution is a more symmetric training design whose local reconstruction signals focus on image content relevant to the cross-modal interaction.
summary.tldr: SyCoCa adds text-guided image reconstruction and attentive masking to strengthen bidirectional local image-text alignment.

title: SyCoCa: Symmetrizing Contrastive Captioners with Attentive Masking for Multimodal Alignment

abstract: We study the probabilistic modeling performed by Autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) through the angle of time directionality, addressing a question first raised in (Shannon, 1951). For large enough models, we empirically find a time asymmetry in their ability to learn natural language: a difference in the average log-perplexity when trying to predict the next token versus when trying to predict the previous one. This difference is at the same time subtle and very consistent across various modalities (language, model size, training time, ...). Theoretically, this is surprising: from an information-theoretic point of view, there should be no such difference. We provide a theoretical framework to explain how such an asymmetry can appear from sparsity and computational complexity considerations, and outline a number of perspectives opened by our results.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether language is equally learnable in two directions: predicting the next token from preceding text and predicting the previous token from following text. It studies this question through autoregressive language models, comparing their average log-perplexity. This measure captures how well each model assigns probabilities to the tokens it must predict.

For sufficiently large models, the authors find a small but consistent difference between the two directions. The pattern persists across variations in language, model size, and training time. The finding is empirical and qualified by model size; it describes an observed asymmetry in learning rather than a universal rule for every language model.

The result is surprising because information theory alone does not predict such a directional difference. The authors develop a framework showing how sparsity and computational complexity can produce one. This connects the observation to the difficulty of learning a probability distribution with computational resources, beyond the information contained in that distribution itself.
summary.tldr: Sufficiently large language models show a subtle directional learning asymmetry that the paper explains through sparsity and computational complexity.

title: Arrows of Time for Large Language Models

abstract: Kernel conditional mean embeddings (CMEs) offer a powerful framework for representing conditional distributions, but they often face scalability and expressiveness challenges. In this work, we propose a new method that effectively combines the strengths of deep learning with CMEs in order to address these challenges. Specifically, our approach leverages the end-to-end neural network (NN) optimization framework using a kernel-based objective. This design circumvents the computationally expensive Gram matrix inversion required by current CME methods. To further enhance performance, we provide efficient strategies to optimize the remaining kernel hyperparameters. In conditional density estimation tasks, our NN-CME hybrid achieves competitive performance and often surpasses existing deep learning-based methods. Lastly, we showcase its remarkable versatility by seamlessly integrating it into reinforcement learning (RL) contexts. Building on Q-learning, our approach naturally leads to a new variant of distributional RL methods, which demonstrates consistent effectiveness across different environments.

paragraphs: Conditional mean embeddings provide a kernel-based way to represent how a distribution depends on its inputs. Their usefulness can be limited by computational cost and representational flexibility. This paper combines them with neural networks to retain the distributional framework while taking advantage of end-to-end neural optimization.

The proposed hybrid trains a network using a kernel-based objective. This avoids the expensive Gram matrix inversion required by existing conditional mean embedding methods, directly addressing a computational bottleneck. The authors also supply efficient procedures for optimizing the remaining kernel hyperparameters, so the kernel component can be adjusted within the overall approach.

On conditional density estimation tasks, the method is competitive with existing deep learning approaches and often performs better. The paper also extends the construction to reinforcement learning: starting from Q-learning produces a new distributional reinforcement learning variant. Its reported effectiveness across different environments supports the versatility of the hybrid. Together, the results show how neural optimization can make a kernel distribution representation useful across both estimation and decision-making tasks.
summary.tldr: Neural-kernel conditional mean embeddings avoid costly matrix inversion and show competitive results in density estimation and distributional reinforcement learning.

title: Neural-Kernel Conditional Mean Embeddings

abstract: Symbolic models play a key role in cognitive science, expressing computationally precise hypotheses about how the brain implements a cognitive process. Identifying an appropriate model typically requires a great deal of effort and ingenuity on the part of a human scientist. Here, we adapt FunSearch (Romera-Paredes et al. 2024), a recently developed tool that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) in an evolutionary algorithm, to automatically discover symbolic cognitive models that accurately capture human and animal behavior. We consider datasets from three species performing a classic reward-learning task that has been the focus of substantial modeling effort, and find that the discovered programs outperform state-of-the-art cognitive models for each. The discovered programs can readily be interpreted as hypotheses about human and animal cognition, instantiating interpretable symbolic learning and decision-making algorithms. Broadly, these results demonstrate the viability of using LLM-powered program synthesis to propose novel scientific hypotheses regarding mechanisms of human and animal cognition.

paragraphs: Cognitive scientists use symbolic models to express precise hypotheses about learning and decision-making. Finding a model that explains observed behavior usually requires substantial scientific effort. This paper adapts FunSearch, which combines language models with an evolutionary algorithm, to automatically search for programs that describe human and animal behavior.

The authors apply the approach to datasets from three species performing a classic reward-learning task. The resulting programs outperform state-of-the-art cognitive models for each species in the study. The task already has a substantial modeling history, so the comparison tests whether automated program discovery can add useful candidates in an established area of cognitive research.

The discovered programs are interpretable as symbolic learning and decision-making algorithms. Their value therefore extends beyond fitting behavior: researchers can read them as proposed explanations of the processes generating that behavior. The results support language-model-powered program synthesis as a tool for proposing scientific hypotheses. Those programs remain hypotheses about cognition; their predictive performance does not itself establish that brains implement the discovered algorithms.
summary.tldr: An adaptation of FunSearch discovers interpretable cognitive programs that outperform established models on reward-learning data from three species.

title: Discovering Symbolic Cognitive Models from Human and Animal Behavior

abstract: Tabular data generation has attracted significant research interest in recent years, with the tabular diffusion models greatly improving the quality of synthetic data. However, while memorization—where models inadvertently replicate exact or near-identical training data—has been thoroughly investigated in image and text generation, its effects on tabular data remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we conduct the first comprehensive investigation of memorization phenomena in diffusion models for tabular data. Our empirical analysis reveals that memorization appears in tabular diffusion models and increases with larger training epochs. We further examine the influence of factors such as dataset sizes, feature dimensions, and different diffusion models on memorization. Additionally, we provide a theoretical explanation for why memorization occurs in tabular diffusion models. To address this issue, we propose TabCutMix, a simple yet effective data augmentation technique that exchanges randomly selected feature segments between random same-class training sample pairs. Building upon this, we introduce TabCutMixPlus, an enhanced method that clusters features based on feature correlations and ensures that features within the same cluster are exchanged together during augmentation. This clustering mechanism mitigates out-of-distribution (OOD) generation issues by maintaining feature coherence. Experimental results across various datasets and diffusion models demonstrate that TabCutMix effectively mitigates memorization while maintaining high-quality data generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/fangzy96/TabCutMix.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate high-quality tabular data, but generated records may reproduce training examples exactly or nearly exactly. This paper investigates that memorization behavior and finds empirically that it increases with more training epochs. The authors also examine dataset size, feature dimensionality, and model choice, and provide a theoretical explanation for why memorization occurs.

Their proposed remedy, TabCutMix, augments training data by exchanging randomly selected feature segments between randomly chosen examples from the same class. This creates altered training records through combinations of existing examples. TabCutMixPlus refines the procedure by clustering correlated features and moving features in the same cluster together.

Keeping correlated features together helps preserve feature coherence and mitigates the production of out-of-distribution examples during augmentation. Across multiple datasets and diffusion models, experiments show that TabCutMix reduces memorization while maintaining high-quality generation. The work therefore combines an investigation of a previously underexplored behavior in tabular diffusion with a practical augmentation strategy, including a refinement that accounts for relationships among the table’s features.
summary.tldr: TabCutMix reduces memorization in tabular diffusion models by exchanging same-class feature segments, with a refined variant preserving correlated feature groups.

title: Understanding and Mitigating Memorization in Diffusion Models for Tabular Data

abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) generation has made remarkable progress in producing high-quality images, but a fundamental challenge remains: creating backgrounds that naturally accommodate text placement without compromising image quality. This capability is non-trivial for real-world applications like graphic design, where clear visual hierarchy between content and text is essential. Prior work has primarily focused on arranging layouts within existing static images, leaving unexplored the potential of T2I models for generating text-friendly backgrounds. We present TextCenGen, a training-free approach that actively relocates objects before optimizing text regions, rather than directly reducing cross-attention which degrades image quality. Our method introduces: (1) a force-directed graph approach that detects conflicting objects and guides them relocation using cross-attention maps, and (2) a spatial attention constraint that ensures smooth background generation in text regions. Our method is plug-and-play, requiring no additional training while well balancing both semantic fidelity and visual quality. Evaluated on our proposed text-friendly T2I benchmark of 27,000 images across three seed datasets, TextCenGen outperforms existing methods by achieving 23% lower saliency overlap in text regions while maintaining 98% of the original semantic fidelity measured by CLIP score and our proposed Visual-Textual Concordance Metric (VTCM).

paragraphs: An attractive generated image can still make a poor background for text if important objects occupy the intended text region. TextCenGen addresses this graphic-design problem during image generation. It aims to leave suitable space for text while preserving the visual content requested by the prompt and maintaining image quality.

The training-free method first uses cross-attention maps to identify objects that conflict with text placement. A force-directed graph approach guides their relocation, after which a spatial attention constraint encourages a smooth background in the text region. This sequence addresses the image-quality degradation associated with directly reducing cross-attention to clear space.

These results support its ability to make backgrounds more text-friendly while retaining prompt-related content, without additional model training.
summary.tldr: TextCenGen relocates objects during image generation to create text-friendly backgrounds without additional training.

title: TextCenGen: Attention-Guided Text-Centric Background Adaptation for Text-to-Image Generation

abstract: Multilayer matrix factorization (MMF) has recently emerged as a generalized model of, and potentially a more expressive approach than, the classic matrix factorization. This paper considers MMF under a probabilistic formulation, and our focus is on inference methods under variational inference. The challenge in this context lies in determining a variational process that leads to a computationally efficient and accurate approximation of the maximum likelihood inference. One well-known example is the variational autoencoder (VAE), which uses neural networks for the variational process. In this work, we take insight from variational diffusion models in the context of generative models to develop variational inference for MMF. We propose a dimension-reducing diffusion process that results in a new way to interact with the layered structures of the MMF model. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed diffusion variational inference method leads to improved performance scores compared to several existing methods, including the VAE.

paragraphs: Multilayer matrix factorization generalizes classic matrix factorization and may offer a more expressive model. This paper studies its probabilistic formulation, where a central challenge is finding an inference procedure that is both computationally efficient and accurate. The authors focus on variational inference as a way to approximate maximum-likelihood inference.

A variational autoencoder is one established approach, using neural networks to define the variational process. The proposed method instead draws inspiration from variational diffusion models developed for generation. It introduces a diffusion process that reduces dimension, creating a different way for the inference procedure to interact with the factorization model's layered structure.

Experiments show improved performance scores over several existing approaches, including the variational autoencoder. These results support dimension-reducing diffusion as a useful variational mechanism for multilayer matrix factorization. The contribution concerns how inference is organized within the probabilistic model: it connects diffusion-based inference ideas to the layered structure of factorization and demonstrates empirical benefits from that connection.
summary.tldr: A dimension-reducing diffusion process improves variational inference for probabilistic multilayer matrix factorization in the reported experiments.

title: Multilayer Matrix Factorization via Dimension-Reducing Diffusion Variational Inference

abstract: While super-resolution (SR) methods based on diffusion models (DM) have demonstrated inspiring performance, their deployment is impeded due to the heavy request of memory and computation. Recent researchers apply two kinds of methods to compress or fasten the DM. One is to compress the DM into 1-bit, aka binarization, alleviating the storage and computation pressure. The other distills the multi-step DM into only one step, significantly speeding up inference process. Nonetheless, it remains impossible to deploy DM to resource-limited edge devices. To address this problem, we propose BiMaCoSR, which combines binarization and one-step distillation to obtain extreme compression and acceleration. To prevent the catastrophic collapse of the model caused by binarization, we proposed sparse matrix branch (SMB) and low rank matrix branch (LRM). Both auxiliary branches pass the full-precision (FP) information but in different ways. SMB absorbs the extreme values and its output is high rank, carrying abundant FP information. Whereas, the design of LRMB is inspired by LoRA and is initialized with the top r SVD components, outputting low rank representation. The computation and storage overhead of our proposed branches can be safely ignored. Comprehensive comparison experiments are conducted to exhibit BiMaCoSR outperforms current state-of-the-art binarization methods and gains competitive performance compared with FP one-step model. Moreover, we achieve excellent compression and acceleration. BiMaCoSR achieves a 23.8x compression ratio and a 27.4x speedup ratio compared to FP counterpart. Our code and model are available at https://github.com/Kai-Liu001/BiMaCoSR

Our code and model are available at https://github.com/Kai-Liu001/BiMaCoSR

paragraphs: Diffusion models can produce strong super-resolution results, but their memory and computation demands complicate deployment on constrained devices. BiMaCoSR combines two compression strategies: representing model weights with one bit and distilling a process with multiple diffusion steps into a single step. The challenge is preserving image-generation capability when these aggressive reductions are applied together.

The method adds two auxiliary branches that retain full-precision information. A sparse matrix branch absorbs extreme values and supplies a high-rank output carrying richer information. A low-rank matrix branch, inspired by LoRA and initialized from leading singular-value decomposition components, supplies a compact representation. These branches provide complementary information to counter the model collapse that binarization can cause, with overhead the authors describe as negligible.

Experiments report better performance than existing state-of-the-art binarization methods and competitive results against a full-precision one-step model. Relative to its full-precision counterpart, BiMaCoSR achieves 23.8-fold compression and a 27.4-fold speedup. The findings demonstrate a substantial efficiency gain while retaining competitive super-resolution performance in the reported comparisons.
summary.tldr: BiMaCoSR combines one-bit compression and one-step diffusion with two full-precision auxiliary branches to accelerate super-resolution while preserving competitive quality.

title: BiMaCoSR: Binary One-Step Diffusion Model Leveraging Flexible Matrix Compression for Real Super-Resolution

abstract: We revisit the problem of selecting $k$-out-of-$n$ elements with the goal of optimizing an objective function, and ask whether it can be solved approximately with sublinear query complexity. For objective functions that are monotone submodular, [Li, Feldman, Kazemi, Karbasi, NeurIPS’22; Kuhnle, AISTATS’21] gave an $\Omega(n/k)$ query lower bound for approximating to within any constant factor. We strengthen their lower bound to a nearly tight $\tilde{\Omega}(n)$. This lower bound holds even for estimating the value of the optimal subset. When the objective function is additive, we prove that finding an approximately optimal subset still requires near-linear query complexity, but we can estimate the value of the optimal subset in $\tilde{O}(n/k)$ queries, and that this is tight up to polylog factors.

paragraphs: The paper asks how much information an algorithm must obtain to choose a good group of k elements from n candidates. Its main setting involves monotone submodular objectives, where adding elements cannot reduce value and additional elements offer diminishing returns. The question is whether a constant-factor approximation can use substantially fewer than n queries to the objective.

The authors prove a lower bound that is nearly linear in n, strengthening an earlier bound proportional to n/k. Here, “nearly” allows polylogarithmic factors. The result applies even when the algorithm only estimates the best achievable value, without identifying a subset that achieves it. This makes the information requirement relevant to both optimization and value estimation.

For additive objectives, the paper identifies a different relationship between these tasks. Finding an approximately optimal subset still needs nearly linear query complexity, but estimating its value takes roughly n/k queries, up to polylogarithmic factors. The matching bounds establish when estimating an answer can be substantially cheaper than constructing one.
summary.tldr: Nearly linear query complexity is required for constant-factor submodular maximization, even for value estimation, while additive objectives permit cheaper value estimates.

title: A Near Linear Query Lower Bound for Submodular Maximization

abstract: We present a conformal inference method for constructing lower prediction bounds for survival times from right-censored data, extending recent approaches designed for more restrictive type-I censoring scenarios. The proposed method imputes unobserved censoring times using a machine learning model, and then analyzes the imputed data using a survival model calibrated via weighted conformal inference. This approach is theoretically supported by an asymptotic double robustness property. Empirical studies on simulated and real data demonstrate that our method leads to relatively informative predictive inferences and is especially robust in challenging settings where the survival model may be inaccurate.

This approach is theoretically supported by an asymptotic double robustness property. Empirical studies on simulated and real data demonstrate that our method leads to relatively informative predictive inferences and is especially robust in challenging settings where the survival model may be inaccurate.

paragraphs: Survival prediction becomes harder when observation ends before the event of interest occurs. Such right-censored records provide incomplete information about survival times. This paper develops a method for producing lower prediction bounds from these data, extending conformal survival approaches that were designed for the more restrictive setting of type-I censoring.

The procedure first uses a machine learning model to impute censoring times that are not observed. It then applies a survival model to the imputed data and calibrates its predictions through weighted conformal inference. The intended output is a lower bound on survival time, giving a predictive statement that accounts for uncertainty rather than only a single estimated event time.

The theory establishes an asymptotic double robustness property, providing support that concerns behavior as sample size grows. Experiments on simulated and real data produce relatively informative predictions and show particular robustness when the survival model is inaccurate. Together, the results support combining censoring-time imputation with conformal calibration to broaden the settings where useful survival prediction bounds can be constructed.
summary.tldr: The method combines censoring-time imputation and weighted conformal calibration to construct asymptotically doubly robust survival prediction bounds.

title: Doubly Robust Conformalized Survival Analysis with Right-Censored Data

abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have transformed software development by automatically generating code from natural language. Yet challenges remain in generating fully correct code that aligns with user intent. Our study reveals that LLMs tend to pay less attention to user prompts as more code tokens are generated. We hypothesize that this attention dilution issue is an important reason for code generation errors. To mitigate this issue, we propose S*elective Prompt A*nchoring (SPA) to guide code LLMs to pay more attention to user intent when generating code. We evaluate SPA using six base LLMs across six benchmarks. Our results demonstrate that SPA enhances Pass@1 by up to 12.9%, consistently outperforming SOTA code generation methods in all settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/magic-YuanTian/Selective-Prompt-Anchoring.

paragraphs: Generating code from natural language requires a model to keep the user’s requirements relevant throughout generation. This paper observes that language models tend to devote less attention to the prompt as they produce more code tokens. The authors hypothesize that this attention dilution is an important contributor to code-generation errors.

Selective Prompt Anchoring, or SPA, is designed to guide code models back toward the user’s intent during generation. Its focus is the connection between the growing code output and the original request. The motivating distinction is between the measured decline in prompt attention and the proposed explanation that this decline contributes to incorrect code.

The authors evaluate SPA with six base language models across six benchmarks. They report Pass@1 improvements of up to 12.9% and consistent superiority over state-of-the-art code-generation methods in all evaluated settings. Pass@1 concerns success from a single generated attempt, so the result speaks to the usefulness of the first answer. The experiments support prompt anchoring as an effective intervention while the causal explanation remains framed as the authors’ hypothesis.
summary.tldr: Selective Prompt Anchoring reinforces attention to user intent during code generation, improving Pass@1 by up to 12.9% in the reported evaluations.

title: Selective Prompt Anchoring for Code Generation

abstract: A key property of reasoning systems is the ability to make sharp decisions on their input data. For contemporary AI systems, a key carrier of sharp behaviour is the softmax function, with its capability to perform differentiable query-key lookups. It is a common belief that the predictive power of networks leveraging softmax arises from "circuits" which sharply perform certain kinds of computations consistently across many diverse inputs. However, for these circuits to be robust, they would need to generalise well to arbitrary valid inputs. In this paper, we dispel this myth: even for tasks as simple as finding the maximum key, any learned circuitry must disperse as the number of items grows at test time. We attribute this to a fundamental limitation of the softmax function to robustly approximate sharp functions with increasing problem size, prove this phenomenon theoretically, and propose adaptive temperature as an ad-hoc technique for improving the sharpness of softmax at inference time.

paragraphs: Softmax allows neural networks to make differentiable selections among alternatives, making it central to query-key lookups. A sharply focused selection can look like a reliable computational rule. This paper asks whether that sharp behavior persists when the number of input items grows beyond the sizes encountered during training.

The authors prove a limitation: even for a task as simple as selecting the maximum key, learned softmax circuitry disperses as problem size increases. They attribute this to softmax's inability to robustly approximate sharp functions as the number of alternatives grows. Thus, sharp behavior at one input size does not by itself establish robust size generalization.

The paper proposes adapting temperature during inference as an ad hoc way to improve sharpness. This is presented as a technique for improvement, rather than a general resolution of the theoretical limitation. The contribution clarifies why a seemingly crisp learned selection mechanism can become less decisive on larger inputs, and identifies temperature adaptation as one practical response to that problem.
summary.tldr: Softmax-based selections lose sharpness as input size grows, and adaptive inference-time temperature is proposed as a partial practical remedy.

title: Softmax is not Enough (for Sharp Size Generalisation)

abstract: Flow matching models have emerged as a powerful method for generative modeling on domains like images or videos, and even on irregular or unstructured data like 3D point clouds or even protein structures. These models are commonly trained in two stages: first, a data compressor is trained, and in a subsequent training stage a flow matching generative model is trained in the latent space of the data compressor. This two-stage paradigm sets obstacles for unifying models across data domains, as hand-crafted compressors architectures are used for different data modalities. To this end, we introduce INRFlow, a domain-agnostic approach to learn flow matching transformers directly in ambient space. Drawing inspiration from INRs, we introduce a conditionally independent point-wise training objective that enables INRFlow to make predictions continuously in coordinate space. Our empirical results demonstrate that INRFlow effectively handles different data modalities such as images, 3D point clouds and protein structure data, achieving strong performance in different domains and outperforming comparable approaches. INRFlow is a promising step towards domain-agnostic flow matching generative models that can be trivially adopted in different data domains.

paragraphs: INRFlow targets a design obstacle in generative modeling across different data types. Many flow-matching systems first train a compressor and then train a generator in the compressor’s latent space. Because different modalities use specially designed compressors, this two-stage process makes it harder to develop one approach that transfers naturally across domains.

The paper proposes training flow-matching transformers directly in the data’s ambient space. Inspired by implicit neural representations, it introduces a conditionally independent, pointwise training objective that supports predictions continuously over coordinates. This gives the model a coordinate-based way to represent data without first relying on a separately trained, modality-specific compressor.

Experiments cover images, three-dimensional point clouds, and protein structures. The authors report strong performance across these domains and improvements over comparable approaches. These results support the feasibility of a shared generative design for substantially different kinds of data. The paper presents INRFlow as a step toward domain-agnostic flow matching, with the demonstrated breadth coming from the modalities evaluated.
summary.tldr: INRFlow trains coordinate-based flow-matching transformers directly in ambient space, demonstrating strong generation across images, point clouds, and protein structures.

title: INRFlow: Flow Matching for INRs in Ambient Space

abstract: Vision-Language Retrieval-Augmented Generation (VLRAG) systems have been widely applied to Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) to enhance their generation ability. However, the reliance on external multimodal knowledge databases renders VLRAG systems vulnerable to malicious poisoning attacks. In this paper, we introduce PoisonedEye, the first knowledge poisoning attack designed for VLRAG systems. Our attack successfully manipulates the response of the VLRAG system for the target query by injecting only one poison sample into the knowledge database. To construct the poison sample, we follow two key properties for the retrieval and generation process, and identify the solution by satisfying these properties. Besides, we also introduce a class query targeted poisoning attack, a more generalized strategy that extends the poisoning effect to an entire class of target queries. Extensive experiments on multiple query datasets, retrievers, and LVLMs demonstrate that our attack is highly effective in compromising VLRAG systems.

paragraphs: Vision-language retrieval-augmented generation systems consult external multimodal knowledge to improve their responses. That dependence also creates an attack surface: malicious content added to the knowledge database can influence what the system retrieves and generates. PoisonedEye studies this vulnerability through a knowledge poisoning attack designed specifically for these systems.

The paper reports that a single injected poison sample can manipulate the response to a target query. Its construction accounts for two properties associated with retrieval and generation, linking the inserted sample to both stages of the system. The authors also introduce a broader class-targeted variant intended to affect an entire category of queries.

Experiments cover multiple query datasets, retrievers, and large vision-language models, and show that the attacks are highly effective in the evaluated settings. The findings identify the external knowledge database as a consequential part of system security. They also distinguish a narrowly targeted response manipulation from an attack with effects across a query class, broadening the scope of the demonstrated vulnerability.
summary.tldr: PoisonedEye demonstrates that one poisoned database sample can manipulate a vision-language retrieval system’s response to a target query.

title: PoisonedEye: Knowledge Poisoning Attack on Retrieval-Augmented Generation based Large Vision-Language Models

abstract: We present a unified framework for quantifying the similarity between representations through the lens of usable information, offering a rigorous theoretical and empirical synthesis across three key dimensions. First, addressing functional similarity, we establish a formal link between stitching performance and conditional mutual information. We further reveal that stitching is inherently asymmetric, demonstrating that robust functional comparison necessitates a bidirectional analysis rather than a unidirectional mapping. Second, concerning representational similarity, we find that reconstruction-based metrics and standard tools (e.g., CKA, RSA) act as estimators of usable information under specific constraints. Crucially, we show that similarity is relative to the capacity of the predictive family: representations that appear distinct to a rigid observer may be identical to a more expressive one. Third, we demonstrate that representational similarity is sufficient but not necessary for functional similarity. We unify these concepts through a task-granularity hierarchy: similarity on a complex task guarantees similarity on any coarser derivative, establishing representational similarity as the limit of maximum granularity: input reconstruction.

paragraphs: Two neural representations can look different while supporting the same task. This paper connects comparisons of internal representations with comparisons of what those representations let models do. Its organizing idea is usable information: similarity depends on the information that a specified family of predictors can extract, making the observer's capacity part of the comparison.

For functional similarity, the authors formally connect model stitching performance to conditional mutual information. They show that stitching is asymmetric, so testing a mapping in one direction does not provide a robust comparison by itself. For representational similarity, they interpret reconstruction metrics and tools such as CKA and RSA as estimators of usable information under particular constraints.

The framework establishes that representational similarity is sufficient, but not necessary, for functional similarity. It also organizes tasks by granularity: similarity on a complex task guarantees similarity on a coarser derivative of that task. Input reconstruction sits at the most detailed end of this hierarchy, explaining how closely matched representations can imply shared functionality without requiring every functionally similar pair to share equally similar representations.
summary.tldr: Usable information connects representation similarity to shared functionality while showing why comparisons depend on predictor capacity and task granularity.

title: Bridging Functional and Representational Similarity via Usable Information

abstract: Multi-modal remote sensing imagery provides complementary observations of the same geographic scene, yet such observations are frequently incomplete in practice. Existing cross-modal translation methods treat each modality pair as an independent task, resulting in quadratic complexity and limited generalization to unseen modality combinations. We formulate Any-to-Any translation as inference over a shared latent representation of the scene, where different modalities correspond to partial observations of the same underlying semantics. Based on this formulation, we propose Any2Any, a unified latent diffusion framework that projects heterogeneous inputs into a geometrically aligned latent space. Such structure performs anchored latent regression with a shared backbone, decoupling modality-specific representation learning from semantic mapping. Moreover, lightweight target-specific residual adapters are used to correct systematic latent mismatches without increasing inference complexity. To support learning under sparse but connected supervision, we introduce RST-1M, the first million-scale remote sensing dataset with paired observations across five sensing modalities, providing supervision anchors for any-to-any translation. Experiments across 14 translation tasks show that Any2Any consistently outperforms pairwise translation methods and exhibits strong zero-shot generalization to unseen modality pairs. Code and models are available at https://github.com/MiliLab/Any2Any.

paragraphs: Remote sensing instruments provide different views of the same geographic scene, but some observations are often missing. Training a separate translator for every pair of sensing modalities becomes increasingly expensive as modalities are added. Any2Any instead treats translation as recovering a shared scene representation from whichever observations are available.

The framework uses latent diffusion and maps heterogeneous inputs into a geometrically aligned representation space. A shared backbone learns semantic mappings, while modality-specific representation learning handles differences between input types. summary.tldr: Any2Any shares a latent scene representation across remote sensing modalities, improving translation and generalization to unseen modality pairs.

title: Any2Any: Unified Arbitrary Modality Translation for Remote Sensing

abstract: We study bilinear bandits with partially observable features on both the user and item sides. In each of $T$ rounds, the learner selects a user–item pair and observes only the reward for the chosen pair. The reward model is bilinear in the user and item features with an unknown parameter matrix. Existing work commonly reduces this problem to a linear bandit via Kronecker-product features, increasing dimensionality and losing bilinear structure. We propose BiRoLF, an algorithm robust to latent features, which directly leverages the bilinear structure without such linearization. It augments observed feature spaces on both sides with orthogonal complement bases and employs doubly robust (DR) estimation to impute rewards for unselected pairs, constructing matrix-valued pseudo-rewards. We estimate the effective parameter using a bilinear DR-Lasso estimator, which promotes sparsity in components orthogonal to observed features. BiRoLF achieves a $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{(d_x + d_{h_x})(d_y + d_{h_y}) T})$ regret bound, where $d_x$ and $d_y$ are observable feature dimensions, and $d_{h_x}$ and $d_{h_y}$ denote effective orthogonal-complement dimensions. By exploiting the induced block-diagonal Gram structure, BiRoLF performs an exact blockwise update that preserves the full DR-Lasso objective. Numerical experiments show strong regret performance and computational gains.

paragraphs: The paper studies repeated selection of user–item pairs when some features on both sides are hidden. Each round reveals only the selected pair’s reward, which depends bilinearly on user and item features through an unknown matrix. Converting this into a standard linear bandit expands the feature space and loses the explicit bilinear structure.

Those dimensions include observable features and effective complement dimensions. An exact blockwise update exploits the resulting Gram structure while preserving the full estimation objective. Numerical experiments report strong regret performance and computational gains, supporting the value of retaining bilinear structure throughout estimation and updating.
summary.tldr: BiRoLF handles partially hidden user and item features while preserving bilinear structure, with regret guarantees and reported computational gains.

title: Bilinear Bandits with Partially Observable Features

abstract: Many high-stakes AI deployments proceed only if every stakeholder deems the system acceptable relative to their own minimum standard. With randomization over a finite menu of options, this becomes a feasibility question: does there exist a lottery over options that clears all stakeholders’ acceptability bars? We study a query model where the algorithm proposes lotteries and receives only binary accept/reject feedback. We give deterministic and randomized algorithms that either find a unanimously acceptable lottery or certify infeasibility; adaptivity can avoid eliciting many stakeholders’ constraints, and randomization further reduces the expected elicitation cost relative to full elicitation. We complement these upper bounds with worst-case lower bounds (in particular, linear dependence on the number of stakeholders and logarithmic dependence on precision are unavoidable). Finally, we develop learning-augmented algorithms that exploit natural forms of advice (e.g., likely binding stakeholders or a promising lottery), improving query complexity when predictions are accurate while preserving worst-case guarantees.

With randomization over a finite menu of options, this becomes a feasibility question: does there exist a lottery over options that clears all stakeholders’ acceptability bars? We study a query model where the algorithm proposes lotteries and receives only binary accept/reject feedback. We give deterministic and randomized algorithms that either find a unanimously acceptable lottery or certify infeasibility; adaptivity can avoid eliciting many stakeholders’ constraints, and randomization further reduces the expected elicitation cost relative to full elicitation. We complement these upper bounds with worst-case lower bounds (in particular, linear dependence on the number of stakeholders and logarithmic dependence on precision are unavoidable). Finally, we develop learning-augmented algorithms that exploit natural forms of advice (e.g., likely binding stakeholders or a promising lottery), improving query complexity when predictions are accurate while preserving worst-case guarantees.

paragraphs: Some decisions can proceed only when every stakeholder considers the outcome acceptable by their own minimum standard. This paper studies whether randomizing over a finite set of options can satisfy everyone. The algorithm proposes lotteries over those options and receives binary accept-or-reject feedback, rather than starting with a full description of each stakeholder's requirements.

The authors develop deterministic and randomized algorithms that either find a unanimously acceptable lottery or certify that none exists. Adaptive querying can avoid eliciting many stakeholders' constraints, and randomization further reduces expected elicitation cost compared with collecting everything. The approach therefore makes the amount of consultation needed part of the computational problem, alongside finding a feasible decision.

Worst-case lower bounds establish unavoidable costs, including linear dependence on stakeholder count and logarithmic dependence on precision. Learning-augmented algorithms additionally use advice, such as likely binding stakeholders or a promising lottery, to reduce queries when predictions are accurate while preserving worst-case guarantees. The results distinguish opportunities for efficient elicitation from costs that cannot generally be eliminated.
summary.tldr: Query-based algorithms find unanimously acceptable lotteries or certify infeasibility, using adaptivity, randomization, and advice to reduce stakeholder elicitation costs.

title: Learning Unanimously Acceptable Lotteries via Queries

abstract: The persistent storage requirements for high-resolution, spatiotemporally evolving fields governed by large-scale and high-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs) have reached the petabyte-to-exabyte scale. Transient simulations modeling Navier-Stokes equations, magnetohydrodynamics, plasma physics, or binary black hole mergers generate data volumes that are prohibitive for modern high-performance computing (HPC) infrastructures. To address this bottleneck, we introduce ANTIC (Adaptive Neural Temporal in situ Compressor), an end-to-end in situ compression pipeline. ANTIC consists of an adaptive temporal selector tailored to high-dimensional physics that identifies and filters informative snapshots at simulation time, combined with a spatial neural compression module based on continual fine-tuning that learns residual updates between adjacent snapshots using neural fields. By operating in a single streaming pass, ANTIC enables a combined compression of temporal and spatial components and effectively alleviates the need for explicit on-disk storage of entire time-evolved trajectories. Experimental results demonstrate that ANTIC achieves storage reductions of approximately $\sim 400\times$ for 2D Kolmogorov flow simulations and $\sim 7000\times$ for large-scale physics simulations such as binary black hole mergers.

paragraphs: Large physics simulations generate fields that change across both space and time, producing trajectories whose storage requirements can reach petabyte or exabyte scales. Saving these outputs becomes a major computing bottleneck. ANTiC addresses that problem by compressing simulation data as it is generated, instead of requiring the entire evolving trajectory to be stored explicitly.

The pipeline combines two components. An adaptive temporal selector identifies informative snapshots during the simulation, reducing what must be retained over time. A spatial neural compressor then uses neural fields and continual fine-tuning to learn residual changes between adjacent snapshots. This design uses both the selection of time points and the relationships between their spatial fields.

Because ANTiC operates in a single streaming pass, its temporal and spatial compression work together during data production. The reported experiments achieve storage reductions of approximately 400-fold for two-dimensional Kolmogorov flow and approximately 7000-fold for large-scale physics simulations such as binary black hole mergers. These results demonstrate substantial storage savings in the evaluated simulations through compression integrated into the simulation workflow.
summary.tldr: ANTiC compresses physics simulations as they run by selecting informative snapshots and learning spatial changes between them.

title: ANTiC: Adaptive Neural Temporal In Situ Compressor

abstract: Integrating graph knowledge into Large Language Models (LLMs) via passive representation faces critical bottlenecks: limited context windows, unreliable numerical computation, and structural hallucinations. To solve this, we propose GRASP (Graph Reasoning via Agentic Solving and Probing), shifting the paradigm from passive ingestion to proactive agentic exploration. By interleaving Neighbor Retrieval for on-demand probing with Code Interpreter as a deterministic solver, GRASP enables LLMs to autonomously navigate and compute over complex topologies. We employ a staged reinforcement learning strategy (GRPO) that transitions from visible tuning to a structure-blind environment, forcing the agent to develop genuine topological awareness. Evaluated on multi-domain graph reasoning benchmarks, our 4B model achieves a 53.06% average performance boost, surpassing SOTA baselines like DeepSeek-V3.2 and successfully generalizing to unseen tasks, with high potential for tackling sampling on million-node graphs and solving Hard-level LeetCode graph problems. Our implementation is open-sourced at https://github.com/PKU-ML/GRASP, with models hosted on Huggingface collection https://huggingface.co/collections/PKU-ML/grasp.

Training uses a staged Group Relative Policy Optimization strategy. It moves from a setting where structure is visible to a structure-blind environment, encouraging the agent to acquire topological information through exploration. The combination connects information gathering with computation: retrieval determines what the model needs to inspect, while executable code handles the solving step.

On graph-reasoning benchmarks spanning multiple domains, the authors report a 53.06% average performance boost for their four-billion-parameter model and results exceeding baselines including DeepSeek-V3.2. They also report generalization to unseen tasks. Sampling on million-node graphs and solving hard LeetCode graph problems are described as promising possibilities. The demonstrated contribution is a trained workflow that couples active graph probing with computational tools.
summary.tldr: GRASP trains language models to explore graphs on demand and use code execution to solve graph-reasoning tasks.

title: GRASP: Graph Reasoning via Agentic Solving and Probing of LLMs

abstract: This paper studies a constrained linear best arm identification problem with covariate selection in the fixed-confidence setting, where each arm is evaluated across multiple performance metrics. The mean performance of each metric depends linearly on the feature vectors of both arms and covariates. The goal is to identify the arm with the highest expected value of one targeted metric while ensuring that the means of the remaining metrics stay below specified thresholds for each covariate. We first establish an instance-dependent lower bound on the sample complexity, formulated as a multi-level optimization problem that captures both feasibility and optimality. We then prove that this bound is tight by designing an algorithm that asymptotically matches it. Since the original algorithm is computationally intensive, we develop a relaxed version of the bound through a surrogate optimization problem and derive its convex dual. Using this bound, we propose a duality-based decomposition algorithm that is computationally efficient, updating only two coordinates and performing a single gradient step per iteration. We further show that the algorithm achieves the relaxed bound in theory and demonstrates its practical effectiveness through numerical experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to identify the best option while satisfying several performance constraints. The goal is to maximize one metric while keeping the others below specified thresholds for every covariate, at a fixed confidence level.

The authors first derive an instance-dependent lower bound on how many samples this task requires. Its multi-level optimization accounts for both whether an arm is feasible and whether it is best. They then design an algorithm that asymptotically matches the bound, establishing that the bound is tight.

Because that algorithm is computationally demanding, the paper develops a relaxed bound through a surrogate problem and its convex dual. The resulting decomposition algorithm updates only two coordinates and takes one gradient step per iteration. It theoretically achieves the relaxed bound and performs effectively in numerical experiments, providing a computationally efficient counterpart to the original sample-optimal construction.
summary.tldr: The paper derives sample-complexity limits for constrained best-arm identification and uses convex duality to build an efficient relaxed algorithm.

title: Learning the Best Under Constraints: A Duality-Based Framework

abstract: Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) have recently emerged as a powerful approach for Bayesian prediction tasks, approximating the posterior predictive distribution (PPD) through in-context learning. Despite their strong empirical performance and ability to go beyond point predictions, theoretical understandings of the algorithmic capability of transformers to learn distributions in context are still lacking. Focusing on Gaussian process regression problems, we show by construction that transformers can implement a gradient descent algorithm targeting the posterior predictive mean and variance, followed by nonlinear mappings that yield binned probabilities of PPD. We study the error bounds of the approximated PPD in terms of attention depth and bin resolution. Based on these results, we further demonstrate the key role of normalization and the choice of attention depth in enabling the extrapolation abilities of transformers beyond the pretraining sample size range. We conduct simulations that corroborate our findings, providing insight into the expressivity of PFNs targeting PPDs and how architectural choices may influence generalization capabilities.

paragraphs: Prior-data fitted networks use examples in their context to approximate a Bayesian predictive distribution, providing uncertainty information as well as a point prediction. This paper investigates the computational capacity behind that behavior. Its analysis focuses specifically on Gaussian process regression.

The authors construct a transformer that implements gradient descent targeting the posterior predictive mean and variance. Nonlinear mappings then convert those quantities into probabilities for discrete output bins. This construction shows how a transformer can represent a distribution-producing procedure. The paper also bounds approximation error in terms of attention depth and bin resolution, linking architectural computation and output discretization to predictive accuracy.

The analysis further identifies normalization and the choice of attention depth as important for handling context sample sizes beyond the range encountered during pretraining. Simulations corroborate the theoretical findings. The contribution is a constructive account of distributional in-context prediction in the studied regression setting, together with insight into architectural choices that influence extrapolation. It establishes capability through a construction rather than claiming that every trained transformer necessarily learns this procedure.
summary.tldr: A constructive analysis shows how transformers can approximate Gaussian-process predictive distributions and links error and extrapolation to architectural choices.

title: Transformers Can Learn Posterior Predictive Distributions In-Context

abstract: Reward design remains a significant bottleneck in applying reinforcement learning (RL) to real-world problems. A popular alternative is reward learning, where reward functions are inferred from human feedback rather than manually specified. Recent work has proposed learning reward functions from human ratings rather than traditional binary preferences, enabling richer and potentially less cognitively demanding supervision. Building on this paradigm, we introduce a new rating-based RL method, Ranked Return Regression for RL (R4). At its core, R4 uses a novel ranking mean squared error loss that learns from a dataset of trajectory–rating pairs, treating the human-provided discrete ratings (e.g., "bad," "neutral," "good") as ordinal targets. Unlike prior rating-based approaches, R4 offers formal guarantees: its solution set is provably minimal and complete under mild assumptions. Empirically, using both human-provided and simulated ratings, we demonstrate that R4 consistently matches or outperforms existing rating and preference-based RL methods on robotic benchmarks from OpenAI Gym and the DeepMind Control Suite.

paragraphs: Designing rewards by hand can make reinforcement learning difficult to apply. Human feedback offers another route, and discrete ratings can provide richer supervision than choosing between two trajectories. This paper develops Ranked Return Regression for RL, or R4, to learn rewards from trajectory–rating pairs such as sequences of behavior labeled bad, neutral, or good.

R4 uses a ranking mean squared error loss that treats ratings as ordinal targets. The ordering of the categories is therefore central to what the method learns. The authors also provide a formal characterization of the method’s solution set: under mild assumptions, it is both minimal and complete. These guarantees distinguish the approach from prior rating-based methods described in the paper.

The empirical evaluation uses both human-provided and simulated ratings on robotic benchmarks from OpenAI Gym and the DeepMind Control Suite. R4 consistently matches or outperforms existing rating-based and preference-based reinforcement-learning methods. The results support ordinal ratings as a practical source of reward supervision, paired with an objective that has stated theoretical guarantees.
summary.tldr: R4 learns rewards from ordered human ratings using a ranking loss with formal guarantees and competitive robotic-benchmark performance.

title: Reward Learning through Ranking Mean Squared Error

abstract: Wasserstein metrics are increasingly adopted as similarity scores for images. We consider the sensitivity of Wasserstein metrics with respect to pixel-wise additive noise when the images are treated as discrete measures on the pixel grid. We derive finite-sample expectation bounds for a Gaussian noise model. Among other results, we prove that the error in the signed 2-Wasserstein distance scales with the square root of the noise standard deviation. This is favorable compared to the Euclidean metric that scales linearly, and thus provides a theoretical basis for the benefits of optimal transport distances in noisy settings. We present experiments that support our theoretical findings and point to a peculiar phenomenon where increasing the level of noise can decrease the Wasserstein distance. A case study on cryo-electron microscopy images demonstrates that the Wasserstein metric can capture the geometry of the data manifold in high noise settings even when the Euclidean metric fails.

paragraphs: Wasserstein distances are increasingly used to compare images, but their response to pixel noise needs theoretical explanation. This paper treats images as discrete measures on a pixel grid and studies how additive noise changes the resulting distances. Its analysis derives finite-sample bounds on expected error under a Gaussian noise model.

One result shows that error in the signed 2-Wasserstein distance scales with the square root of the noise standard deviation. The authors contrast this with the linear scaling of the Euclidean metric and identify it as favorable behavior in noisy settings. The result gives a theoretical basis for using optimal transport distances when image comparisons are affected by substantial noise.

A case study using cryo-electron microscopy images further shows that Wasserstein comparisons can capture the geometry of the data manifold at high noise levels where Euclidean comparisons fail. These findings connect the mathematical sensitivity analysis to a concrete image-analysis setting.
summary.tldr: Gaussian-noise bounds and imaging experiments explain favorable noise scaling of Wasserstein distances, including cases where more noise reduces distance.

title: Quantifying the noise sensitivity of the Wasserstein metric for images

abstract: Optimization modeling underpins decision-making in logistics, manufacturing, energy, and finance, yet translating natural-language requirements into correct optimization formulations and solver-executable code remains labor-intensive. Although large language models (LLMs) have been explored for this task, evaluation is still dominated by toy-sized or synthetic benchmarks, masking the difficulty of industrial problems with $10^{3}$–$10^{6}$ (or more) variables and constraints. A key bottleneck is the lack of benchmarks that align natural-language specifications with reference formulations/solver code grounded in real optimization models. To fill in this gap, we introduce MIPLIB-NL, built via a structure-aware reverse construction methodology from real mixed-integer linear programs in MIPLIB 2017. Our pipeline (i) recovers compact, reusable model structure from flat solver formulations, (ii) reverse-generates natural-language specifications explicitly tied to this recovered structure under a unified model–data separation format, and (iii) performs iterative semantic validation through expert review and human–LLM interaction with independent reconstruction checks. This yields 223 one-to-one reconstructions that preserve the mathematical content of the original instances while enabling realistic natural-language-to-optimization evaluation. Experiments show substantial performance degradation on MIPLIB-NL for systems that perform strongly on existing benchmarks, exposing failure modes invisible at toy scale.

This paper constructs MIPLIB-NL to connect natural-language descriptions with real mathematical optimization instances.

The resulting benchmark contains 223 one-to-one reconstructions. Systems that perform strongly on existing benchmarks show substantial deterioration on MIPLIB-NL, exposing failures that smaller problems do not reveal. The contribution is both a benchmark and a construction methodology: grounding descriptions in existing optimization models makes it possible to evaluate whether language-to-optimization systems can recover realistic formulations rather than succeed mainly on simplified examples.
summary.tldr: MIPLIB-NL reconstructs natural-language specifications for real optimization models and reveals weaknesses hidden by smaller benchmarks.

title: Constructing Industrial-Scale Optimization Modeling Benchmark

abstract: Although causal discovery from multivariate time series is widely used, it remains challenging under noise. Convergent cross mapping (CCM) infers causality by reconstructing shadow manifolds via time-delay embedding (TDE) and evaluating cross-map skill between manifolds. Despite Takens’ theorem guarantees in ideal settings, TDE effectively attempts to recover system state from a single noisy view, often yielding geometrically degraded manifolds and unreliable distance-based neighborhoods, which in turn weakens causal identification. We propose TopoDistill, a topology-informed knowledge distillation framework that improves univariate shadow-manifold reconstruction by aligning local neighborhood structure to a multivariate system representation. A global embedder trained on multivariate observations captures a global attractor representation, while a delay embedder is distilled to produce embeddings whose neighborhood distributions match the global topology. This cross-view alignment yields smoother and more reliable neighborhoods, improving cross mapping under noise while maintaining specificity against spurious correlations. Theoretical analysis and experimental results demonstrate that our method enables effective causal discovery.

paragraphs: Convergent cross mapping investigates causal relationships in time series by reconstructing representations of a system’s state from delayed observations. With noisy measurements of a single variable, those reconstructions can have distorted geometry. Points that appear nearby may then provide unreliable information, weakening the causal conclusions drawn from cross mapping.

TopoDistill improves these single-variable reconstructions using information from multiple observed variables. A global embedder learns a representation of the system’s attractor from multivariate observations. A delay embedder then learns to reproduce its neighborhood distributions. This transfers information about the system’s broader organization into the local neighborhoods used by the single-variable representation.

The paper reports that this alignment produces smoother, more reliable neighborhoods and improves cross mapping under noise while retaining specificity against spurious correlations. Theoretical analysis and experiments support its effectiveness for causal discovery. The central contribution is to improve the geometry on which causal inference relies, using a multivariate view to guide a reconstruction that would otherwise depend on one noisy view.
summary.tldr: TopoDistill transfers multivariate neighborhood structure into single-variable time-series embeddings to improve causal discovery under noise.

title: TopoDistill: Distilling Global System Topology for Causal Discovery in Multivariate Time Series

abstract: Building mathematical optimization models is critical in operations research (OR), while it requires substantial human expertise. Recent advancements have utilized large language models (LLMs) to automate this modeling process. However, existing works often struggle to verify the correctness of the generated optimization models, without checking the rationality of the constraints and variables or the validity of solutions to the generated models. This hampers the subsequent verification and correction steps, and thus it severely hurts the modeling accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose a novel LLM-based framework with Dual-side Verification (OptiVer) from both structure and solution perspectives, thereby improving the modeling accuracy. The structure-side verification ensures that the modeling structure of the generated optimization models aligns with the original problem description, accurately capturing the problem’s constraints and requirements. Meanwhile, the solution-side verification interprets and evaluates the validity of the solutions, confirming that the optimization models are logically and mathematically sound. Extensive experiments on several popular benchmarks demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art, achieving over 20% improvement in accuracy.

paragraphs: OptiVer addresses the difficulty of checking mathematical optimization models generated by language models. Translating a problem description into variables and constraints requires substantial expertise. A generated formulation can fail to capture the original requirements, and its solutions can expose additional problems. Weak verification makes subsequent correction less effective.

The framework checks the formulation from two perspectives. Structure-side verification examines whether the variables, constraints, and overall model reflect the original problem description. Solution-side verification interprets the model’s solutions and evaluates their validity. The two views connect what the formulation says with what it actually permits as an answer, giving the correction process evidence about both representation and consequences.

Experiments on several popular benchmarks report an accuracy improvement of over 20% compared with the state of the art. The abstract does not specify that this is a percentage-point increase, so the result is best retained in its reported form. The main methodological finding is that checking both model structure and solution validity improves automated optimization modeling beyond relying on an unchecked generated formulation.
summary.tldr: OptiVer improves language-model-generated optimization formulations by checking both their structure and the validity of their solutions.

title: Opt-Verifier: Unleashing the Power of LLMs for Optimization Modeling via Dual-Side Verification

abstract: Predictive coding networks are neural models that perform inference through an iterative energy minimization process, whose operations are local in space and time. While effective in shallow architectures, they suffer significant performance degradation beyond five to seven layers. In this work, we show that this degradation is caused by exponentially imbalanced errors between layers during weight updates, and by predictions from the previous layers not being effective in guiding updates in deeper layers. Furthermore, when training models with skip connections, the energy propagated by the residuals reaches higher layers faster than that propagated by the main pathway, affecting test accuracy. We address the first issue by introducing a novel precision-weighted optimization of latent variables that balances error distributions during the relaxation phase, the second issue by proposing a novel weight update mechanism that reduces error accumulation in deeper layers, and the third one by using auxiliary neurons that slow down the propagation of the energy in the residual connections. Empirically, our methods achieve performance comparable to backpropagation on deep models such as ResNets, opening new possibilities for predictive coding in complex tasks.

paragraphs: Predictive coding networks infer internal states through repeated energy minimization using operations that are local in space and time. They work well in shallow architectures, but performance deteriorates beyond roughly five to seven layers. This paper investigates why increasing depth disrupts their training and proposes targeted changes for the identified causes.

The authors find exponentially imbalanced errors across layers and predictions from earlier layers that inadequately guide deeper weight updates. They address these problems with precision-weighted latent-variable optimization during relaxation and a revised weight-update mechanism that reduces error accumulation. For architectures with skip connections, they identify a further timing mismatch: energy travels through residual paths faster than through the main pathway.

Auxiliary neurons slow energy propagation through those residual connections, addressing that third issue. In experiments, the combined methods achieve performance comparable to backpropagation on deep architectures including ResNets. The findings indicate that depth-related failures can be addressed through the balance and propagation of learning signals, providing empirical support for extending predictive coding to more complex models rather than restricting it to shallow networks.
summary.tldr: Balancing errors, revising weight updates, and slowing residual energy propagation enables deep predictive coding models to perform comparably to backpropagation.

title: Towards the Training of Deeper Predictive Coding Neural Networks

abstract: Performative predictions influence the very outcomes they aim to forecast. We study performative predictions that affect a sample (e.g., only existing users of an app) and/or the whole population (e.g., all potential app users). This raises the question of how well models generalize under performativity. For example, how well can we draw insights about new app users based on existing users when both of them react to the app’s predictions? We address this question by embedding performative predictions into statistical learning theory. We prove generalization bounds under performative effects on the sample, on the population, and on both. A key intuition behind our proofs is that in the worst case, the population negates predictions, while the sample deceptively fulfills them. We cast such self-negating and self-fulfilling predictions as min-max and min-min risk functionals in Wasserstein space, respectively. Our analysis reveals both a fundamental trade-off between performatively changing the world and learning from it, as well as a surprising insight on how to improve generalization guarantees by retraining on performatively distorted samples. We illustrate our bounds using real data on prediction-informed assignments to job trainings.
