For example, existing app users and potential new users may each react to an app’s predictions, complicating what the existing users reveal about future ones.

The authors incorporate these feedback effects into statistical learning theory and prove generalization bounds for all three cases. Their worst-case intuition distinguishes a sample that deceptively confirms predictions from a population that works against them. They formalize these self-fulfilling and self-negating behaviors through different optimization-based risk formulations in Wasserstein space.

The analysis identifies a fundamental trade-off between changing the world through predictions and learning from the resulting observations. It also shows how retraining on samples already altered by predictions can improve generalization guarantees. Real data on prediction-informed job-training assignments illustrate the bounds. The contribution provides a framework for reasoning about generalization when deployment itself changes the data that learning depends on.
summary.tldr: The paper derives generalization bounds for predictions that change their own data and identifies benefits from retraining on affected samples.

title: Performative Learning Theory

abstract: Large language models increasingly generate structured outputs, including citation-grounded summaries, multi-step reasoning chains, and tool-augmented responses, where correctness is inherently compositional: a single flawed claim can invalidate an otherwise accurate response. Existing certification methods treat outputs as atomic units, forcing a binary choice between unsafe acceptance and wasteful rejection. We introduce Claim Graph Risk Control (CGRiC), a framework that decomposes responses into dependency graphs of verifiable claims and assigns calibrated per-claim risk bounds via information-lift statistics. By composing these bounds, CGRiC provides explicit guarantees on the probability that any incorrect claim passes verification undetected. When this composed risk exceeds a target threshold, the system triggers localized repairs rather than full abstention, preserving correct content while fixing problematic claims. Our approach explicitly models extraction noise and verifier imperfection, and exploits conditional independence structure for tighter certificates when validated. Empirically, CGRiC achieves target risk levels while reducing abstention by 31% compared to atomic baselines across QA, summarization, and reasoning tasks.
originalAbstract: Large language models increasingly generate structured outputs, including citation-grounded summaries, multi-step reasoning chains, and tool-augmented responses, where correctness is inherently compositional: a single flawed claim can invalidate an otherwise accurate response. Existing certification methods treat outputs as atomic units, forcing a binary choice between unsafe acceptance and wasteful rejection. We introduce Claim Graph Risk Control (CGRiC), a framework that decomposes responses into dependency graphs of verifiable claims and assigns calibrated per-claim risk bounds via information-lift statistics. By composing these bounds, CGRiC provides explicit guarantees on the probability that any incorrect claim passes verification undetected. When this composed risk exceeds a target threshold, the system triggers localized repairs rather than full abstention, preserving correct content while fixing problematic claims. Our approach explicitly models extraction noise and verifier imperfection, and exploits conditional independence structure for tighter certificates when validated. Empirically, CGRiC achieves target risk levels while reducing abstention by 31% compared to atomic baselines across QA, summarization, and reasoning tasks.

paragraphs: CGRiC addresses structured language-model responses whose correctness depends on several connected claims. A response may contain substantial correct material but still fail because one important statement is wrong. Treating the entire response as a single object makes it difficult to preserve useful content while controlling the risk of accepting an error.

The framework represents a response as a dependency graph of verifiable claims. It uses information-lift statistics to assign calibrated risk bounds to individual claims, then combines them into a guarantee on the probability that any incorrect claim escapes detection. If the combined risk exceeds a chosen threshold, the system initiates repairs to particular claims instead of rejecting the whole response.

The analysis accounts for noisy claim extraction and imperfect verification. It can also use conditional independence to tighten certificates when that structure has been validated. Across question answering, summarization, and reasoning experiments, CGRiC meets the target risk levels while reducing abstention by 31% relative to atomic baselines. This supports repairing responses at the same granularity at which their errors occur.
summary.tldr: CGRiC combines claim-level risk bounds to certify structured responses and repair problematic claims while reducing whole-response abstention.

title: CGRiC: Compositional Risk Certification for Structured LLM Outputs

abstract: Cross-modal Hashing (CMH) typically assumes a perfectly complete data annotation, whereas noisy labels are unavoidable in practical scenarios. Existing CMH methods often overlook the uncertainty introduced by noise or semantic ambiguity, making models susceptible to overfitting noisy labels and yielding unreliable similarity judgments during inference. To address this issue, we propose a Robust Self-reflective Hashing (RSH) framework that prudently analyzes semantic discrepancies while accounting for uncertainty, thereby effectively mitigating interference from noisy labels. Specifically, the Double Feature Representation (DFR) method is introduced, employing semantic and uncertainty features to represent the semantic representation and fuzziness of samples. With a double feature, we propose a novel cross-modal similarity metric - the Self-reflective Similarity Metric (SSM), which judges sample similarity by integrating semantic discrepancy and fuzziness, enabling the model to adaptively weaken semantic discrepancy according to uncertainty level. The proposed method is plug-and-play, enabling seamless integration into diverse objective functions to enhance model robustness and reliability. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that RSH outperforms existing methods. Code is available at https://github.com/QinLab-WFU/RSH.

paragraphs: Robust Self-reflective Hashing addresses unreliable similarity judgments in cross-modal retrieval when training labels contain noise. If a model treats every semantic distinction as equally trustworthy, it can fit annotation mistakes or ambiguous examples too closely. The paper makes uncertainty an explicit part of how similarity is represented and assessed.

Its Double Feature Representation gives each sample both semantic features and uncertainty features. A Self-reflective Similarity Metric then combines semantic discrepancy with the sample’s fuzziness. The metric can weaken the contribution of semantic differences according to uncertainty, allowing the similarity calculation to account for how reliable those differences appear.

The method is designed as a plug-and-play component that can be integrated into different objective functions. This makes uncertainty-aware similarity usable across multiple training formulations rather than restricting it to one fixed loss. Experiments on benchmark datasets report improvements over existing methods. The findings support jointly modeling what an example means and how ambiguous that meaning is when learning cross-modal retrieval representations.
summary.tldr: RSH combines semantic and uncertainty features so noisy or ambiguous examples have a more cautious influence on cross-modal similarity.

title: Robust Self-reflective Hashing for Cross-modal Retrieval with Noisy Label

abstract: Grokking, the phenomenon where models suddenly generalize long after overfitting training data, remains a puzzling challenge in neural network dynamics. Through mechanistic analysis, we find that this transition is fundamentally driven by a structural reorganization of token representations, with the onset of grokking entailing a shift toward a well-defined geometry, and reveal the model’s distinct understanding of data’s dual characteristics. Building on these geometric insights, we propose R2G (Repel-to-Grokking) Loss, an active intervention that reshapes the representation manifold by enforcing structural repulsion. The versatility of R2G is empirically validated in both algorithmic and linguistic tasks, while our theoretical analysis and ablation studies jointly demonstrate that angular reorganization is the primary driver of grokking. Our work offers a novel mechanistic perspective on the evolution of grokking and provides a useful tool for enhancing model efficiency and reliability.

paragraphs: Grokking describes a delayed transition: a model fits its training data well before it suddenly begins to generalize. This paper examines what changes inside the model during that transition. Its mechanistic analysis identifies a reorganization of token representations, with the onset of generalization accompanied by movement toward a well-defined geometric structure.

The authors use this observation to design R2G, or Repel-to-Grokking, Loss. It actively reshapes the representation manifold by imposing structural repulsion. The intervention targets how token representations are arranged, making their organization an explicit part of training. The paper's theoretical analysis and ablation studies identify angular reorganization as the primary driver of the grokking transition.

Experiments on both algorithmic and linguistic tasks support the intervention's versatility. Together, the analysis and experiments offer a mechanism for delayed generalization and a way to intervene in that process. The practical implication is that representation geometry can be an actionable training target: encouraging its reorganization offers a route toward accelerating generalization and improving model efficiency and reliability in the studied settings.
summary.tldr: The paper links grokking to angular reorganization of token representations and introduces a loss that actively encourages this transition.

title: The Geometric Origin of Grokking: Accelerating Generalization via Active Structural Reorganization

abstract: Recent years have seen a surge in data-driven surrogates for dynamical systems that can be orders of magnitude faster than numerical solvers. However, many machine learning-based models such as neural operators exhibit spectral bias, attenuating high-frequency components that often encode small-scale structure. This limitation is particularly damaging in applications such as weather forecasting, where misrepresented high frequencies can induce long-horizon instability. To address this issue, we propose multi-scale wavelet transformers (MSWTs), which learn system dynamics in a tokenized wavelet domain. The wavelet transform explicitly separates low- and high-frequency content across scales. MSWTs leverage a wavelet-preserving downsampling scheme that retains high-frequency features and employ wavelet-based attention to capture dependencies across scales and frequency bands. Experiments on chaotic dynamical systems show substantial error reductions and improved long-horizon spectral fidelity. On the ERA5 climate reanalysis, MSWTs further reduce climatological bias, demonstrating their effectiveness in a real-world forecasting setting.

paragraphs: Learned surrogates can simulate dynamical systems much faster than numerical solvers, but they often underrepresent high-frequency components. Those components carry small-scale structure, so losing them can damage forecasts over long horizons. The paper addresses this spectral bias by changing how the model represents and processes system dynamics.

Multi-scale wavelet transformers operate on tokens in a wavelet representation, which separates low- and high-frequency information across scales. Their downsampling scheme preserves high-frequency features instead of discarding them as the representation becomes coarser. Wavelet-based attention then models dependencies among scales and frequency bands, allowing broad behavior and fine detail to inform one another.

On chaotic dynamical systems, the authors report substantial error reductions and better preservation of frequency content over long forecasts. On ERA5 climate reanalysis, the models also reduce climatological bias. These findings support the value of explicitly retaining small-scale information throughout the architecture. The contribution is more than a different input representation: both downsampling and attention are designed to keep the separated frequency information useful during prediction.
summary.tldr: Multi-scale wavelet transformers preserve fine-scale frequency information to improve dynamical-system forecasts and reduce climate prediction bias.

title: Multi-Scale Wavelet Transformers for Operator Learning of Dynamical Systems

abstract: $U$-statistics play a central role in statistical inference. In many modern applications, however, acquiring the labels required for $U$-statistics is costly. Motivated by recent advances in active inference, we develop an active inference framework for $U$-statistics that selectively queries informative labels to improve estimation efficiency under a fixed labeling budget, while preserving valid statistical inference. Our approach is built on the augmented inverse probability weighting $U$-statistic, which is proposed to incorporate the sampling rule and machine learning predictions. We characterize the optimal sampling rule that minimizes its variance and design practical sampling strategies. We further extend the framework to $U$-statistic-based empirical risk minimization. Experiments on real datasets demonstrate substantial gains in estimation efficiency over baseline methods, while maintaining target coverage.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to estimate U-statistics efficiently when obtaining the necessary labels is expensive. Its framework actively selects informative labels within a fixed budget while preserving valid statistical inference. The aim is to extract more estimation value from each queried label without losing the reliability of the resulting uncertainty statements.

The central estimator is an augmented inverse probability weighting U-statistic. It incorporates both the rule used to select labels and predictions supplied by a machine learning model. This explicitly connects estimation to the selective sampling process. The authors characterize the sampling rule that minimizes variance and develop practical strategies based on that characterization, turning the statistical objective into guidance for deciding which labels to acquire.

The framework also extends to empirical risk minimization based on U-statistics, connecting label acquisition with learning objectives. Experiments on real datasets show substantial improvements in estimation efficiency over baseline methods while maintaining target coverage. The findings support a combination of selective labeling, predictive models, and sampling-aware estimation as a way to use limited annotation resources more effectively.
summary.tldr: An active-labeling framework improves U-statistic estimation efficiency under a fixed budget while preserving valid statistical inference.

title: Learning $U$-Statistics with Active Inference

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can be influenced by harmful or irrelevant context, which can significantly harm model performance on downstream tasks. This motivates principled designs in which LLM systems include built-in mechanisms to guard against such "garbage in, garbage out" scenarios. We propose a novel approach to limit the degree to which harmful context can degrade model performance. First, we define a baseline "safe" behavior for the model – the model’s performance given no context at all (zero-shot). Next, we apply distribution-free risk control (DFRC) to control the extent to which the user-provided context can decay performance below this safe zero-shot baseline. We achieve this by leveraging dynamic early exit prediction, ignoring later attention heads that attend the most to the unsafe inputs. Finally, we propose modifications to DFRC that allow it to both control risk for harmful inputs and leverage performance and efficiency gains on helpful inputs. We present both theoretical and empirical results across 9 tasks spanning in-context learning and open-ended question answering, showing that our approach can effectively control risk for harmful context and simultaneously achieve substantial computational efficiency gains with helpful context.

paragraphs: Additional context can make a language model less accurate when that context is irrelevant or harmful. This paper defines a concrete reference for protection: the model’s performance without any supplied context. Here, “safe” refers to that zero-shot performance baseline, giving the method a measurable target for limiting context-induced degradation.

The approach combines distribution-free risk control with dynamic early exiting. It avoids later attention heads that attend most strongly to unsafe inputs, limiting how much those inputs influence the prediction. The authors also modify the risk-control procedure so that protection against harmful context can coexist with benefits from useful context. This matters because a system that simply ignores every input would lose the advantages of contextual information.

The paper presents theoretical and empirical results across nine tasks covering in-context learning and open-ended question answering. Those results show effective control of performance risk from harmful context, alongside substantial computational savings when context is helpful. The contribution connects statistical control of degradation with a mechanism that can also reduce inference work.
summary.tldr: The method combines risk control and early exiting to limit damage from harmful context while retaining efficiency gains from helpful inputs.

title: Controlling the Risk of Corrupted Contexts for Language Models via Early-Exiting

abstract: While on-policy distillation offers dense supervision for training small reasoning models, its optimization dynamics in the multimodal domain remain under-explored. In this work, we challenge the standard monolithic view of Vision-Language Model (VLM) distillation by mathematically decomposing the loss into two distinct components: the language prior and visual grounding. Our analysis uncovers that gradient vectors for these components are nearly orthogonal, indicating that the objective of aligning with the teacher’s language distribution is geometrically independent from the objective of matching its visual perception. Consequently, standard optimization passively follows a suboptimal compromise trajectory that implicitly balances the two objectives. Hypothesizing that visual grounding constitutes the primary bottleneck for vision-language reasoning, we introduce Visual Gradient Steering (VGS), a method that dynamically reorients the update vector to prioritize the visual subspace. Experimental results on multiple distillation settings and complex multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that VGS significantly outperforms the standard monolithic formulation of on-policy distillation, achieving superior grounding with minimal training overhead.

paragraphs: On-policy distillation trains a smaller reasoning model using dense guidance from a teacher. For vision-language models, that guidance involves both language behavior and understanding visual evidence. This paper separates the usual combined distillation loss into a language-prior component and a visual-grounding component to examine how each affects learning.

The analysis finds that the gradients of these components are nearly orthogonal. Improving agreement with the teacher's language distribution therefore points in a largely independent direction from improving agreement with its visual perception. Standard optimization implicitly balances these directions, producing what the authors identify as a suboptimal compromise trajectory. They hypothesize that visual grounding is the main bottleneck for vision-language reasoning.

Visual Gradient Steering responds by dynamically rotating the update direction to give greater priority to the visual subspace. Across multiple distillation settings and challenging multimodal benchmarks, the method significantly outperforms the standard combined objective and improves grounding with minimal training overhead. The findings support explicitly managing the two learning signals rather than assuming their ordinary combination provides the best training direction.
summary.tldr: Visual Gradient Steering separates language and visual learning signals, then prioritizes visual grounding to improve vision-language distillation.

title: Decomposed On-Policy Distillation for Vision-Language Reasoning: Steering Gradients for Visual Grounding

abstract: Deterministic inference is increasingly critical for Large language model (LLM) applications such as LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, multi-agent systems, and reinforcement learning (RL). However, existing LLM serving frameworks can produce different outputs for identical inputs when tensor parallel (TP) size or batch size changes, even under greedy decoding. This arises from the non-associativity of floating-point arithmetic and inconsistent reduction orders across GPUs. While prior work has addressed batch-size–related nondeterminism through batch-invariant kernels, determinism across different TP sizes remains an open problem, particularly in RL settings, where the training engine typically uses Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) (i.e., TP = 1) while the rollout engine relies on multi-GPU TP to maximize the inference throughput, creating a probability mismatch that can degrade or even collapse training. We identify and analyze the root causes of TP-induced inconsistency and propose Tree-Based Invariant Kernels (TBIK), a set of custom matrix multiplication and reduction kernels that guarantee bit-wise identical results across TP sizes. Our key insight is to enforce a consistent reduction order across and within GPUs. We implement TBIK in Triton and integrate it into vLLM and FSDP, achieving bit-wise deterministic inference across different TP sizes and zero probability divergence between rollout and training engines in RL pipelines. By eliminating mismatches caused by different parallelization strategies, TBIK enables true on-policy RL at scale for the first time, leading to improved model performance and faster convergence.

paragraphs: Identical prompts can produce different model outputs when inference is distributed across different numbers of GPUs, even with greedy decoding. The paper traces this to floating-point arithmetic: changing the order in which partial results are combined can change the final numerical result. In reinforcement learning, differing training and rollout configurations can consequently assign different probabilities to the same behavior.

Tree-Based Invariant Kernels, or TBIK, enforce a consistent order for reductions both within and across GPUs. The authors implement custom matrix multiplication and reduction kernels in Triton and integrate them into vLLM and Fully Sharded Data Parallel training. Eliminating this source of mismatch enables the authors' claimed on-policy reinforcement learning at scale, with improved performance and faster convergence. The contribution links low-level arithmetic ordering to whether the probabilities used for learning match those that generated the training experience.
summary.tldr: TBIK makes arithmetic reduction order invariant across tensor-parallel sizes, eliminating the resulting probability mismatch between rollout and training.

abstract: Quite a bit is known about minimizing different kinds of regret in experts problems, and how these regret types relate to types of equilibria in the multiagent setting of repeated matrix games. Much less is known about the possible kinds of regret in online convex programming problems (OCPs), or about equilibria in the analogous multiagent setting of repeated convex games. This gap is unfortunate, since convex games are much more expressive than matrix games, and since many important machine learning problems can be expressed as OCPs. In this paper, we work to close this gap: we analyze a spectrum of regret types which lie between external and swap regret, along with their corresponding equilibria, which lie between coarse correlated and correlated equilibrium. We also analyze algorithms for minimizing these regret types. As examples of our framework, we derive algorithms for learning correlated equilibria in polyhedral convex games and extensive-form correlated equilibria in extensive-form games. The former is exponentially more efficient than previous algorithms, and the latter is the first of its type.

paragraphs: Learning in repeated games connects individual regret to the equilibria that players collectively approach. The paper extends this line of analysis to online convex programming and repeated convex games, where those connections were less developed than for experts problems and matrix games. Convex games matter here because they offer a more expressive setting for problems arising in machine learning.

The authors examine a range of regret notions between external regret and swap regret. They connect these to equilibrium notions between coarse correlated and correlated equilibrium, and analyze algorithms that minimize the corresponding regrets. The framework therefore organizes several learning objectives and collective outcomes together instead of treating only the endpoints.

Two applications make the framework concrete. The paper derives algorithms for learning correlated equilibria in polyhedral convex games and extensive-form correlated equilibria in extensive-form games. The first is reported to be exponentially more efficient than previous algorithms; the second is presented as the first algorithm of its type. These claims concern the specified game classes and equilibrium-learning tasks.
summary.tldr: A spectrum of regret notions links learning algorithms to equilibria in convex games and yields improved algorithms for two equilibrium-learning tasks.

title: No-regret learning in convex games

abstract: We present a general PAC-Bayes theorem from which all known PAC-Bayes bounds are simply obtained as particular cases. We also propose different learning algorithms for finding linear classifiers that minimize these PAC-Bayes risk bounds. These learning algorithms are generally competitive with both AdaBoost and the SVM.
originalAbstract: We present a general PAC-Bayes theorem from which all known PAC-Bayes bounds are simply obtained as particular cases. We also propose different learning algorithms for finding linear classifiers that minimize these PAC-Bayes risk bounds. These learning algorithms are generally competitive with both AdaBoost and the SVM.

paragraphs: This paper connects a general theoretical result about prediction risk with algorithms for learning linear classifiers. Its first contribution is a PAC-Bayes theorem that encompasses all the PAC-Bayes bounds described as known in the abstract. Those bounds can be recovered as particular cases, placing separate results within a common mathematical framework.

The second contribution uses these risk bounds as learning objectives. The authors propose different algorithms that search for linear classifiers by minimizing PAC-Bayes bounds. This makes the theory part of the construction of a classifier: the bound is something the training procedure tries to improve, rather than only a statement used to assess a finished model.

The resulting learning algorithms are reported to be generally competitive with AdaBoost and support vector machines. That qualified comparison supports the practical relevance of bound-driven learning without claiming superiority in every case. The paper's central link is between unifying generalization guarantees and turning those guarantees into concrete optimization targets for familiar linear prediction models.
summary.tldr: A general PAC-Bayes theorem unifies existing bounds and motivates linear-classifier learning algorithms that are generally competitive with AdaBoost and SVMs.

title: PAC-Bayesian learning of linear classifiers

abstract: Online representational expansion techniques have improved the learning speed of existing reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms in low dimensional domains, yet existing online expansion methods do not scale well to high dimensional problems. We conjecture that one of the main difficulties limiting this scaling is that features defined over the full-dimensional state space often generalize poorly. Hence, we introduce incremental Feature Dependency Discovery (iFDD) as a computationally-inexpensive method for representational expansion that can be combined with any online, value-based RL method that uses binary features. Unlike other online expansion techniques, iFDD creates new features in low dimensional subspaces of the full state space where feedback errors persist. We provide convergence and computational complexity guarantees for iFDD, as well as showing empirically that iFDD scales well to high dimensional multi-agent planning domains with hundreds of millions of state-action pairs.

We conjecture that one of the main difficulties limiting this scaling is that features defined over the full-dimensional state space often generalize poorly. Hence, we introduce incremental Feature Dependency Discovery (iFDD) as a computationally-inexpensive method for representational expansion that can be combined with any online, value-based RL method that uses binary features. Unlike other online expansion techniques, iFDD creates new features in low dimensional subspaces of the full state space where feedback errors persist. paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning methods can expand their feature representations during learning, but existing expansion methods struggle in high-dimensional problems. The authors conjecture that one reason is poor generalization from features defined over the entire state space. They introduce incremental Feature Dependency Discovery, or iFDD, to create new features in smaller subspaces instead.

The method expands the representation where feedback errors persist. Its design focuses new features on low-dimensional parts of the state space, addressing the proposed generalization difficulty while keeping computation inexpensive. It can be combined with any online, value-based reinforcement-learning method that uses binary features. That compatibility claim is broad within the stated class of methods.

The paper supplies convergence and computational-complexity guarantees and evaluates scalability empirically. In high-dimensional multi-agent planning domains containing hundreds of millions of state-action pairs, iFDD scales well in the reported experiments. The findings support targeted feature expansion as a practical approach to large planning problems. They do not turn the authors' proposed explanation for earlier scaling difficulties into an established universal cause.
summary.tldr: iFDD adds low-dimensional features where errors persist and demonstrates scalable online reinforcement learning in large multi-agent planning domains.

title: Online Discovery of Feature Dependencies

abstract: We propose a novel problem formulation of learning a single task when the data are provided in different feature spaces. Each such space is called an outlook, and is assumed to contain both labeled and unlabeled data. The objective is to take advantage of the data from all the outlooks to better classify each of the outlooks. We devise an algorithm that computes optimal affine mappings from different outlooks to a target outlook by matching moments of the empirical distributions. We further derive a probabilistic interpretation of the resulting algorithm and a sample complexity bound indicating how many samples are needed to adequately find the mapping. We report the results of extensive experiments on activity recognition tasks that show the value of the proposed approach in boosting performance.

Each such space is called an outlook, and is assumed to contain both labeled and unlabeled data. The objective is to take advantage of the data from all the outlooks to better classify each of the outlooks. We devise an algorithm that computes optimal affine mappings from different outlooks to a target outlook by matching moments of the empirical distributions. We further derive a probabilistic interpretation of the resulting algorithm and a sample complexity bound indicating how many samples are needed to adequately find the mapping. We report the results of extensive experiments on activity recognition tasks that show the value of the proposed approach in boosting performance.

paragraphs: The paper studies a single classification task whose data appear in different feature spaces, called outlooks. Each outlook is assumed to contain both labeled and unlabeled examples. The objective is to use information from all these spaces to improve classification within each of them, despite their differing representations.

The proposed algorithm computes optimal affine mappings from the different outlooks into a target outlook. It finds these mappings by matching moments of the empirical distributions, using distributional summaries to relate the spaces. This gives a concrete way to bring information expressed in different coordinates into a common target representation.

The authors also derive a probabilistic interpretation and a sample-complexity bound describing how many examples are needed to find the mapping adequately. Extensive activity-recognition experiments show improvements in performance. Together, these contributions provide an alignment method, a theoretical account of its data requirements, and empirical evidence that sharing information across outlooks can benefit the classification task.
summary.tldr: Moment-matching affine mappings let a classifier benefit from data describing the same task in different feature spaces.
